I COME no more to make you laugh: things now / That bear a weighty and a serious brow, / Sad, high, and working, full of state and woe, / Such noble scenes as draw the eye to flow, / We now present. Those that can pity, here / May, if they think it well, let fall a tear; / The subject will deserve it. Such as give / Their money out of hope they may believe, / May here find truth too. Those that come to see / Only a show or two, and so agree / The play may pass, if they be still and willing, / I'll undertake may see away their shilling / Richly in two short hours. Only they / That come to hear a merry bawdy play, / A noise of targets, or to see a fellow / In a long motley coat guarded with yellow, / Will be deceiv'd; for, gentle hearers, know, / To rank our chosen truth with such a show / As fool and fight is, beside forfeiting / Our own brains, and the opinion that we bring / To make that only true we now intend, / Will leave us never an understanding friend. / Therefore, for goodness' sake, and as you are known / The first and happiest hearers of the town, / Be sad, as we would make ye; think ye see / The very persons of our noble story / As they were living; think you see them great, / And follow'd with the general throng and sweat / Of thousand friends; then, in a moment, see / How soon this mightiness meets misery; / And if you can be merry then, I'll say / A man may weep upon his wedding-day.

I have not come to make you laugh this time. We now present serious, weighty scenes, sad and lofty, full of state affairs and grief, noble scenes that will bring tears to your eyes. Those of you who can feel pity may shed a tear here if you like; the subject deserves it. Those who pay hoping to see something true will find truth here too. Those who come only for a spectacle or two, and are willing to let the play pass, I promise will get their shilling's worth in two short hours. Only those who come to hear a merry, bawdy play, the clash of shields, or a clown in a long motley coat trimmed with yellow will be disappointed. For, gentle audience, if we mixed our chosen true story with such foolery and fighting, we would throw away our own wits and our aim of showing only what is true, and no thinking person would stay our friend. So, for goodness' sake, and since you are known as the best and most discerning audience in the city, be as sad as we want to make you. Imagine you see the real people of our noble story as if they were alive; see them great, followed by crowds of thousands of sweating friends; then see how in a moment this greatness meets misery. And if you can be merry then, I'll say a man can weep on his wedding day.
Good morrow, and well met. How have ye done / Since last we saw in France?
Good morning, and well met. How have you been since we last saw each other in France?
I thank your Grace, / Healthful; and ever since a fresh admirer / Of what I saw there.
Healthy, thank you, your Grace, and ever since then a fresh admirer of what I saw there.
An untimely ague / Stay'd me a prisoner in my chamber when / Those suns of glory, those two lights of men, / Met in the vale of Andren.
A badly timed fever kept me a prisoner in my room when those two glorious suns, those two shining kings, met in the valley of Andren.

'Twixt Guynes and Arde. / I was then present, saw them salute on horseback; / Beheld them, when they lighted, how they clung / In their embracement, as they grew together; / Which had they, what four thron'd ones could have weigh'd / Such a compounded one?

Between Guisnes and Ardres. I was there. I saw them greet each other on horseback, and when they dismounted, how they hugged, clinging together as if they had grown into one. If they had become one, what four kings could have outweighed such a compound?
All the whole time / I was my chamber's prisoner.
The whole time I was a prisoner in my room.

Then you lost / The view of earthly glory. Men might say, / Till this time pomp was single, but now married / To one above itself. Each following day / Became the next day's master, till the last / Made former wonders its. To-day the French, / All clinquant, all in gold, like heathen gods, / Shone down the English; and, to-morrow, they / Made Britain India: every man that stood / Show'd like a mine. Their dwarfish pages were / As cherubins, all gilt; the madams too, / Not us'd to toil, did almost sweat to bear / The pride upon them, that their very labour / Was to them as a painting. Now this masque / Was cried incomparable; and the ensuing night / Made it a fool and beggar. The two kings, / Equal in lustre, were now best, now worst, / As presence did present them; him in eye, / Still him in praise; and, being present both, / 'Twas said they saw but one; and no discerner / Durst wag his tongue in censure. When these suns— / For so they phrase 'em—by their heralds challeng'd / The noble spirits to arms, they did perform / Beyond thought's compass, that former fabulous story, / Being now seen possible enough, got credit, / That Bevis was believ'd.

Then you missed the sight of earthly glory. You could say that until then splendour had been single, but now it married something greater than itself. Each day outdid the one before, until the last one gathered up all the earlier wonders as its own. One day the French, all glittering, all in gold like pagan gods, outshone the English; the next, the English made Britain look like India: every man standing there shone like a gold mine. Their little pages were like cherubs, all gilded; the ladies too, not used to work, almost sweated under the weight of their finery, so that the effort of carrying it made them blush as if painted. One night's masque was called beyond compare, and the next night's made it look poor and foolish. The two kings, equal in splendour, were now one the best, now the other, depending on who was in sight; whichever you were looking at got the praise, and when both were present people said they saw only one, and no critic dared say a word against either. When these two suns, as they called them, had their heralds challenge the nobles to joust, they performed beyond belief, so that old fabulous legends, now seen to be possible, were believed, and even the tale of Bevis was credited.

As I belong to worship and affect / In honour honesty, the tract of ev'rything / Would by a good discourser lose some life, / Which action's self was tongue to. All was royal; / To the disposing of it nought rebell'd, / Order gave each thing view; the office did / Distinctly his full function.

On my honour as a gentleman who loves honesty, the telling of every detail would lose some life in the mouth of even a good storyteller, because the event itself spoke better than words. Everything was royal; nothing went against the arrangements; good order made everything visible; every official carried out his duty exactly.
Who did guide, / I mean, who set the body and the limbs / Of this great sport together, as you guess?
Who was in charge? I mean, who put together the body and limbs of this great entertainment, do you think?
One, certes, that promises no element / In such a business.
Someone, certainly, whom you would not expect to have any part in such business.
I pray you, who, my lord?
All this was ord'red by the good discretion / Of the right reverend Cardinal of York.
All this was arranged by the wise judgement of the right reverend Cardinal of York.

The devil speed him! no man's pie is freed / From his ambitious finger. What had he / To do in these fierce vanities? I wonder / That such a keech can with his very bulk / Take up the rays o' th' beneficial sun, / And keep it from the earth.

The devil take him! No one's pie is safe from his ambitious finger. What business did he have in these wild vanities? I wonder how such a lump of fat can block the rays of the life-giving sun with his bulk and keep them from the earth.

Surely, sir, / There's in him stuff that puts him to these ends; / For, being not propp'd by ancestry, whose grace / Chalks successors their way, nor call'd upon / For high feats done to the crown; neither allied / To eminent assistants; but, spider-like, / Out of his self-drawing web, he gives us note, / The force of his own merit makes his way; / A gift that heaven gives for him, which buys / A place next to the King.

Surely, sir, he has qualities that drive him to these ends. He isn't supported by noble ancestry, whose favour marks out the way for heirs; he isn't called on for great services to the crown; he isn't connected to powerful allies. Like a spider spinning a web out of itself, he shows us that the force of his own merit makes his way, a gift from heaven that buys him the place next to the King.

I cannot tell / What heaven hath given him,—let some graver eye / Pierce into that; but I can see his pride / Peep through each part of him. Whence has he that? / If not from hell, the devil is a niggard, / Or has given all before, and he begins / A new hell in himself.

I can't say what heaven has given him; let some wiser eye look into that. But I can see his pride peeping out of every part of him. Where did he get it? If not from hell, then the devil is a miser, or has given all his pride away already, and Wolsey is starting a new hell in himself.

Why the devil, / Upon this French going out, took he upon him, / Without the privity o' the King, to appoint / Who should attend on him? He makes up the file / Of all the gentry; for the most part such / To whom as great a charge as little honour / He meant to lay upon; and his own letter, / The honourable board of council out, / Must fetch him in the papers.

Why the devil, for this French trip, did he take it on himself, without the King's knowledge, to choose who should go with him? He drew up the list of all the gentry, mostly men he meant to load with great expense and little honour; and his own letter, without the honourable council being consulted, was enough to summon whoever he named in his papers.
I do know / Kinsmen of mine, three at the least, that have / By this so sicken'd their estates, that never / They shall abound as formerly.
I know kinsmen of mine, at least three, who have so ruined their estates by this that they will never be as rich as before.
O, many / Have broke their backs with laying manors on 'em / For this great journey. What did this vanity / But minister communication of / A most poor issue?
Oh, many have broken their backs by wearing whole estates on their backs for this great journey. And what did this vanity achieve but talks that came to a very poor result?
Grievingly I think / The peace between the French and us not values / The cost that did conclude it.
Sadly I think the peace between France and us is not worth what it cost to make.

Every man, / After the hideous storm that follow'd, was / A thing inspir'd; and, not consulting, broke / Into a general prophecy, that this tempest, / Dashing the garment of this peace, aboded / The sudden breach on't.

After the terrible storm that followed, every man became a prophet; without consulting each other, they all predicted that this storm, tearing the robe of this peace, foretold that it would soon be broken.
Which is budded out; / For France hath flaw'd the league, and hath attach'd / Our merchants' goods at Bordeaux.
And so it has begun; France has broken the treaty and has seized our merchants' goods at Bordeaux.
Is it therefore / The ambassador is silenc'd?
Is that why the French ambassador has been silenced?
A proper title of a peace, and purchas'd / At a superfluous rate!
A fine sort of peace, and bought at an excessive price!
Why, all this business / Our reverend Cardinal carried.
And our reverend Cardinal managed all this business.

Like it your Grace, / The state takes notice of the private difference / Betwixt you and the Cardinal. I advise you— / And take it from a heart that wishes towards you / Honour and plenteous safety—that you read / The Cardinal's malice and his potency / Together, to consider further that / What his high hatred would effect wants not / A minister in his power. You know his nature, / That he's revengeful, and I know his sword / Hath a sharp edge; it's long, and, 't may be said, / It reaches far, and where 'twill not extend, / Thither he darts it. Bosom up my counsel, / You'll find it wholesome. Lo, where comes that rock / That I advise your shunning.

If your Grace pleases, the government has noticed the private quarrel between you and the Cardinal. I advise you, and take this from a heart that wishes you honour and safety, to weigh the Cardinal's malice and his power together, and to consider that whatever his great hatred wants done, he has someone in his power to do it. You know his nature, that he is revengeful, and I know his sword has a sharp edge; it is long, and you might say it reaches far, and where it won't reach he throws it. Keep my advice close; you'll find it healthy. Look, here comes the rock I advise you to steer around.
The Duke of Buckingham's surveyor, ha? / Where's his examination?
The Duke of Buckingham's surveyor, ha? Where is the record of his questioning?
Is he here in person, ready?
Yes, if it please your Grace.
Well, we shall then know more; and Buckingham / Shall lessen this big look.
Good, then we'll learn more, and Buckingham will have to lower that proud look.
This butcher's cur is venom-mouth'd, and I / Have not the power to muzzle him; therefore best / Not wake him in his slumber. A beggar's book / Outworths a noble's blood.

This butcher's dog has a poisonous mouth, and I don't have the power to muzzle him; so it's best not to wake him while he sleeps. A beggar's book learning is worth more than a noble's blood these days.
What, are you chaf'd? / Ask God for temp'rance; that's the appliance only / Which your disease requires.
What, are you angry? Ask God for self-control; that's the only medicine your illness needs.
I read in 's looks / Matter against me, and his eye revil'd / Me as his abject object. At this instant / He bores me with some trick. He's gone to the King; / I'll follow, and outstare him.

I read in his looks something against me; his eye scorned me as something low and contemptible. At this moment he is working some trick against me. He's gone to the King; I'll follow and stare him down.

Stay, my lord, / And let your reason with your choler question / What 'tis you go about. To climb steep hills / Requires slow pace at first. Anger is like / A full hot horse, who being allow'd his way, / Self-mettle tires him. Not a man in England / Can advise me like you; be to yourself / As you would to your friend.

Wait, my lord, and let your reason question your anger about what you are doing. To climb steep hills you must go slowly at first. Anger is like a hot-blooded horse: let it have its head and its own spirit tires it out. No man in England can advise me as well as you can; be to yourself what you would be to a friend.
I'll to the King, / And from a mouth of honour quite cry down / This Ipswich fellow's insolence, or proclaim / There's difference in no persons.
I'll go to the King, and with the voice of a nobleman shout down this Ipswich fellow's insolence, or else declare that there is no difference in rank between people.

Be advis'd; / Heat not a furnace for your foe so hot / That it do singe yourself. We may outrun, / By violent swiftness, that which we run at, / And lose by over-running. Know you not, / The fire that mounts the liquor till 't run o'er, / In seeming to augment it wastes it? Be advis'd. / I say again, there is no English soul / More stronger to direct you than yourself, / If with the sap of reason you would quench, / Or but allay, the fire of passion.

Be careful. Don't heat the furnace for your enemy so hot that it scorches you. We can overshoot what we are running at by running too fast, and lose by overrunning. Don't you know that the fire that makes liquid boil over seems to increase it but actually wastes it? Be careful. I say again, there is no English soul better able to guide you than yourself, if you would quench, or just cool, the fire of passion with the sap of reason.

Sir, / I am thankful to you; and I'll go along / By your prescription; but this top-proud fellow, / Whom from the flow of gall I name not, but / From sincere motions, by intelligence, / And proofs as clear as founts in July when / We see each grain of gravel, I do know / To be corrupt and treasonous.

Sir, I am thankful to you, and I'll follow your advice. But this arrogant fellow, whom I call so not out of bitterness but from honest motives, I know from information and proofs as clear as springs in July, when we can see every grain of gravel, to be corrupt and treasonous.

To the King I'll say't, and make my vouch as strong / As shore of rock. Attend. This holy fox, / Or wolf, or both,—for he is equal ravenous / As he is subtle, and as prone to mischief / As able to perform't; his mind and place / Infecting one another, yea, reciprocally— / Only to show his pomp as well in France / As here at home, suggests the King our master / To this last costly treaty, the interview, / That swallowed so much treasure, and like a glass / Did break i' the rinsing.

I'll say it to the King, and make my claim as firm as a rocky shore. Listen. This holy fox, or wolf, or both, for he is as greedy as he is cunning, and as ready for mischief as he is able to carry it out, his mind and his position infecting each other, just to show off his splendour in France as well as at home, urged the King our master into this last expensive treaty, the meeting that swallowed so much treasure and broke like a glass in the rinsing.

Pray, give me favour, sir. This cunning Cardinal / The articles o' the combination drew / As himself pleas'd; and they were ratified / As he cried "Thus let be," to as much end / As give a crutch to the dead. But our count-cardinal / Has done this, and 'tis well; for worthy Wolsey, / Who cannot err, he did it. Now this follows,— / Which, as I take it, is a kind of puppy / To the old dam, treason,—Charles the Emperor, / Under pretence to see the Queen his aunt,— / For 'twas indeed his colour, but he came / To whisper Wolsey,—here makes visitation. / His fears were, that the interview betwixt / England and France might, through their amity, / Breed him some prejudice; for from this league / Peep'd harms that menac'd him. He privily / Deals with our Cardinal; and, as I trow,— / Which I do well, for I am sure the Emperor / Paid ere he promis'd; whereby his suit was granted / Ere it was ask'd—but when the way was made, / And pav'd with gold, the Emperor thus desir'd, / That he would please to alter the King's course, / And break the foresaid peace. Let the King know, / As soon he shall by me, that thus the Cardinal / Does buy and sell his honour as he pleases / And for his own advantage.

Please, let me go on, sir. This cunning Cardinal drew up the terms of the alliance just as he liked, and they were ratified as soon as he said "Let it be so," with as much use as giving a crutch to a dead man. But our cardinal-count did it, so it must be good, for worthy Wolsey, who can't make mistakes, did it. Now this follows, which I take to be a puppy of the old bitch treason: Charles the Emperor, pretending to visit his aunt the Queen, though that was only his excuse, came to whisper with Wolsey. He feared that the meeting between England and France might, through their friendship, do him harm, since threats to him peeped out of this alliance. He deals secretly with our Cardinal, and, as I believe, and I'm sure of it, for the Emperor paid before he promised, so his request was granted before it was asked, when the way had been made and paved with gold, the Emperor asked that Wolsey turn the King's course and break that peace. Let the King know, as he soon will from me, that this is how the Cardinal buys and sells the King's honour as he likes, for his own profit.
I am sorry / To hear this of him; and could wish he were / Something mistaken in't.
I'm sorry to hear this about him, and I wish there were some mistake in it.
No, not a syllable: / I do pronounce him in that very shape / He shall appear in proof.
No, not a syllable. I describe him exactly as he will be proved to be.
Do your duty, sergeant; carry it out.
Sir, / My lord the Duke of Buckingham, and Earl / Of Hereford, Stafford, and Northampton, I / Arrest thee of high treason, in the name / Of our most sovereign king.
Sir, my lord the Duke of Buckingham, Earl of Hereford, Stafford and Northampton, I arrest you for high treason, in the name of our most sovereign king.
Lo, you, my lord, / The net has fall'n upon me! I shall perish / Under device and practice.
There, my lord, you see: the net has fallen on me! I shall die through plotting and trickery.
I am sorry / To see you ta'en from liberty, to look on / The business present. 'Tis his Highness' pleasure / You shall to the Tower.
I am sorry to see you lose your liberty and to watch this business. It is his Highness's wish that you go to the Tower.

It will help nothing / To plead mine innocence; for that dye is on me / Which makes my whit'st part black. The will of Heaven / Be done in this and all things! I obey. / O my Lord Abergavenny, fare you well!
It will do no good to plead my innocence, for I am stained with a dye that makes my whitest part black. God's will be done in this and in everything! I obey. Oh, my Lord Abergavenny, farewell!
Nay, he must bear you company. / [To Abergavenny] The King / Is pleas'd you shall to the Tower, till you know / How he determines further.
No, he must go with you. (To Abergavenny) The King wishes you to go to the Tower until you learn what he decides next.
As the Duke said, / The will of Heaven be done, and the King's pleasure / By me obey'd!
As the Duke said, God's will be done, and I obey the King's wishes!
Here is warrant from / The King to attach Lord Montacute, and the bodies / Of the Duke's confessor, John de la Car, / One Gilbert Peck, his chancellor,—
Here is a warrant from the King to arrest Lord Montacute, and the persons of the Duke's confessor, John de la Car, and one Gilbert Peck, his chancellor —
So, so; / These are the limbs o' the plot. No more, I hope?
So, so; these are the limbs of the plot. No more, I hope?

My surveyor is false; the o'er-great Cardinal / Hath show'd him gold; my life is spann'd already. / I am the shadow of poor Buckingham, / Whose figure even this instant cloud puts on, / By dark'ning my clear sun. My lord, farewell.

My surveyor has betrayed me; the overmighty Cardinal has shown him gold. My life is already measured out. I am now only the shadow of poor Buckingham, whose shape this sudden cloud takes on by darkening my bright sun. My lord, farewell.

My life itself, and the best heart of it, / Thanks you for this great care. I stood i' the level / Of a full-charg'd confederacy, and give thanks / To you that chok'd it. Let be call'd before us / That gentleman of Buckingham's; in person / I'll hear his confessions justify; / And point by point the treasons of his master / He shall again relate.

My life itself, and the very core of it, thanks you for this great care. I stood in the firing line of a fully loaded conspiracy, and I thank you for choking it off. Have that gentleman of Buckingham's called before us; I'll hear him confirm his confession in person, and he shall repeat, point by point, his master's treasons.
Nay, we must longer kneel; I am a suitor.
No, I must kneel longer; I have a request to make.
Arise, and take place by us. Half your suit / Never name to us, you have half our power; / The other moiety, ere you ask, is given. / Repeat your will and take it.
Get up and sit beside us. Never mention half your request to us: you have half our power. The other half is granted before you ask. Say what you want and take it.
Thank your Majesty. / That you would love yourself, and in that love / Not unconsidered leave your honour, nor / The dignity of your office, is the point / Of my petition.
Thank you, your Majesty. My request is that you love yourself, and in that love do not neglect your honour or the dignity of your office.

I am solicited, not by a few, / And those of true condition, that your subjects / Are in great grievance. There have been commissions / Sent down among 'em, which hath flaw'd the heart / Of all their loyalties; wherein, although, / My good Lord Cardinal, they vent reproaches / Most bitterly on you, as putter on / Of these exactions, yet the King our master— / Whose honour Heaven shield from soil!—even he escapes not / Language unmannerly, yea, such which breaks / The sides of loyalty, and almost appears / In loud rebellion.

I am being petitioned, not by a few people, and those honest ones, that your subjects are in great distress. Commissions have been sent among them that have cracked the heart of their loyalty. In this, although they pour bitter reproaches on you, my good Lord Cardinal, as the one who urged these demands, yet even the King our master, whose honour heaven keep from stain, does not escape rude language, language that breaks the bounds of loyalty and almost appears as open rebellion.

Not "almost appears," / It doth appear; for, upon these taxations, / The clothiers all, not able to maintain / The many to them longing, have put off / The spinsters, carders, fullers, weavers, who, / Unfit for other life, compell'd by hunger / And lack of other means, in desperate manner / Daring the event to the teeth, are all in uproar, / And danger serves among them.

Not "almost appears"; it does appear. Because of these taxes, the cloth-makers, unable to keep their many workers, have laid off the spinners, carders, fullers and weavers. Fit for no other work, driven by hunger and lack of other means, they are desperately defying the consequences and are all in uproar, and danger is among them.
Taxation! / Wherein? and what taxation? My Lord Cardinal, / You that are blam'd for it alike with us, / Know you of this taxation?
Taxation! On what? What taxation? My Lord Cardinal, you who are blamed for it together with us, do you know about this taxation?
Please you, sir, / I know but of a single part, in aught / Pertains to the state, and front but in that file / Where others tell steps with me.
If you please, sir, I know only my own part of what concerns the state, and I only walk in the front of a line where others keep step with me.

No, my lord? / You know no more than others? But you frame / Things that are known alike, which are not wholesome / To those which would not know them, and yet must / Perforce be their acquaintance. These exactions, / Whereof my sovereign would have note, they are / Most pestilent to the hearing; and, to bear 'em, / The back is sacrifice to the load. They say / They are devis'd by you; or else you suffer / Too hard an exclamation.

No, my lord? You know no more than others? But you devise things that everyone then knows, which are harmful to those who would rather not know them but are forced to become familiar with them. These demands, which my sovereign wants to hear about, are poisonous even to hear of, and bearing them breaks the back under the load. They say you devised them; if not, you are blamed too harshly.
Still exaction! / The nature of it? In what kind, let's know, / Is this exaction?
Demands again! What kind? Let us know what sort of demand this is.

I am much too venturous / In tempting of your patience; but am bold'ned / Under your promis'd pardon. The subjects' grief / Comes through commissions, which compels from each / The sixth part of his substance, to be levied / Without delay; and the pretence for this / Is nam'd, your wars in France. This makes bold mouths; / Tongues spit their duties out, and cold hearts freeze / Allegiance in them; their curses now / Live where their prayers did; and it's come to pass / This tractable obedience is a slave / To each incensed will. I would your Highness / Would give it quick consideration, for / There is no primer business.

I am too bold in testing your patience, but your promised pardon gives me courage. The subjects' grievance comes from commissions that force each man to pay a sixth of all he owns, to be collected without delay, and the reason given is your wars in France. This makes mouths bold; tongues spit out their duty, and cold hearts freeze their allegiance. Their curses now live where their prayers used to, and it has come to this: their willing obedience has become a slave to every angry impulse. I wish your Highness would consider it quickly, for there is no more urgent business.
By my life, / This is against our pleasure.
On my life, this is against our wishes.

And for me, / I have no further gone in this than by / A single voice; and that not pass'd me but / By learned approbation of the judges. If I am / Traduc'd by ignorant tongues, which neither know / My faculties nor person, yet will be / The chronicles of my doing, let me say / 'Tis but the fate of place, and the rough brake / That virtue must go through. We must not stint / Our necessary actions, in the fear / To cope malicious censurers; which ever, / As ravenous fishes, do a vessel follow / That is new-trimm'd, but benefit no further / Than vainly longing. What we oft do best, / By sick interpreters, once weak ones, is / Not ours, or not allow'd; what worst, as oft, / Hitting a grosser quality, is cried up / For our best act. If we shall stand still, / In fear our motion will be mock'd or carp'd at, / We should take root here where we sit, or sit / State-statues only.

As for me, I went no further in this than casting a single vote, and that only with the learned approval of the judges. If I am slandered by ignorant tongues that know neither my abilities nor me, yet set themselves up as historians of what I do, let me say that this is simply the fate of high office, the thorny thicket that virtue must go through. We must not hold back necessary actions for fear of facing malicious critics, who always follow like greedy fish behind a newly fitted ship but gain nothing except useless longing. What we often do best, sick or weak interpreters say is not ours or not good; what we do worst, because it appeals to cruder minds, is often praised as our best act. If we stand still for fear our actions will be mocked or criticised, we should take root where we sit, or sit like statues of statesmen.

Things done well, / And with a care, exempt themselves from fear; / Things done without example, in their issue / Are to be fear'd. Have you a precedent / Of this commission? I believe, not any. / We must not rend our subjects from our laws, / And stick them in our will. Sixth part of each? / A trembling contribution! Why, we take / From every tree lop, bark, and part o' the timber; / And, though we leave it with a root, thus hack'd, / The air will drink the sap. To every county / Where this is question'd send our letters, with / Free pardon to each man that has deni'd / The force of this commission. Pray, look to't; / I put it to your care.

Things done well and carefully have nothing to fear; things done without precedent are to be feared in their results. Do you have a precedent for this commission? I believe not. We must not tear our subjects away from our laws and fix them on our mere will. A sixth of everything? A contribution to make men tremble! Why, it is as if we took from every tree its branches, bark and part of the trunk; though we leave the root, the tree so hacked will have its sap drunk by the air. Send our letters to every county where this is disputed, with a free pardon for every man who has refused this commission. Please see to it; I leave it in your care.

A word with you. [To the Secretary, aside] / Let there be letters writ to every shire, / Of the King's grace and pardon. The grieved commons / Hardly conceive of me; let it be nois'd / That through our intercession this revokement / And pardon comes. I shall anon advise you / Further in the proceeding.

A word with you. (To the Secretary, aside) Have letters written to every county about the King's grace and pardon. The aggrieved common people think badly of me; let it be spread about that this repeal and pardon came about through my pleading. I'll give you further instructions soon.
I am sorry that the Duke of Buckingham / Is run in your displeasure.
I am sorry that the Duke of Buckingham has fallen out of your favour.

It grieves many. / The gentleman is learn'd, and a most rare speaker; / To nature none more bound; his training such / That he may furnish and instruct great teachers, / And never seek for aid out of himself. Yet see, / When these so noble benefits shall prove / Not well dispos'd, the mind growing once corrupt, / They turn to vicious forms, ten times more ugly / Than ever they were fair. This man so complete, / Who was enroll'd 'mongst wonders, and when we, / Almost with ravish'd list'ning, could not find / His hour of speech a minute; he, my lady, / Hath into monstrous habits put the graces / That once were his, and is become as black / As if besmear'd in hell. Sit by us; you shall hear— / This was his gentleman in trust—of him / Things to strike honour sad. Bid him recount / The fore-recited practices, whereof / We cannot feel too little, hear too much.

It grieves many. The gentleman is learned and a remarkably fine speaker, more gifted by nature than anyone; his education is such that he could teach great teachers and never need help from outside himself. Yet see: when such noble gifts are badly used and the mind once becomes corrupt, they turn into vicious forms ten times uglier than they were ever beautiful. This man, so complete, who was counted among the wonders, whom we listened to almost entranced so that an hour of his speech seemed a minute, has, my lady, turned the graces that were once his into monstrous habits and has become as black as if smeared in hell. Sit beside us; you shall hear things about him, from this man who was his trusted servant, that would sadden honour itself. Tell him to repeat the plots he already described, which we cannot be too little moved by, nor hear too much of.
Stand forth, and with bold spirit relate what you, / Most like a careful subject, have collected / Out of the Duke of Buckingham.
Step forward, and boldly tell what you, like a careful subject, have gathered about the Duke of Buckingham.

First, it was usual with him, every day / It would infect his speech, that if the King / Should without issue die, he'll carry it so / To make the sceptre his. These very words / I've heard him utter to his son-in-law, / Lord Abergavenny; to whom by oath he menac'd / Revenge upon the Cardinal.

First, it was his habit, every day it tainted his talk, to say that if the King died without children he would manage things so as to make the sceptre his. I've heard him say these very words to his son-in-law, Lord Abergavenny, to whom he swore he would take revenge on the Cardinal.
Please your Highness, note / This dangerous conception in this point. / Not friended by his wish, to your high person / His will is most malignant; and it stretches / Beyond you, to your friends.
If your Highness pleases, note this dangerous idea. Since his wish isn't granted, his will is deeply malicious toward your royal person, and it reaches beyond you to your friends.
My learn'd Lord Cardinal, / Deliver all with charity.
My learned Lord Cardinal, tell everything with charity.
Speak on. / How grounded he his title to the crown? / Upon our fail? To this point hast thou heard him / At any time speak aught?
Go on. On what did he base his claim to the crown? On our having no heir? Have you ever heard him say anything about that?
He was brought to this / By a vain prophecy of Nicholas Henton.
He was led to this by an empty prophecy of Nicholas Henton.
Sir, a Chartreux friar, / His confessor; who fed him every minute / With words of sovereignty.
Sir, a Carthusian friar, his confessor, who fed him every minute with talk of becoming king.

Not long before your Highness sped to France, / The Duke being at the Rose, within the parish / Saint Lawrence Poultney, did of me demand / What was the speech among the Londoners / Concerning the French journey. I repli'd, / Men fear the French would prove perfidious, / To the King's danger. Presently the Duke / Said, 'twas the fear, indeed; and that he doubted / 'Twould prove the verity of certain words / Spoke by a holy monk, "that oft," says he, / "Hath sent to me, wishing me to permit / John de la Car, my chaplain, a choice hour / To hear from him a matter of some moment; / Whom after under the confession's seal / He solemnly had sworn, that what he spoke / My chaplain to no creature living but / To me should utter, with demure confidence / This pausingly ensu'd: 'Neither the King nor's heirs, / Tell you the Duke, shall prosper. Bid him strive / To gain the love o' the commonalty. The Duke / Shall govern England."'

Not long before your Highness went to France, the Duke, at the Rose in the parish of Saint Lawrence Poultney, asked me what the Londoners were saying about the French journey. I replied that people feared the French would prove treacherous, endangering the King. At once the Duke said that was indeed the fear, and he suspected it would prove the truth of certain words spoken by a holy monk. "He has often sent to me," he said, "asking me to allow my chaplain, John de la Car, a convenient hour to hear something important from him. After he had made my chaplain swear solemnly, under the seal of confession, to tell what he said to no living creature but me, he said slowly and with grave confidence: 'Neither the King nor his heirs, tell the Duke, shall prosper. Tell him to work to win the love of the common people. The Duke shall govern England.'"

If I know you well, / You were the Duke's surveyor, and lost your office / On the complaint o' the tenants. Take good heed / You charge not in your spleen a noble person / And spoil your nobler soul; I say, take heed; / Yes, heartily beseech you.

If I know you rightly, you were the Duke's surveyor and lost your post because his tenants complained. Be careful not to accuse a noble person out of spite and ruin your own nobler soul. I say, be careful; yes, I beg you with all my heart.

On my soul, I'll speak but truth. / I told my lord the Duke, by the devil's illusions / The monk might be deceiv'd; and that 'twas dangerous for him / To ruminate on this so far, until / It forg'd him some design; which, being believ'd, / It was much like to do. He answer'd, "Tush, / It can do me no damage;" adding further / That, had the King in his last sickness fail'd, / The Cardinal's and Sir Thomas Lovell's heads / Should have gone off.

On my soul, I'll speak only the truth. I told my lord the Duke that the monk might have been deceived by the devil's tricks, and that it was dangerous for him to brood on this so long that it led him into some plot, which, if he believed it, it was very likely to do. He answered, "Nonsense, it can do me no harm," and added that if the King had died in his last illness, the Cardinal's and Sir Thomas Lovell's heads would have come off.
Ha! what, so rank? Ah ha! / There's mischief in this man. Canst thou say further?
Ha! What, as foul as that? Aha! There's mischief in this man. Can you tell more?
Being at Greenwich, / After your Highness had reprov'd the Duke / About Sir William Bulmer,—
At Greenwich, after your Highness had rebuked the Duke about Sir William Bulmer —
I remember / Of such a time; being my sworn servant, / The Duke retain'd him his. But on; what hence?
I remember that time; Bulmer was my sworn servant and the Duke took him into his own service. But go on; what came of it?

"If," quoth he, "I for this had been committed," / —As, to the Tower, I thought,—"I would have play'd / The part my father meant to act upon / The usurper Richard; who, being at Salisbury, / Made suit to come in 's presence; which if granted, / As he made semblance of his duty, would / Have put his knife into him."

"If," he said, "I had been imprisoned for this," in the Tower, I took it, "I would have played the part my father meant to play against the usurper Richard. When Richard was at Salisbury, my father asked to come into his presence; if that had been granted, he would have pretended to pay his respects and put his knife into him."
Now, madam, may his Highness live in freedom, / And this man out of prison?
Now, madam, can his Highness live safely with this man out of prison?
There's something more would out of thee; what say'st?
There's something more you want to say; what is it?

After "the Duke his father," with "the knife," / He stretch'd him, and, with one hand on his dagger, / Another spread on 's breast, mounting his eyes, / He did discharge a horrible oath; whose tenour / Was, were he evil us'd, he would outgo / His father by as much as a performance / Does an irresolute purpose.

After saying "the Duke his father" and "the knife," he drew himself up, one hand on his dagger and the other spread on his chest, lifted his eyes, and swore a horrible oath, the gist of which was that if he were badly treated he would outdo his father as much as a deed outdoes an uncertain intention.

There's his period, / To sheathe his knife in us. He is attach'd. / Call him to present trial. If he may / Find mercy in the law, 'tis his; if none, / Let him not seek 't of us. By day and night, / He's traitor to th' height.

That's his aim: to sheathe his knife in us. He is under arrest. Bring him to trial at once. If he can find mercy in the law, he may have it; if not, let him not look for it from us. By day and night, he is a traitor to the highest degree.
Is't possible the spells of France should juggle / Men into such strange mysteries?
Is it possible that the spells of France can trick men into such strange fashions?
New customs, / Though they be never so ridiculous, / Nay, let 'em be unmanly, yet are follow'd.
New customs, however ridiculous, even unmanly ones, are still followed.

As far as I see, all the good our English / Have got by the late voyage is but merely / A fit or two o' the face; but they are shrewd ones; / For when they hold 'em, you would swear directly / Their very noses had been counsellors / To Pepin or Clotharius, they keep state so.

As far as I can see, all the good our Englishmen have got from the recent trip is a grimace or two; but they're sharp ones, for when they put them on you'd swear their very noses had been advisers to Pepin or Clotharius, they look so grand.
They have all new legs, and lame ones. One would take it, / That never saw 'em pace before, the spavin / Or springhalt reign'd among 'em.
They all have new ways of walking, and lame ones. Anyone who had never seen them walk before would think they all suffered from horse diseases like spavin or stringhalt.
Death! my lord, / Their clothes are after such a pagan cut too, / That, sure, they've worn out Christendom.
Death! My lord, their clothes are so outlandishly cut, too, that they must have worn out all Christian fashions.
How now! / What news, Sir Thomas Lovell?
Hello! What's the news, Sir Thomas Lovell?
Faith, my lord, / I hear of none, but the new proclamation / That's clapp'd upon the court-gate.
Indeed, my lord, I've heard none except the new proclamation nailed up on the court gate.
The reformation of our travell'd gallants, / That fill the court with quarrels, talk, and tailors.
The reform of our well-travelled young dandies, who fill the court with quarrels, chatter and tailors.
I'm glad 'tis there. Now I would pray our monsieurs / To think an English courtier may be wise, / And never see the Louvre.
I'm glad it's there. Now I'd ask our "monsieurs" to believe an English courtier can be wise without ever seeing the Louvre.

They must either, / For so run the conditions, leave those remnants / Of fool and feather that they got in France, / With all their honourable points of ignorance / Pertaining thereunto, as fights and fireworks, / Abusing better men than they can be, / Out of a foreign wisdom, renouncing clean / The faith they have in tennis and tall stockings, / Short blist'red breeches, and those types of travel, / And understand again like honest men, / Or pack to their old playfellows. There, I take it, / They may, "cum privilegio," wear away / The lag end of their lewdness and be laugh'd at.

By the terms of it, they must either give up the scraps of folly and feathers they picked up in France, with all the honourable bits of ignorance that go with them, such as duelling and fireworks and insulting better men than themselves with foreign wisdom; renounce completely their faith in tennis, tall stockings, short puffed breeches and those other badges of travel, and behave like honest men again; or else pack off to their old playmates. There, I suppose, they may, "with privilege," wear out the last of their lewdness and be laughed at.
'Tis time to give 'em physic, their diseases / Are grown so catching.
It's time to give them medicine; their diseases have become so catching.
What a loss our ladies / Will have of these trim vanities!
What a loss our ladies will suffer from these smart vanities!
Ay, marry, / There will be woe indeed, lords; the sly whoresons / Have got a speeding trick to lay down ladies. / A French song and a fiddle has no fellow.
Yes indeed, there will be grief, lords; the sly rascals have a quick trick for laying ladies down. A French song and a fiddle have no equal.

The devil fiddle 'em! I am glad they are going, / For, sure, there's no converting of 'em. Now / An honest country lord, as I am, beaten / A long time out of play, may bring his plainsong / And have an hour of hearing; and, by 'r Lady, / Held current music too.

The devil fiddle them! I'm glad they're going, for there's certainly no converting them. Now an honest country lord like me, kept out of the game for a long time, can bring his plain tune, get an hour's hearing and, by Our Lady, be thought good music too.
Well said, Lord Sandys; / Your colt's tooth is not cast yet.
Well said, Lord Sandys; you still have your colt's tooth, your youthful appetite.
No, my lord; / Nor shall not, while I have a stump.
No, my lord, and I won't lose it while I have a stump left.
Sir Thomas, / Whither were you a-going?
Sir Thomas, where were you going?
To the Cardinal's. / Your lordship is a guest too.
To the Cardinal's. Your lordship is a guest too.
O, 'tis true: / This night he makes a supper, and a great one, / To many lords and ladies; there will be / The beauty of this kingdom, I'll assure you.
Oh, that's true. Tonight he's giving a supper, a great one, for many lords and ladies. All the beauty of this kingdom will be there, I promise you.
That churchman bears a bounteous mind indeed, / A hand as fruitful as the land that feeds us; / His dews fall everywhere.
That churchman has a generous mind indeed, a hand as fruitful as the land that feeds us; his dew falls everywhere.
No doubt he's noble; / He had a black mouth that said other of him.
No doubt he's noble; anyone who said otherwise would have a slanderous mouth.
He may, my lord; has wherewithal; in him / Sparing would show a worse sin than ill doctrine. / Men of his way should be most liberal; / They are set here for examples.
He can afford it, my lord; he has the means. In him meanness would be a worse sin than false doctrine. Men in his position should be very generous; they are set here as examples.

True, they are so; / But few now give so great ones. My barge stays; / Your lordship shall along. Come, good Sir Thomas, / We shall be late else; which I would not be, / For I was spoke to, with Sir Henry Guildford, / This night to be comptrollers.

True, they are; but few set such great ones now. My barge is waiting; your lordship shall come with me. Come, good Sir Thomas, or we'll be late, which I don't want to be, because I was asked, along with Sir Henry Guildford, to be master of ceremonies tonight.
I am at your lordship's service.

Ladies, a general welcome from his Grace / Salutes ye all; this night he dedicates / To fair content and you. None here, he hopes, / In all this noble bevy, has brought with her / One care abroad. He would have all as merry / As, first, good company, good wine, good welcome, / Can make good people.

Ladies, his Grace greets you all with a warm welcome. He dedicates this night to pleasure and to you. He hopes none of this noble company has brought a single care out with her. He wants everyone as merry as good company, good wine and a good welcome can make good people.
O, my lord, you're tardy; / The very thought of this fair company / Clapp'd wings to me.
Oh, my lord, you're late. The mere thought of this lovely company gave me wings.
You are young, Sir Harry Guildford.
You are young, Sir Harry Guildford.

Sir Thomas Lovell, had the Cardinal / But half my lay thoughts in him, some of these / Should find a running banquet ere they rested, / I think would better please 'em. By my life, / They are a sweet society of fair ones.

Sir Thomas Lovell, if the Cardinal had only half my worldly thoughts, some of these ladies would get a quick snack of a different kind before they went to bed, which I think would please them more. On my life, they are a sweet company of beauties.
O, that your lordship were but now confessor / To one or two of these!
Oh, if only your lordship were confessor to one or two of them now!
I would I were; / They should find easy penance.
I wish I were; they'd get an easy penance.
As easy as a down-bed would afford it.
As easy as a feather bed could make it.

Sweet ladies, will it please you sit? Sir Harry, / Place you that side; I'll take the charge of this. / His Grace is ent'ring. Nay, you must not freeze; / Two women plac'd together makes cold weather. / My Lord Sandys, you are one will keep 'em waking; / Pray, sit between these ladies.

Sweet ladies, will you please sit down? Sir Harry, you seat that side; I'll take charge of this one. His Grace is coming in. No, you mustn't freeze; two women seated together make cold weather. My Lord Sandys, you're one who'll keep them awake; please sit between these ladies.
By my faith, / And thank your lordship. By your leave, sweet ladies. / If I chance to talk a little wild, forgive me; / I had it from my father.
Gladly, and thank you, my lord. With your permission, sweet ladies. If I happen to talk a little wildly, forgive me; I got it from my father.
O, very mad, exceeding mad; in love too; / But he would bite none. Just as I do now, / He would kiss you twenty with a breath.
Oh, very mad, extremely mad, and in love too; but he never bit anyone. Just as I do now, he would kiss you twenty times in one breath.
Well said, my lord. / So, now you're fairly seated. Gentlemen, / The penance lies on you, if these fair ladies / Pass away frowning.
Well done, my lord. So, now you're nicely seated. Gentlemen, it will be your fault if these lovely ladies go away frowning.
For my little cure, / Let me alone.
For my small part of the cure, leave it to me.
You're welcome, my fair guests. That noble lady / Or gentleman that is not freely merry / Is not my friend. This, to confirm my welcome; / And to you all, good health.
Welcome, my fair guests. Any noble lady or gentleman who isn't freely merry is no friend of mine. This, to confirm my welcome; and good health to you all.
Your Grace is noble. / Let me have such a bowl may hold my thanks, / And save me so much talking.
Your Grace is noble. Give me a bowl big enough to hold my thanks, and save me so much talking.
My Lord Sandys, / I am beholding to you; cheer your neighbours. / Ladies, you are not merry. Gentlemen, / Whose fault is this?
My Lord Sandys, I am obliged to you; cheer up your neighbours. Ladies, you aren't merry. Gentlemen, whose fault is this?
The red wine first must rise / In their fair cheeks, my lord; then we shall have 'em / Talk us to silence.
First the red wine must rise into their pretty cheeks, my lord; then they'll talk us into silence.
You are a merry gamester, / My Lord Sandys.
You are a merry player, my Lord Sandys.
Yes, if I make my play. / Here's to your ladyship; and pledge it, madam, / For 'tis to such a thing,—
Yes, if I win my game. Here's to your ladyship; and drink to it, madam, for it's to such a thing —
I told your Grace they would talk anon.
I told your Grace they'd start talking soon.
Look out there, some of ye.
Look out there, some of you.
What warlike voice, / And to what end, is this? Nay, ladies, fear not; / By all the laws of war you're privileg'd.
What warlike sound is this, and what is it for? No, ladies, don't be afraid; by all the laws of war you're protected.
A noble troop of strangers, / For so they seem. They've left their barge and landed, / And hither make, as great ambassadors / From foreign princes.
A noble troop of foreigners, or so they seem. They've left their barge, landed, and are coming here like great ambassadors from foreign princes.

Good Lord Chamberlain, / Go, give 'em welcome; you can speak the French tongue; / And, pray, receive 'em nobly, and conduct 'em / Into our presence, where this heaven of beauty / Shall shine at full upon them. Some attend him.

Good Lord Chamberlain, go and welcome them; you speak French. And please receive them nobly and bring them into our presence, where this heaven of beauty shall shine fully on them. Some of you go with him.
You have now a broken banquet; but we'll mend it. / A good digestion to you all; and once more / I shower a welcome on ye. Welcome all!
Now your banquet has been interrupted, but we'll make up for it. Good digestion to you all, and once again I shower welcome on you. Welcome, all!
A noble company! What are their pleasures?
A noble company! What do they wish?

Because they speak no English, thus they pray'd / To tell your Grace, that, having heard by fame / Of this so noble and so fair assembly / This night to meet here, they could do no less, / Out of the great respect they bear to beauty, / But leave their flocks; and, under your fair conduct, / Crave leave to view these ladies and entreat / An hour of revels with 'em.

Since they speak no English, they asked me to tell your Grace this: having heard by report of this noble and lovely gathering meeting here tonight, they could do no less, out of their great respect for beauty, than leave their flocks; and with your kind permission they ask leave to see these ladies and beg an hour of dancing with them.
Say, Lord Chamberlain, / They have done my poor house grace; for which I pay 'em / A thousand thanks, and pray 'em take their pleasures.
Tell them, Lord Chamberlain, that they have honoured my poor house, for which I give them a thousand thanks, and ask them to enjoy themselves.
The fairest hand I ever touch'd! O beauty, / Till now I never knew thee!
The fairest hand I ever touched! Oh beauty, I never knew you until now!
Pray, tell 'em thus much from me: / There should be one amongst 'em, by his person, / More worthy this place than myself; to whom, / If I but knew him, with my love and duty / I would surrender it.
Please tell them this from me: there must be one among them, by his bearing, more worthy of this seat than I am, and if I only knew who he was I would give it up to him with love and duty.
Such a one, they all confess, / There is indeed; which they would have your Grace / Find out, and he will take it.
They all admit there is such a one, and they would like your Grace to find him out; then he will take the seat.
Let me see, then. / By all your good leaves, gentlemen; here I'll make / My royal choice.
Let me see, then. With your permission, gentlemen, here I'll make my royal choice.
Ye have found him, Cardinal. [Unmasking] / You hold a fair assembly; you do well, lord. / You are a churchman, or, I'll tell you, Cardinal, / I should judge now unhappily.
You've found him, Cardinal. (Unmasking) You hold a fine gathering; you do well, lord. You are a churchman, or else, I tell you, Cardinal, I would think badly of you now.
I am glad / Your Grace is grown so pleasant.
I'm glad your Grace has become so merry.
My Lord Chamberlain, / Prithee come hither. What fair lady's that?
My Lord Chamberlain, please come here. Who is that lovely lady?
An't please your Grace, Sir Thomas Bullen's daughter,— / The Viscount Rochford,—one of her Highness' women.
If it please your Grace, Sir Thomas Bullen's daughter, Viscount Rochford's, one of her Highness's ladies-in-waiting.
By heaven, she is a dainty one. Sweetheart, / I were unmannerly to take you out / And not to kiss you. A health, gentlemen / Let it go round.
By heaven, she is a delicate one. Sweetheart, it would be bad manners to lead you out to dance and not kiss you. A toast, gentlemen; let it go round.
Sir Thomas Lovell, is the banquet ready / I' the privy chamber?
Sir Thomas Lovell, is the banquet ready in the private room?
Your Grace, / I fear, with dancing is a little heated.
I'm afraid your Grace is a little heated from dancing.
There's fresher air, my lord, / In the next chamber.
There's fresher air in the next room, my lord.

Lead in your ladies, every one. Sweet partner, / I must not yet forsake you; let's be merry. / Good my Lord Cardinal, I have half a dozen healths / To drink to these fair ladies, and a measure / To lead 'em once again; and then let's dream / Who's best in favour. Let the music knock it.

Lead in your ladies, every one of you. Sweet partner, I mustn't leave you yet; let's be merry. My good Lord Cardinal, I have half a dozen toasts to drink to these lovely ladies, and a dance to lead them in once more; and then let's dream about who is most in favour. Let the music strike up.
Where are you going so fast?
O, God save ye! / Even to the hall, to hear what shall become / Of the great Duke of Buckingham.
Oh, God save you! To the hall, to hear what will become of the great Duke of Buckingham.
I'll save you / That labour, sir. All's now done, but the ceremony / Of bringing back the prisoner.
I'll save you the trouble, sir. It's all over, except for the ceremony of bringing the prisoner back.
Yes, truly is he, and condemn'd upon't.
Yes, he has, and condemned for it.
But please, how did it go?

I'll tell you in a little. The great Duke / Came to the bar; where to his accusations / He pleaded still not guilty and alleged / Many sharp reasons to defeat the law. / The King's attorney on the contrary / Urg'd on the examinations, proofs, confessions / Of divers witnesses; which the Duke desir'd / To have brought viva voce to his face; / At which appear'd against him his surveyor; / Sir Gilbert Peck his chancellor; and John Car, / Confessor to him, with that devil-monk, / Hopkins, that made this mischief.

I'll tell you briefly. The great Duke came to the bar, where he kept pleading not guilty to the charges and offered many sharp arguments to defeat the law. The King's attorney, on the other side, pressed the statements, proofs and confessions of various witnesses, whom the Duke asked to have brought to his face to speak in person. Then his surveyor appeared against him, Sir Gilbert Peck his chancellor, and John Car his confessor, along with that devil of a monk, Hopkins, who caused this mischief.
That was he / That fed him with his prophecies?
Was he the one who fed him with prophecies?

The same. / All these accus'd him strongly; which he fain / Would have flung from him, but, indeed, he could not. / And so his peers, upon this evidence, / Have found him guilty of high treason. Much / He spoke, and learnedly, for life; but all / Was either pitied in him or forgotten.

The same. All of these accused him strongly, and he would gladly have thrown off their charges, but in truth he couldn't. So his fellow peers, on this evidence, found him guilty of high treason. He spoke much, and learnedly, for his life, but it was all either pitied or ignored.
After all this, how did he bear himself?
After all this, how did he behave?

When he was brought again to the bar, to hear / His knell rung out, his judgment, he was stirr'd / With such an agony, he sweat extremely, / And something spoke in choler, ill, and hasty. / But he fell to himself again, and sweetly / In all the rest show'd a most noble patience.

When he was brought back to the bar to hear his death knell rung, his sentence, he was so shaken with agony that he sweated heavily and said something angry, bitter and rash. But he recovered himself, and for the rest showed a most noble and gentle patience.
I do not think he fears death.
I don't think he's afraid of death.
Sure, he does not; / He never was so womanish. The cause / He may a little grieve at.
Surely he isn't; he was never so womanish. He may grieve a little at the cause of it.
Certainly / The Cardinal is the end of this.
Surely the Cardinal is behind this.
'Tis likely, / By all conjectures: first, Kildare's attainder, / Then deputy of Ireland; who remov'd, / Earl Surrey was sent thither, and in haste too, / Lest he should help his father.

It's likely, by every guess. First there was the condemnation of Kildare, then Deputy of Ireland; once he was removed, the Earl of Surrey was sent there, and in a hurry too, so that he couldn't help his father-in-law.
That trick of state / Was a deep envious one.
That political trick was a deep and spiteful one.
At his return / No doubt he will requite it. This is noted, / And generally, whoever the King favours, / The Cardinal instantly will find employment, / And far enough from court too.
No doubt he will pay it back when he returns. People have noticed that, as a rule, whoever the King favours, the Cardinal will at once find a job for, and far enough from court too.
All the commons / Hate him perniciously, and, o' my conscience, / Wish him ten fathom deep. This duke as much / They love and dote on; call him bounteous Buckingham, / The mirror of all courtesy,—

All the common people hate him deadly and, on my conscience, wish him sixty feet under the sea. They love and adore this duke just as much; they call him bountiful Buckingham, the model of all courtesy —
Stay there, sir, / And see the noble ruin'd man you speak of.
Stop there, sir, and see the noble ruined man you're talking about.
Let's stand close, and behold him.
Let's stand aside and watch him.

All good people, / You that thus far have come to pity me, / Hear what I say, and then go home and lose me. / I have this day receiv'd a traitor's judgement, / And by that name must die; yet, Heaven bear witness, / And if I have a conscience, let it sink me, / Even as the axe falls, if I be not faithful! / The law I bear no malice for my death; / 'T has done, upon the premises, but justice; / But those that sought it I could wish more Christians. / Be what they will, I heartily forgive 'em; / Yet let 'em look they glory not in mischief, / Nor build their evils on the graves of great men, / For then my guiltless blood must cry against 'em. / For further life in this world I ne'er hope, / Nor will I sue, although the King have mercies / More than I dare make faults. You few that lov'd me / And dare be bold to weep for Buckingham, / His noble friends and fellows, whom to leave / Is only bitter to him, only dying, / Go with me, like good angels, to my end; / And, as the long divorce of steel falls on me, / Make of your prayers one sweet sacrifice, / And lift my soul to heaven. Lead on, o' God's name.

All you good people who have come this far out of pity for me, hear what I say, and then go home and forget me. Today I have received a traitor's sentence and must die under that name; yet heaven be my witness, and if I have a conscience, let it sink me as the axe falls if I am not loyal! I bear the law no grudge for my death; on the evidence it has done only justice. But I wish those who sought it were better Christians. Whoever they are, I forgive them with all my heart; but let them take care not to glory in mischief, nor build their evil on great men's graves, for then my innocent blood will cry out against them. I never hope for more life in this world, nor will I beg for it, although the King has more mercy than I dare commit faults. You few who loved me and dare to weep for Buckingham, his noble friends and companions, whom it is the only bitterness, the only death, to leave, go with me like good angels to my end; and as the long divorce of the steel falls on me, make your prayers one sweet offering and lift my soul to heaven. Lead on, in God's name.
I do beseech your Grace, for charity, / If ever any malice in your heart / Were hid against me, now to forgive me frankly.
I beg your Grace, out of charity, if any malice against me was ever hidden in your heart, to forgive me freely now.

Sir Thomas Lovell, I as free forgive you / As I would be forgiven. I forgive all. / There cannot be those numberless offences / 'Gainst me, that I cannot take peace with; no black envy / Shall mark my grave. Commend me to his Grace; / And, if he speak of Buckingham, pray, tell him / You met him half in heaven. My vows and prayers / Yet are the King's; and, till my soul forsake, / Shall cry for blessings on him. May he live / Longer than I have time to tell his years! / Ever belov'd and loving may his rule be! / And when old Time shall lead him to his end, / Goodness and he fill up one monument!

Sir Thomas Lovell, I forgive you as freely as I would be forgiven. I forgive everyone. There cannot be so many offences against me that I cannot make peace with them; no dark hatred shall mark my grave. Give my respects to his Grace, and if he speaks of Buckingham, please tell him you met him half in heaven. My vows and prayers are still the King's, and until my soul leaves me they will cry for blessings on him. May he live longer than I have time to count his years! May his rule be always loved and loving! And when old Time leads him to his end, may goodness and he share one monument!
To the water side I must conduct your Grace; / Then give my charge up to Sir Nicholas Vaux, / Who undertakes you to your end.
I must take your Grace to the riverside, then hand over my charge to Sir Nicholas Vaux, who will take you to your end.
Prepare there, / The Duke is coming. See the barge be ready; / And fit it with such furniture as suits / The greatness of his person.
Get ready there, the Duke is coming. See that the barge is ready, and furnish it with such fittings as suit the greatness of his person.

Nay, Sir Nicholas, / Let it alone; my state now will but mock me. / When I came hither, I was Lord High Constable / And Duke of Buckingham; now, poor Edward Bohun. / Yet I am richer than my base accusers, / That never knew what truth meant. I now seal it; / And with that blood will make 'em one day groan for't. / My noble father, Henry of Buckingham, / Who first rais'd head against usurping Richard, / Flying for succour to his servant Banister, / Being distress'd, was by that wretch betray'd, / And without trial fell; God's peace be with him! / Henry the Seventh succeeding, truly pitying / My father's loss, like a most royal prince, / Restor'd me to my honours, and, out of ruins, / Made my name once more noble. Now his son, / Henry the Eighth, life, honour, name, and all / That made me happy, at one stroke has taken / For ever from the world. I had my trial, / And, must needs say, a noble one; which makes me / A little happier than my wretched father. / Yet thus far we are one in fortunes: both / Fell by our servants, by those men we lov'd most; / A most unnatural and faithless service. / Heaven has an end in all; yet, you that hear me, / This from a dying man receive as certain: / Where you are liberal of your loves and counsels / Be sure you be not loose; for those you make friends / And give your hearts to, when they once perceive / The least rub in your fortunes, fall away / Like water from ye; never found again / But where they mean to sink ye. All good people, / Pray for me! I must now forsake ye. The last hour / Of my long weary life is come upon me. / Farewell! / And when you would say something that is sad, / Speak how I fell. I have done; and God forgive me!

No, Sir Nicholas, leave it; my former rank would only mock me now. When I came here I was Lord High Constable and Duke of Buckingham; now I'm poor Edward Bohun. Yet I am richer than my low accusers, who never knew what truth meant. I seal my truth now, and with this blood I'll make them groan for it one day. My noble father, Henry of Buckingham, who first raised an army against the usurper Richard, fled for help to his servant Banister when he was in trouble, was betrayed by that wretch, and died without trial; God's peace be with him! Henry the Seventh, who came after, truly pitying my father's loss, like a most royal prince restored me to my honours and made my name noble again out of the ruins. Now his son, Henry the Eighth, has taken life, honour, name and everything that made me happy from the world for ever at one stroke. I had a trial, and I must say a noble one, which makes me a little happier than my wretched father. Yet in this our fortunes are the same: we both fell through our servants, through the men we loved most, a most unnatural and faithless service. Heaven has a purpose in everything; yet you who hear me, take this as certain from a dying man: where you are generous with your love and advice, be sure you are not careless. Those you make friends of and give your hearts to, once they see the least bump in your fortunes, fall away from you like water and are never found again except where they mean to sink you. All good people, pray for me! I must leave you now. The last hour of my long, weary life has come. Farewell! And when you want to tell a sad story, tell how I fell. I have finished; and God forgive me!
O, this is full of pity! Sir, it calls, / I fear, too many curses on their heads / That were the authors.
Oh, this is full of pity! Sir, I fear it calls down too many curses on the heads of those who caused it.
If the Duke be guiltless, / 'Tis full of woe; yet I can give you inkling / Of an ensuing evil, if it fall, / Greater than this.
If the Duke is innocent, it's full of grief; yet I can give you a hint of an evil to come, if it happens, greater than this.
Good angels keep it from us! / What may it be? You do not doubt my faith, sir?
Good angels keep it from us! What could it be? You don't doubt my loyalty, sir?
This secret is so weighty, 'twill require / A strong faith to conceal it.
This secret is so weighty it will need strong loyalty to keep it.
Let me have it. / I do not talk much.
Tell me; I don't talk much.
I am confident; / You shall, sir. Did you not of late days hear / A buzzing of a separation / Between the King and Katherine?
I trust you; you shall have it, sir. Didn't you hear recently a buzz of rumour about a separation between the King and Katherine?
Yes, but it held not; / For when the King once heard it, out of anger / He sent command to the Lord Mayor straight / To stop the rumour, and allay those tongues / That durst disperse it.
Yes, but it didn't last; for when the King heard it he angrily ordered the Lord Mayor at once to stop the rumour and silence the tongues that dared to spread it.

But that slander, sir, / Is found a truth now; for it grows again / Fresher than e'er it was; and held for certain / The King will venture at it. Either the Cardinal, / Or some about him near, have, out of malice / To the good Queen, possess'd him with a scruple / That will undo her. To confirm this too, / Cardinal Campeius is arriv'd, and lately; / As all think, for this business.

But that slander, sir, has now turned out true, for it is growing again, fresher than ever, and people take it as certain that the King will attempt it. Either the Cardinal or someone close to him, out of malice toward the good Queen, has filled him with a doubt of conscience that will ruin her. To confirm this, Cardinal Campeius has arrived, recently, and everyone thinks it is for this business.
'Tis the Cardinal; / And merely to revenge him on the Emperor / For not bestowing on him, at his asking, / The archbishopric of Toledo, this is purpos'd.
It's the Cardinal. This is planned merely to take revenge on the Emperor for not giving him the archbishopric of Toledo when he asked for it.
I think you have hit the mark; but is't not cruel / That she should feel the smart of this? The Cardinal / Will have his will, and she must fall.
I think you've hit the mark. But isn't it cruel that she should suffer for this? The Cardinal will have his way, and she must fall.
'Tis woeful. / We are too open here to argue this; / Let's think in private more.
It's sad. We're too exposed here to discuss this; let's think about it more in private.

"My lord, the horses your lordship sent for, / with all the care had, I saw well chosen, ridden, and furnish'd. / They were young and handsome, and of the best breed in the north. / When they were ready to set out for London, a man of / my Lord Cardinal's, by commission and main power, took / 'em from me, with this reason: His master would be serv'd / before a subject, if not before the King; which stopp'd / our mouths, sir." I fear he will indeed. Well, let him have them: / He will have all, I think.

"My lord, the horses your lordship sent for were, with all possible care, well chosen, broken in and equipped. They were young and handsome, of the best breed in the north. When they were ready to set out for London, a man of my Lord Cardinal's took them from me by warrant and sheer force, with this reason: his master would be served before a subject, if not before the King. That shut our mouths, sir." I'm afraid he will be, indeed. Well, let him have them; he'll have everything, I think.
Good day to both your Graces.
Good day to both your Graces.
I left him private, / Full of sad thoughts and troubles.
I left him alone, full of sad thoughts and troubles.
It seems the marriage with his brother's wife / Has crept too near his conscience.
It seems his marriage to his brother's widow has come too close to his conscience.
No, his conscience / Has crept too near another lady.
No, his conscience has come too close to another lady.
'Tis so. / This is the Cardinal's doing, the king-cardinal. / That blind priest, like the eldest son of Fortune, / Turns what he list. The King will know him one day.
That's it. This is the Cardinal's doing, the king-cardinal. That blind priest, like Fortune's eldest son, turns things whichever way he likes. The King will see him for what he is one day.
Pray God he do! he'll never know himself else.
God grant he does! Otherwise he'll never know himself.

How holily he works in all his business! / And with what zeal! for, now he has crack'd the league / Between us and the Emperor, the Queen's great nephew, / He dives into the King's soul, and there scatters / Dangers, doubts, wringing of the conscience, / Fears, and despairs; and all these for his marriage. / And out of all these to restore the King, / He counsels a divorce; a loss of her / That, like a jewel, has hung twenty years / About his neck, yet never lost her lustre; / Of her that loves him with that excellence / That angels love good men with; even of her / That, when the greatest stroke of fortune falls, / Will bless the King. And is not this course pious?

How holy he is in all his business, and how zealous! Now that he has broken the alliance between us and the Emperor, the Queen's great nephew, he dives into the King's soul and scatters there dangers, doubts, pangs of conscience, fears and despair, all about his marriage. And to rescue the King from all of these, he advises a divorce: losing her who has hung like a jewel round his neck for twenty years without ever losing her shine; her who loves him with the perfect love angels have for good men; her who, even when the heaviest blow of fortune falls, will bless the King. Isn't this a pious course?

Heaven keep me from such counsel! 'Tis most true / These news are everywhere; every tongue speaks 'em, / And every true heart weeps for't. All that dare / Look into these affairs see this main end, / The French king's sister. Heaven will one day open / The King's eyes, that so long have slept upon / This bold bad man.

Heaven keep me from such advice! It's quite true this news is everywhere; every tongue speaks of it and every honest heart weeps for it. Everyone who dares look into these affairs sees the main aim: the French king's sister. Heaven will one day open the King's eyes, which have slept so long on this bold, bad man.
And free us from his slavery.
And free us from slavery to him.

We had need pray, / And heartily, for our deliverance; / Or this imperious man will work us all / From princes into pages. All men's honours / Lie like one lump before him, to be fashion'd / Into what pitch he please.

We need to pray, and heartily, to be delivered; or this domineering man will turn us all from princes into pages. All men's honours lie before him like one lump of clay, to be shaped to whatever level he likes.

For me, my lords, / I love him not, nor fear him; there's my creed. / As I am made without him, so I'll stand, / If the King please; his curses and his blessings / Touch me alike, they'are breath I not believe in. / I knew him, and I know him; so I leave him / To him that made him proud, the Pope.

As for me, my lords, I neither love nor fear him; that's my creed. Just as I was made without him, so I'll stand, if the King pleases. His curses and his blessings touch me equally; they're breath I don't believe in. I knew him and I know him; so I leave him to the one who made him proud, the Pope.
Let's in; / And with some other business put the King / From these sad thoughts, that work too much upon him. / My lord, you'll bear us company?
Let's go in, and with some other business distract the King from these sad thoughts that weigh on him too much. My lord, will you come with us?
Excuse me, / The King has sent me otherwhere. Besides, / You'll find a most unfit time to disturb him. / Health to your lordships!
Excuse me, the King has sent me elsewhere. Besides, you'll find it a very bad time to disturb him. Good health to your lordships!
How sad he looks! Sure, he is much afflicted.
How sad he looks! He must be very troubled.
Pray God he be not angry.
Who's there, I say? How dare you thrust yourselves / Into my private meditations? / Who am I? ha?
Who's there, I say? How dare you push yourselves into my private thoughts? Who do you think I am? Ha?
A gracious king that pardons all offences / Malice ne'er meant. Our breach of duty this way / Is business of estate; in which we come / To know your royal pleasure.
A gracious king who pardons all offences that were not meant in malice. We have broken our duty this way on state business; we come to learn your royal wishes about it.
Ye are too bold. / Go to; I'll make ye know your times of business. / Is this an hour for temporal affairs, ha?
You are too bold. Go on; I'll teach you when the right times for business are. Is this an hour for worldly affairs, ha?

Who's there? My good Lord Cardinal? O my Wolsey, / The quiet of my wounded conscience, / Thou art a cure fit for a King. [To Campeius] You're welcome, / Most learned reverend sir, into our kingdom; / Use us and it. [To Wolsey] My good lord, have great care / I be not found a talker.

Who's there? My good Lord Cardinal? Oh my Wolsey, the comfort of my wounded conscience, you are a cure fit for a king. (To Campeius) You are welcome to our kingdom, most learned reverend sir; make use of us and it. (To Wolsey) My good lord, take great care that I am not found to be all talk.
Sir, you cannot. / I would your Grace would give us but an hour / Of private conference.
