Sir, you cannot be. I wish your Grace would give us just an hour of private conversation.
[To Norfolk and Suffolk] We are busy; go.
(To Norfolk and Suffolk) We are busy; go.
[Aside to Suffolk] This priest has no pride in him?
(Aside to Suffolk) This priest has no pride in him, does he?
[Aside to Norfolk] Not to speak of. / I would not be so sick, though, for his place. / But this cannot continue.
(Aside to Norfolk) None worth mentioning. I wouldn't be so sick with pride as he is, though, to have his position. But this can't go on.
[Aside to Suffolk] If it do, / I'll venture one have-at-him.
(Aside to Suffolk) If it does, I'll take a swing at him.

Your Grace has given a precedent of wisdom / Above all princes, in committing freely / Your scruple to the voice of Christendom. / Who can be angry now? What envy reach you? / The Spaniard, tied by blood and favour to her, / Must now confess, if they have any goodness, / The trial just and noble. All the clerks, / I mean the learned ones, in Christian kingdoms / Have their free voices. Rome, the nurse of judgement, / Invited by your noble self, hath sent / One general tongue unto us, this good man, / This just and learned priest, Cardinal Campeius, / Whom once more I present unto your Highness.

Your Grace has given an example of wisdom above all princes by freely submitting your doubt to the judgement of all Christendom. Who can be angry now? What malice can reach you? The Spanish, tied to her by blood and favour, must now admit, if they have any goodness, that the trial is just and noble. All the clergy, I mean the learned ones, in Christian kingdoms are free to give their opinions. Rome, the nurse of judgement, invited by your noble self, has sent us one voice to speak for all, this good man, this just and learned priest, Cardinal Campeius, whom I present to your Highness once more.
And once more in mine arms I bid him welcome, / And thank the holy conclave for their loves. / They have sent me such a man I would have wish'd for.
And once more I welcome him in my arms, and thank the holy college of cardinals for their love. They have sent me just the man I would have wished for.

Your Grace must needs deserve all strangers' loves, / You are so noble. To your Highness' hand / I tender my commission; by whose virtue, / The court of Rome commanding—you, my Lord / Cardinal of York, are join'd with me their servant / In the unpartial judging of this business.

Your Grace must deserve the love of all foreigners, you are so noble. I hand my commission to your Highness; by its authority, at the command of the court of Rome, you, my Lord Cardinal of York, are joined with me, their servant, in judging this business impartially.
Two equal men. The Queen shall be acquainted / Forthwith for what you come. Where's Gardiner?
Two fair-minded men. The Queen shall be told at once why you have come. Where's Gardiner?
I know your Majesty has always lov'd her / So dear in heart not to deny her that / A woman of less place might ask by law, / Scholars allow'd freely to argue for her.
I know your Majesty has always loved her so dearly that you won't deny her what a woman of lower rank could claim by law: scholars allowed to argue freely on her behalf.
Ay, and the best she shall have; and my favour / To him that does best; God forbid else. Cardinal, / Prithee, call Gardiner to me, my new secretary. / I find him a fit fellow.
Yes, and she shall have the best, and my favour to whoever does best; God forbid otherwise. Cardinal, please call Gardiner to me, my new secretary. I find him a fit fellow.
[Aside to Gardiner] Give me your hand. Much joy and favour to you; / You are the King's now.
(Aside to Gardiner) Give me your hand. Much joy and favour to you; you are the King's man now.
[Aside to Wolsey] But to be commanded / For ever by your Grace, whose hand has rais'd me.
(Aside to Wolsey) But always to be commanded by your Grace, whose hand has raised me.
My Lord of York, was not one Doctor Pace / In this man's place before him?
My Lord of York, wasn't a Doctor Pace in this man's position before him?
Was he not held a learned man?
Wasn't he thought a learned man?
Believe me, there's an ill opinion spread then / Even of yourself, Lord Cardinal.
Believe me, then, there's a bad opinion going around about you, Lord Cardinal.
They will not stick to say you envi'd him, / And fearing he would rise, he was so virtuous, / Kept him a foreign man still; which so griev'd him / That he ran mad and died.
They don't hesitate to say you envied him, and, fearing he would rise because he was so virtuous, kept him always abroad on foreign missions, which grieved him so much that he went mad and died.

Heav'n's peace be with him! / That's Christian care enough. For living murmurers / There's places of rebuke. He was a fool, / For he would needs be virtuous. That good fellow, / If I command him, follows my appointment; / I will have none so near else. Learn this, brother, / We live not to be grip'd by meaner persons.

Heaven's peace be with him! That's enough Christian charity. For living grumblers there are places of punishment. He was a fool, because he insisted on being virtuous. That good fellow there follows my orders when I command him; I'll have no one else so close to the King. Learn this, brother: we don't live to be pushed around by lesser people.
Deliver this with modesty to the Queen.
Give this to the Queen with tact.

The most convenient place that I can think of / For such receipt of learning is Black-Friars; / There ye shall meet about this weighty business. / My Wolsey, see it furnish'd. O, my lord, / Would it not grieve an able man to leave / So sweet a bedfellow? But, conscience, conscience! / O, 'tis a tender place; and I must leave her.

The most suitable place I can think of to receive such learned men is Blackfriars; you shall meet there about this weighty business. My Wolsey, see it is made ready. Oh, my lord, wouldn't it grieve any capable man to leave so sweet a bedfellow? But conscience, conscience! Oh, it's a tender spot, and I must leave her.

Not for that neither. Here's the pang that pinches: / His Highness having liv'd so long with her, and she / So good a lady that no tongue could ever / Pronounce dishonour of her,—by my life, / She never knew harm-doing—O, now, after / So many courses of the sun enthroned, / Still growing in a majesty and pomp, the which / To leave a thousand-fold more bitter than / 'Tis sweet at first to acquire,—after this process, / To give her the avaunt, it is a pity / Would move a monster.

Not for that either. Here's the pain that pinches: his Highness has lived so long with her, and she is so good a lady that no tongue could ever speak of dishonour in her; on my life, she never knew how to do harm. Now, after so many years on the throne, always growing in majesty and splendour, which are a thousand times more bitter to lose than they are sweet to gain at first, after all this, to send her packing is a pity that would move a monster.
Hearts of most hard temper / Melt and lament for her.
The hardest hearts melt and grieve for her.
O, God's will, much better / She ne'er had known pomp! Though't be temporal, / Yet, if that quarrel, fortune, do divorce / It from the bearer, 'tis a sufferance panging / As soul and body's severing.

Oh, God's will, it would have been much better if she'd never known greatness! Though it's only worldly, if fortune, that quarrelsome thing, divorces it from the one who has it, it is as painful a suffering as the soul's separation from the body.
Alas, poor lady! / She's a stranger now again.
Alas, poor lady! She is a foreigner again now.

So much the more / Must pity drop upon her. Verily, / I swear, 'tis better to be lowly born / And range with humble livers in content, / Than to be perk'd up in a glist'ring grief, / And wear a golden sorrow.
All the more reason for pity to fall on her. Truly, I swear it's better to be born humble and live contentedly among humble people than to be perched up in glittering grief and wear a golden sorrow.
Our content / Is our best having.
By my troth and maidenhead, / I would not be a queen.
By my faith and my virginity, I wouldn't be a queen.

Beshrew me, I would, / And venture maidenhead for't; and so would you, / For all this spice of your hypocrisy. / You, that have so fair parts of woman on you, / Have too a woman's heart, which ever yet / Affected eminence, wealth, sovereignty; / Which, to say sooth, are blessings; and which gifts, / Saving your mincing, the capacity / Of your soft cheveril conscience would receive, / If you might please to stretch it.

Curse me, I would, and risk my virginity for it; and so would you, for all this flavour of hypocrisy. You, who have such lovely woman's features, have a woman's heart too, which has always wanted high rank, wealth and power; which, to tell the truth, are blessings; and, for all your primness, your soft, stretchy kid-leather conscience would take in those gifts if you cared to stretch it.
Yes, troth and troth. You would not be a queen?
Yes, truly, truly. You wouldn't be a queen?
No, not for all the riches under heaven.
No, not for all the riches under heaven.
'Tis strange. A three-pence bow'd would hire me, / Old as I am, to queen it. But, I pray you, / What think you of a duchess? Have you limbs / To bear that load of title?
That's strange. A bent threepenny bit would hire me, old as I am, to play the queen. But tell me, what do you think of being a duchess? Do you have the limbs to carry that load of title?

Then you are weakly made; pluck off a little. / I would not be a young count in your way, / For more than blushing comes to. If your back / Cannot vouchsafe this burden, 'tis too weak / Ever to get a boy.
Then you're weakly built; take a little off. I wouldn't want to be a young earl coming your way, for more than a blush is worth. If your back can't carry this burden, it's too weak ever to get a boy.
How you do talk! / I swear again I would not be a queen / For all the world.
How you talk! I swear again I wouldn't be a queen for the whole world.
In faith, for little England / You'd venture an emballing. I myself / Would for Carnarvonshire, although there long'd / No more to the crown but that. Lo, who comes here?
Honestly, for little England you'd risk being given the orb. I would myself for Carnarvonshire, even if nothing else belonged to the crown. Look, who's coming?
Good morrow, ladies. What were't worth to know / The secret of your conference?
Good morning, ladies. What would it cost to know the secret of your conversation?
My good lord, / Not your demand; it values not your asking. / Our mistress' sorrows we were pitying.
My good lord, not even the effort of asking; it isn't worth your question. We were pitying our mistress's sorrows.
It was a gentle business, and becoming / The action of good women. There is hope / All will be well.
That was a kind occupation, and fitting for good women. There is hope that all will be well.
I pray God it will, amen!

You bear a gentle mind, and heavenly blessings / Follow such creatures. That you may, fair lady, / Perceive I speak sincerely, and high note's / Ta'en of your many virtues, the King's Majesty / Commends his good opinion of you, and / Does purpose honour to you no less flowing / Than Marchioness of Pembroke; to which title / A thousand pound a year, annual support, / Out of his grace he adds.

You have a kind heart, and heavenly blessings follow such people. So that you may see I'm sincere, fair lady, and that high notice has been taken of your many virtues: the King's Majesty sends his good opinion of you and intends to give you honour no less than the title of Marchioness of Pembroke, to which title, out of his grace, he adds a thousand pounds a year to support it.

I do not know / What kind of my obedience I should tender. / More than my all is nothing; nor my prayers / Are not words duly hallowed, nor my wishes / More worth than empty vanities; yet prayers and wishes / Are all I can return. Beseech your lordship, / Vouchsafe to speak my thanks and my obedience, / As from a blushing handmaid, to his Highness; / Whose health and royalty I pray for.

I don't know what kind of obedience I should offer. Even more than everything I have would be nothing; my prayers are not properly blessed words, and my wishes are worth no more than empty vanities; yet prayers and wishes are all I can give back. I beg your lordship to give my thanks and obedience to his Highness, as from a blushing servant, whose health and royal state I pray for.

Lady, / I shall not fail to approve the fair conceit / The King hath of you. [Aside] I have perus'd her well. / Beauty and honour in her are so mingled / That they have caught the King; and who knows yet / But from this lady may proceed a gem / To lighten all this isle? I'll to the King, / And say I spoke with you.

Lady, I shall be sure to confirm the good opinion the King has of you. (Aside) I've studied her well. Beauty and honour are so mixed in her that they have captured the King; and who knows whether from this lady may come a jewel to light up all this island? (To Anne) I'll go to the King and say I spoke with you.

Why, this it is: see, see! / I have been begging sixteen years in court, / Am yet a courtier beggarly, nor could / Come pat betwixt too early and too late / For any suit of pounds; and you, O fate! / A very fresh-fish here—fie, fie, fie upon / This compell'd fortune!—have your mouth fill'd up / Before you open it.

Why, that's how it is: look, look! I've been begging at court for sixteen years and am still a beggarly courtier, and I could never hit the right moment between too early and too late for any money request; and you, oh fate, a brand-new fish here, damn this forced fortune, have your mouth filled before you open it.
How tastes it? Is it bitter? Forty pence, no. / There was a lady once, 'tis an old story, / That would not be a queen, that would she not, / For all the mud in Egypt. Have you heard it?
How does it taste? Is it bitter? I bet forty pence it isn't. There was once a lady, it's an old story, who would not be a queen, she would not, for all the mud in Egypt. Have you heard it?

With your theme, I could / O'ermount the lark. The Marchioness of Pembroke! / A thousand pounds a year for pure respect! / No other obligation! By my life, / That promises moe thousands; Honour's train / Is longer than his foreskirt. By this time / I know your back will bear a duchess. Say, / Are you not stronger than you were?

With your subject I could fly higher than the lark. Marchioness of Pembroke! A thousand pounds a year just as a mark of respect! No other obligation! On my life, that promises more thousands; honour's train is longer than its front hem. By now I know your back can carry a duchess. Tell me, aren't you stronger than you were?

Good lady, / Make yourself mirth with your particular fancy, / And leave me out on't. Would I had no being, / If this salute my blood a jot. It faints me, / To think what follows. / The Queen is comfortless, and we forgetful / In our long absence. Pray, do not deliver / What here you've heard to her.

Good lady, amuse yourself with your own fancies and leave me out of them. I wish I didn't exist if this stirs my blood one bit. It makes me faint to think what comes next. The Queen is without comfort, and we are neglectful in being away so long. Please don't tell her what you've heard here.
What do you take me for?
Whilst our commission from Rome is read, / Let silence be commanded.
While our commission from Rome is read, let silence be ordered.
What's the need? / It hath already publicly been read, / And on all sides the authority allow'd; / You may, then, spare that time.
What need is there? It has already been read publicly, and its authority accepted by all sides; so you may save that time.
Say, Henry King of England, come into the court.
Say, "Henry, King of England, come into the court."
Henry, King of England, and so on.
Say, Katherine Queen of England, come into the court.
Say, "Katherine, Queen of England, come into the court."
Katherine, Queen of England, and so on.

Sir, I desire you do me right and justice, / And to bestow your pity on me; for / I am a most poor woman, and a stranger, / Born out of your dominions, having here / No judge indifferent, nor no more assurance / Of equal friendship and proceeding. Alas, sir, / In what have I offended you? What cause / Hath my behaviour given to your displeasure, / That thus you should proceed to put me off / And take your good grace from me? Heaven witness, / I have been to you a true and humble wife, / At all times to your will conformable; / Ever in fear to kindle your dislike, / Yea, subject to your countenance, glad or sorry / As I saw it inclin'd. When was the hour / I ever contradicted your desire, / Or made it not mine too? Or which of your friends / Have I not strove to love, although I knew / He were mine enemy? What friend of mine / That had to him deriv'd your anger, did I / Continue in my liking? nay, gave notice / He was from thence discharg'd? Sir, call to mind / That I have been your wife in this obedience / Upward of twenty years, and have been blest / With many children by you. If, in the course / And process of this time, you can report, / And prove it too, against mine honour aught, / My bond to wedlock, or my love and duty, / Against your sacred person, in God's name, / Turn me away; and let the foul'st contempt / Shut door upon me, and so give me up / To the sharp'st kind of justice. Please you, sir, / The King, your father, was reputed for / A prince most prudent, of an excellent / And unmatch'd wit and judgment; Ferdinand, / My father, King of Spain, was reckon'd one / The wisest prince that there had reign'd by many / A year before; it is not to be question'd / That they had gather'd a wise council to them / Of every realm, that did debate this business, / Who deem'd our marriage lawful; wherefore I humbly / Beseech you, sir, to spare me till I may / Be by my friends in Spain advis'd, whose counsel / I will implore. If not, i' the name of God, / Your pleasure be fulfill'd!

Sir, I ask you to do me right and justice and to take pity on me, for I am a very poor woman and a foreigner, born outside your kingdom, with no impartial judge here and no assurance of fair friendship or fair proceedings. Alas, sir, how have I offended you? What cause has my behaviour given for your displeasure, that you should proceed like this to cast me off and take your good grace from me? Heaven be my witness, I have been a true and humble wife to you, always obedient to your will, always afraid of provoking your dislike, yes, following your expression, glad or sorry as I saw it turn. When did I ever contradict your wishes, or not make them mine too? Which of your friends have I not tried to love, even knowing he was my enemy? Which friend of mine who had earned your anger did I go on liking? No, I let him know he was dismissed. Sir, remember that I have been your wife in this obedience for more than twenty years, and have been blessed with many children by you. If in all that time you can report and prove anything against my honour, my marriage vows, or my love and duty to your sacred person, then in God's name turn me away, let the foulest contempt shut the door on me, and hand me over to the harshest justice. If you please, sir, the King your father was known as a most prudent prince, of excellent, unmatched intelligence and judgement; my father Ferdinand, King of Spain, was thought the wisest prince who had reigned for many years before. There is no question that they gathered wise councillors from each kingdom to debate this business, and these judged our marriage lawful. So I humbly beg you, sir, to spare me until I can be advised by my friends in Spain, whose counsel I will beg for. If not, in God's name, let your will be done!

You have here, lady, / And of your choice, these reverend fathers; men / Of singular integrity and learning, / Yea, the elect o' the land, who are assembled / To plead your cause. It shall be therefore bootless / That longer you desire the court; as well / For your own quiet, as to rectify / What is unsettled in the King.

Lady, you have here, of your own choosing, these reverend fathers, men of rare integrity and learning, the pick of the land, gathered to plead your cause. So it is useless for you to ask the court for more delay, both for your own peace and to settle what is unsettled in the King.
His Grace / Hath spoken well and justly; therefore, madam, / It's fit this royal session do proceed, / And that, without delay, their arguments / Be now produc'd and heard.
His Grace has spoken well and justly; so, madam, it is right for this royal session to go on, and for their arguments to be presented and heard without delay.
Lord Cardinal, / To you I speak.
Lord Cardinal, I am speaking to you.
Sir, / I am about to weep; but, thinking that / We are a queen, or long have dream'd so, certain / The daughter of a king, my drops of tears / I'll turn to sparks of fire.
Sir, I am about to weep; but remembering that I am a queen, or have long dreamed I was, and am certainly a king's daughter, I'll turn my tears into sparks of fire.

I will, when you are humble; nay, before, / Or God will punish me. I do believe, / Induced by potent circumstances, that / You are mine enemy, and make my challenge / You shall not be my judge; for it is you / Have blown this coal betwixt my lord and me, / Which God's dew quench! Therefore I say again, / I utterly abhor, yea, from my soul / Refuse you for my judge; whom, yet once more, / I hold my most malicious foe, and think not / At all a friend to truth.

I will, when you are humble; no, even before, or God will punish me. I believe, persuaded by strong evidence, that you are my enemy, and I object that you shall not be my judge, for it is you who have blown on this coal between my lord and me; may God's dew put it out! So I say again: I utterly loathe you, and from my soul I refuse you as my judge, you whom once more I consider my most malicious enemy and no friend at all to truth.

I do profess / You speak not like yourself, who ever yet / Have stood to charity and display'd the effects / Of disposition gentle, and of wisdom / O'ertopping woman's pow'r. Madam, you do me wrong. / I have no spleen against you, nor injustice / For you or any. How far I have proceeded, / Or how far further shall, is warranted / By a commission from the consistory, / Yea, the whole consistory of Rome. You charge me / That I have blown this coal. I do deny it. / The King is present: if it be known to him / That I gainsay my deed, how may he wound, / And worthily, my falsehood! yea, as much / As you have done my truth. If he know / That I am free of your report, he knows / I am not of your wrong. Therefore in him / It lies to cure me; and the cure is, to / Remove these thoughts from you; the which before / His Highness shall speak in, I do beseech / You, gracious madam, to unthink your speaking / And to say so no more.

I declare you are not speaking like yourself; you have always been charitable and shown a gentle nature and a wisdom beyond a woman's. Madam, you wrong me. I have no malice against you, and intend no injustice to you or anyone. How far I have gone, and how much further I shall go, is authorised by a commission from the papal court, the whole court of Rome. You accuse me of blowing on this coal. I deny it. The King is here. If he knows that I am denying what I did, how rightly he could punish my falsehood, as much as you have wounded my truth! If he knows I am innocent of what you say, he knows I am not guilty of wronging you. So it is in his power to cure me, and the cure is to remove these thoughts from you. Before his Highness speaks on this, I beg you, gracious madam, to take back what you said and say it no more.

My lord, my lord, / I am a simple woman, much too weak / To oppose your cunning. You're meek and humble-mouth'd; / You sign your place and calling, in full seeming, / With meekness and humility; but your heart / Is cramm'd with arrogancy, spleen, and pride. / You have, by fortune and his Highness' favours, / Gone slightly o'er low steps and now are mounted / Where powers are your retainers, and your words, / Domestics to you, serve your will as 't please / Yourself pronounce their office. I must tell you, / You tender more your person's honour than / Your high profession spiritual; that again / I do refuse you for my judge; and here, / Before you all, appeal unto the Pope, / To bring my whole cause 'fore his Holiness, / And to be judg'd by him.

My lord, my lord, I am a simple woman, far too weak to stand against your cunning. You are mild and humble in speech; you mark your position and calling, to all appearances, with meekness and humility; but your heart is crammed with arrogance, malice and pride. Through luck and his Highness's favours you have skipped lightly over the low steps and now sit so high that powerful men are your servants, and your words, like household servants, do whatever you tell them. I must tell you, you care more for your own honour than for your high spiritual calling. So again I refuse you as my judge, and here, before you all, I appeal to the Pope, to bring my whole case before his Holiness and be judged by him.
The Queen is obstinate, / Stubborn to justice, apt to accuse it, and / Disdainful to be tried by't; 'tis not well. / She's going away.
The Queen is obstinate, stubborn against justice, quick to accuse it and too proud to be tried by it; that is not good. She is leaving.
Katherine Queen of England, come into the court.
Katherine, Queen of England, come into the court.
Madam, you are being called back.

What need you note it? Pray you keep your way; / When you are call'd, return. Now, the Lord help! / They vex me past my patience. Pray you, pass on. / I will not tarry; no, nor ever more / Upon this business my appearance make / In any of their courts.

Why do you need to notice it? Please go on your way; return when you are called. Now, Lord help me! They provoke me past my patience. Please, go on. I will not stay; no, nor will I ever appear in any of their courts on this business again.

Go thy ways, Kate. / That man i' the world who shall report he has / A better wife, let him in nought be trusted, / For speaking false in that. Thou art, alone, / If thy rare qualities, sweet gentleness, / Thy meekness saint-like, wife-like government, / Obeying in commanding, and thy parts / Sovereign and pious else, could speak thee out, / The queen of earthly queens. She's noble born; / And, like her true nobility, she has / Carried herself towards me.

Go your way, Kate. Any man in the world who claims he has a better wife should not be trusted in anything, for lying about that. If your rare qualities, your sweet gentleness, your saintly meekness, your wifely self-command, obedient while commanding, and your other royal and devout qualities could speak for you, you alone would be the queen of earthly queens. She is nobly born, and she has behaved toward me with true nobility.

Most gracious sir, / In humblest manner I require your Highness, / That it shall please you to declare, in hearing / Of all these ears,—for, where I am robb'd and bound, / There must I be unloos'd, although not there / At once and fully satisfied,—whether ever I / Did broach this business to your Highness, or / Laid any scruple in your way, which might / Induce you to the question on't? or ever / Have to you, but with thanks to God for such / A royal lady, spake one the least word that might / Be to the prejudice of her present state, / Or touch of her good person?

Most gracious sir, I humbly ask your Highness to declare in the hearing of everyone here, for where I was robbed and bound I must be set free there, though not at once fully compensated, whether I ever raised this business with your Highness or put any doubt in your way that might lead you to question your marriage; or whether I ever said to you, except to thank God for so royal a lady, the smallest word that might harm her present position or touch her good person.

My Lord Cardinal, / I do excuse you; yea, upon mine honour, / I free you from't. You are not to be taught / That you have many enemies, that know not / Why they are so, but, like to village-curs, / Bark when their fellows do: by some of these / The Queen is put in anger. You're excus'd; / But will you be more justifi'd? You ever / Have wish'd the sleeping of this business; never desir'd / It to be stirr'd; but oft have hind'red, oft, / The passages made toward it. On my honour, / I speak my good Lord Cardinal to this point, / And thus far clear him. Now, what mov'd me to't, / I will be bold with time and your attention: / Then mark the inducement. Thus it came; give heed to't: / My conscience first receiv'd a tenderness, / Scruple, and prick, on certain speeches utter'd / By the Bishop of Bayonne, then French ambassador; / Who had been hither sent on the debating / A marriage 'twixt the Duke of Orleans and / Our daughter Mary. I' the progress of this business, / Ere a determinate resolution, he, / I mean the Bishop, did require a respite; / Wherein he might the King his lord advertise / Whether our daughter were legitimate, / Respecting this our marriage with the dowager, / Sometimes our brother's wife. This respite shook / The bosom of my conscience, enter'd me, / Yea, with a splitting power, and made to tremble / The region of my breast; which forc'd such way, / That many maz'd considerings did throng / And press'd in with this caution. First, methought / I stood not in the smile of Heaven; who had / Commanded nature, that my lady's womb, / If it conceiv'd a male child by me, should / Do no more offices of life to't than / The grave does to the dead; for her male issue / Or died where they were made, or shortly after / This world had air'd them. Hence I took a thought / This was a judgement on me; that my kingdom, / Well worthy the best heir o' the world, should not / Be gladded in't by me. Then follows, that / I weigh'd the danger which my realms stood in / By this my issue's fail; and that gave to me / Many a groaning throe. Thus hulling in / The wild sea of my conscience, I did steer / Toward this remedy, whereupon we are / Now present here together; that's to say, / I meant to rectify my conscience,—which / I then did feel full sick, and yet not well,— / By all the reverend fathers of the land / And doctors learn'd. First I began in private / With you, my Lord of Lincoln. You remember / How under my oppression I did reek, / When I first mov'd you.

My Lord Cardinal, I excuse you; yes, on my honour, I clear you of it. You don't need telling that you have many enemies who don't know why they are your enemies, but like village dogs bark when the others do; some of these have made the Queen angry. You are excused. But would you like to be cleared further? You have always wished this business to stay asleep, never wanted it stirred, but often, often blocked the moves toward it. On my honour, I speak for my good Lord Cardinal on this point and so far clear him. Now, as to what moved me to it, I'll take some time and your attention; so mark the cause. It came like this; listen. My conscience first felt a tenderness, a doubt and a prick, at certain words spoken by the Bishop of Bayonne, then the French ambassador, who had been sent here to negotiate a marriage between the Duke of Orleans and our daughter Mary. In the course of this business, before a firm decision, the Bishop asked for a delay in which he could tell the King his master whether our daughter was legitimate, considering our marriage to the widow who was once our brother's wife. This delay shook my conscience to its heart, entered me with a splitting force and made my whole breast tremble; it forced such a way in that many bewildered thoughts crowded in after this warning. First, I thought I was not in Heaven's favour, which had ordered nature that if my lady's womb conceived a male child by me it should do no more to keep it alive than the grave does for the dead; for her sons either died in the womb or shortly after this world had given them air. So I thought this was a judgement on me: that my kingdom, worthy of the best heir in the world, should not be made glad by one from me. Then I considered the danger my kingdoms were in through my lack of an heir, and that gave me many groaning pangs. So, drifting on the wild sea of my conscience, I steered toward this remedy, which is why we are here together; that is, I meant to set right my conscience, which I then felt was very sick and still is not well, with the help of all the reverend fathers of the land and learned doctors. I began first in private with you, my Lord of Lincoln. You remember how I sweated under my burden when I first raised it with you.
I have spoke long; be pleas'd yourself to say / How far you satisfi'd me.
I have spoken long; please say yourself how far you satisfied me.

So please your Highness, / The question did at first so stagger me, / Bearing a state of mighty moment in't / And consequence of dread, that I committed / The daring'st counsel which I had to doubt; / And did entreat your Highness to this course / Which you are running here.

If it please your Highness, the question at first so staggered me, involving such a weighty matter and such fearful consequences, that I doubted even my boldest advice, and urged your Highness to take the course you are now following here.

I then mov'd you, / My Lord of Canterbury; and got your leave / To make this present summons. Unsolicited / I left no reverend person in this court; / But by particular consent proceeded / Under your hands and seals. Therefore, go on; / For no dislike i' the world against the person / Of the good queen, but the sharp thorny points / Of my alleged reasons, drives this forward. / Prove but our marriage lawful, by my life / And kingly dignity, we are contented / To wear our mortal state to come with her, / Katherine our queen, before the primest creature / That's paragon'd o' the world.

Then I raised it with you, my Lord of Canterbury, and got your permission to call this present hearing. I left no reverend person in this court unasked, but went ahead with the agreement of each, under your signatures and seals. So go on; for it is no dislike in the world of the good Queen's person, but the sharp, thorny points of the reasons I have given, that drives this forward. Only prove our marriage lawful, and on my life and royal dignity we are content to spend the rest of our mortal life with her, Katherine our queen, rather than with the most perfect creature in the world.

So please your Highness, / The Queen being absent, 'tis a needful fitness / That we adjourn this court till further day. / Meanwhile must be an earnest motion / Made to the Queen, to call back her appeal / She intends unto his Holiness.

If it please your Highness, since the Queen is absent, it is necessary and proper that we adjourn this court until a later day. Meanwhile an earnest appeal must be made to the Queen to withdraw the appeal she intends to make to his Holiness.

[Aside] I may perceive / These Cardinals trifle with me; I abhor / This dilatory sloth and tricks of Rome. / My learn'd and well-beloved servant, Cranmer, / Prithee, return. With thy approach, I know, / My comfort comes along.—Break up the court! / I say, set on.

(Aside) I can see these Cardinals are toying with me; I hate this delaying laziness and these tricks of Rome. My learned and well-loved servant Cranmer, please come back. I know my comfort comes with you. (Aloud) Break up the court! I say, go on.
Take thy lute, wench; my soul grows sad with troubles. / Sing, and disperse 'em, if thou canst. Leave working.
Take your lute, girl; my soul grows sad with troubles. Sing, and scatter them if you can. Stop working.

Orpheus with his lute made trees / And the mountain tops that freeze / Bow themselves when he did sing. / To his music plants and flowers / Ever sprung; as sun and showers / There had made a lasting spring. / Every thing that heard him play, / Even the billows of the sea, / Hung their heads, and then lay by. / In sweet music is such art, / Killing care and grief of heart / Fall asleep, or hearing, die.

Orpheus with his lute made trees and frozen mountain tops bow down when he sang. Plants and flowers always sprang up to his music, as if sun and showers had made an everlasting spring there. Everything that heard him play, even the waves of the sea, hung their heads and then lay still. In sweet music there is such art that care and heartache, hearing it, fall asleep or die.
An't please your Grace, the two great Cardinals / Wait in the presence.
If it please your Grace, the two great Cardinals are waiting in the audience room.
Do they wish to speak with me?
They will'd me say so, madam.
They told me to say so, madam.

Pray their Graces / To come near. [Exit Gentleman] What can be their business / With me, a poor weak woman, fallen from favour? / I do not like their coming. Now I think on't, / They should be good men, their affairs as righteous. / But all hoods make not monks.

Ask their Graces to come in. (The Gentleman leaves) What business can they have with me, a poor weak woman fallen out of favour? I don't like their coming. Now that I think of it, they ought to be good men, and their business righteous. But a hood doesn't make a monk.
Your Graces find me here part of housewife; / I would be all, against the worst may happen. / What are your pleasures with me, reverend lords?
Your Graces find me here partly a housewife; I'd like to be wholly one, in case the worst happens. What do you want with me, reverend lords?
May it please you, noble madam, to withdraw / Into your private chamber, we shall give you / The full cause of our coming.
If it please you, noble madam, to withdraw into your private room, we will tell you the full reason for our coming.

Speak it here; / There's nothing I have done yet, o' my conscience, / Deserves a corner. Would all other women / Could speak this with as free a soul as I do! / My lords, I care not, so much I am happy / Above a number, if my actions / Were tried by every tongue, every eye saw 'em, / Envy and base opinion set against 'em, / I know my life so even. If your business / Seek me out, and that way I am wife in, / Out with it boldly. Truth loves open dealing.

Say it here. Nothing I have done yet, on my conscience, needs a corner to hide in. I wish all other women could say this with as clear a soul as I do! My lords, I don't care, and in this I am happier than many, if my actions were judged by every tongue and seen by every eye, with malice and low opinion set against them; I know my life is so blameless. If your business is about me and my position as a wife, out with it boldly. Truth loves plain dealing.
Tanta est erga te mentis integritas, regina serenissima,—
Most serene queen, so upright is our intention toward you —

O, good my lord, no Latin; / I am not such a truant since my coming, / As not to know the language I have liv'd in. / A strange tongue makes my cause more strange, suspicious; / Pray, speak in English. Here are some will thank you, / If you speak truth, for their poor mistress' sake. / Believe me, she has had much wrong. Lord Cardinal, / The willing'st sin I ever yet committed / May be absolv'd in English.

Oh, my good lord, no Latin. I haven't been so idle since I came here as not to know the language I have lived in. A foreign tongue makes my case seem stranger and more suspicious. Please speak English. There are people here who will thank you for their poor mistress's sake, if you speak the truth. Believe me, she has been greatly wronged. Lord Cardinal, the most deliberate sin I ever committed can be absolved in English.

Noble lady, / I am sorry my integrity should breed, / And service to his Majesty and you, / So deep suspicion, where all faith was meant. / We come not by the way of accusation / To taint that honour every good tongue blesses, / Nor to betray you any way to sorrow; / You have too much, good lady; but to know / How you stand minded in the weighty difference / Between the King and you; and to deliver, / Like free and honest men, our just opinions / And comforts to your cause.

Noble lady, I am sorry that my honesty and my service to his Majesty and you should cause such deep suspicion when only good faith was meant. We don't come to accuse you or to stain the honour every good tongue blesses, nor to lead you into sorrow in any way; you have too much, good lady. We come to learn your mind on the serious dispute between the King and you, and to give you, as free and honest men, our sincere opinions and comfort for your cause.

Most honour'd madam, / My Lord of York, out of his noble nature, / Zeal and obedience he still bore your Grace, / Forgetting, like a good man, your late censure / Both of his truth and him, which was too far, / Offers, as I do, in a sign of peace, / His service and his counsel.

Most honoured madam, my Lord of York, out of his noble nature and the devotion and obedience he has always had for your Grace, forgetting like a good man your recent attack on his honesty and himself, which went too far, offers, as I do, his service and advice as a sign of peace.

[Aside] To betray me.— / My lords, I thank you both for your good wills. / Ye speak like honest men; pray God, ye prove so! / But how to make ye suddenly an answer, / In such a point of weight, so near mine honour,— / More near my life, I fear,—with my weak wit, / And to such men of gravity and learning, / In truth I know not. I was set at work / Among my maids; full little, God knows, looking / Either for such men or such business. / For her sake that I have been,—for I feel / The last fit of my greatness—good your Graces, / Let me have time and counsel for my cause. / Alas, I am a woman, friendless, hopeless!

(Aside) To betray me. (Aloud) My lords, I thank you both for your good will. You speak like honest men; God grant you prove to be! But how to give you a quick answer on such a serious matter, so close to my honour, and closer to my life, I fear, with my weak wits, and to such grave and learned men, I really don't know. I was working among my maids, little expecting, God knows, such men or such business. For the sake of what I have been, for I feel the last throes of my greatness, good your Graces, let me have time and counsel for my cause. Alas, I am a woman, friendless and hopeless!
Madam, you wrong the King's love with these fears. / Your hopes and friends are infinite.
Madam, you wrong the King's love with these fears. Your hopes and friends are countless.

In England / But little for my profit. Can you think, lords, / That any Englishman dare give me counsel? / Or be a known friend, 'gainst his Highness' pleasure, / Though he be grown so desperate to be honest, / And live a subject? Nay, forsooth; my friends, / They that much weigh out my afflictions, / They that my trust must grow to, live not here; / They are, as all my other comforts, far hence / In mine own country, lords.

In England they are of little use to me. Can you believe, lords, that any Englishman would dare give me advice, or be known as my friend against his Highness's wishes, even if he had become desperate enough to be honest, and still live as a subject? No, indeed. My friends, those who truly weigh my troubles, those I can trust, don't live here; they are, like all my other comforts, far away in my own country, lords.
I would your Grace / Would leave your griefs, and take my counsel.
I wish your Grace would put aside your grief and take my advice.

Put your main cause into the King's protection; / He's loving and most gracious. 'Twill be much / Both for your honour better and your cause; / For if the trial of the law o'ertake ye, / You'll part away disgrac'd.

Place your whole case under the King's protection. He is loving and most gracious. It will be much better both for your honour and for your cause, for if the law's judgement overtakes you, you'll leave in disgrace.
Ye tell me what ye wish for both,—my ruin. / Is this your Christian counsel? Out upon ye! / Heaven is above all yet; there sits a judge / That no king can corrupt.
You tell me what you both want: my ruin. Is this your Christian advice? Shame on you! Heaven is still above everything; there sits a judge no king can corrupt.

The more shame for ye! Holy men I thought ye, / Upon my soul, two reverend cardinal virtues; / But cardinal sins and hollow hearts I fear ye. / Mend 'em, for shame, my lords! Is this your comfort, / The cordial that ye bring a wretched lady, / A woman lost among ye, laugh'd at, scorn'd? / I will not wish ye half my miseries; / I have more charity; but say, I warn'd ye. / Take heed, for heaven's sake, take heed, lest at once / The burden of my sorrows fall upon ye.

The more shame on you! I thought you were holy men, on my soul, two reverend cardinal virtues; but I fear you are cardinal sins and hollow hearts. Mend them, for shame, my lords! Is this your comfort, the medicine you bring a miserable lady, a woman lost among you, laughed at and scorned? I won't wish you half my miseries; I have more charity than that. But remember, I warned you. Take care, for heaven's sake, take care that the whole weight of my sorrows doesn't fall on you at once.
Madam, this is a mere distraction; / You turn the good we offer into envy.
Madam, this is sheer madness; you turn the good we offer into malice.

Ye turn me into nothing. Woe upon ye / And all such false professors! Would you have me— / If you have any justice, any pity; / If ye be anything but churchmen's habits— / Put my sick cause into his hands that hates me? / Alas, he's banish'd me his bed already, / His love, too, long ago! I am old, my lords, / And all the fellowship I hold now with him / Is only my obedience. What can happen / To me above this wretchedness? All your studies / Make me a curse like this.

You turn me into nothing. A curse on you and on all such false believers! Would you have me, if you have any justice or pity, if you are anything more than churchmen's robes, put my sick case into the hands of the man who hates me? Alas, he has already banished me from his bed, and from his love long ago! I am old, my lords, and the only bond I have with him now is my obedience. What can happen to me worse than this misery? All your efforts bring me this kind of curse.
Your fears make it worse than it is.

Have I liv'd thus long—let me speak myself, / Since virtue finds no friends—a wife, a true one? / A woman, I dare say without vain-glory, / Never yet branded with suspicion? / Have I with all my full affections / Still met the King? lov'd him next Heav'n? obey'd him? / Been, out of fondness, superstitious to him? / Almost forgot my prayers to content him? / And am I thus rewarded! 'Tis not well, lords. / Bring me a constant woman to her husband, / One that ne'er dream'd a joy beyond his pleasure; / And to that woman, when she has done most, / Yet will I add an honour,—a great patience.

Have I lived so long, let me speak for myself, since virtue finds no friends, as a wife, a true one? A woman, I dare say without boasting, never once branded with suspicion? Have I always met the King with all my love? Loved him next to Heaven? Obeyed him? Out of fondness, almost worshipped him? Almost forgotten my prayers to please him? And am I rewarded like this? It isn't right, lords. Show me a woman faithful to her husband, one who never dreamed of any joy beyond his pleasure, and to that woman, when she has done her utmost, I will still add one honour more: a great patience.
Madam, you wander from the good we aim at.
Madam, you are straying from the good we intend.
My lord, I dare not make myself so guilty, / To give up willingly that noble title / Your master wed me to. Nothing but death / Shall e'er divorce my dignities.
My lord, I dare not make myself so guilty as to give up willingly the noble title your master married me to. Nothing but death shall ever divorce me from my dignities.

Would I had never trod this English earth, / Or felt the flatteries that grow upon it! / Ye have angels' faces, but Heaven knows your hearts. / What will become of me now, wretched lady! / I am the most unhappy woman living. / Alas, poor wenches, where are now your fortunes! / Shipwreck'd upon a kingdom, where no pity, / No friends, no hope; no kindred weep for me; / Almost no grave allow'd me. Like the lily, / That once was mistress of the field and flourish'd, / I'll hang my head and perish.

I wish I had never set foot on this English soil, or felt the flattery that grows on it! You have angels' faces, but Heaven knows your hearts. What will become of me now, wretched lady? I am the unhappiest woman alive. Alas, poor girls, where are your fortunes now! Shipwrecked in a kingdom where there is no pity, no friends, no hope; no relatives weep for me; I'm hardly allowed a grave. Like the lily that was once mistress of the field and flourished, I'll hang my head and die.

If your Grace / Could but be brought to know our ends are honest, / You'd feel more comfort. Why should we, good lady, / Upon what cause, wrong you? Alas, our places, / The way of our profession is against it; / We are to cure such sorrows, not to sow 'em. / For goodness' sake, consider what you do; / How you may hurt yourself, ay, utterly / Grow from the King's acquaintance, by this carriage. / The hearts of princes kiss obedience, / So much they love it; but to stubborn spirits / They swell, and grow as terrible as storms. / I know you have a gentle, noble temper, / A soul as even as a calm; pray, think us / Those we profess, peacemakers, friends, and servants.

If your Grace could only be brought to see that our purposes are honest, you would feel more comfort. Why should we wrong you, good lady, and for what reason? Alas, our positions and the nature of our calling are against it; we are meant to cure such sorrows, not to sow them. For goodness' sake, think what you are doing: how you may harm yourself, yes, and lose the King's acquaintance completely by behaving like this. The hearts of princes kiss obedience, they love it so much; but against stubborn spirits they swell and grow as terrible as storms. I know you have a gentle, noble temper, a soul as smooth as a calm sea; please think of us as what we claim to be, peacemakers, friends and servants.

Madam, you'll find it so. You wrong your virtues / With these weak women's fears. A noble spirit / As yours was, put into you, ever casts / Such doubts, as false coin, from it. The King loves you; / Beware you lose it not. For us, if you please / To trust us in your business, we are ready / To use our utmost studies in your service.

Madam, you'll find it so. You wrong your virtues with these weak womanish fears. A noble spirit such as was put into you always throws out such doubts like counterfeit coins. The King loves you; take care you don't lose that love. As for us, if you will trust us in your business, we are ready to do our very best in your service.

Do what ye will, my lords; and, pray, forgive me / If I have us'd myself unmannerly; / You know I am a woman, lacking wit / To make a seemly answer to such persons. / Pray, do my service to his Majesty; / He has my heart yet, and shall have my prayers / While I shall have my life. Come, reverend fathers, / Bestow your counsels on me. She now begs, / That little thought, when she set footing here, / She should have bought her dignities so dear.

Do what you will, my lords, and please forgive me if I have behaved rudely; you know I am a woman, without the wit to give a proper answer to men like you. Please give my respects to his Majesty; he still has my heart, and shall have my prayers as long as I live. Come, reverend fathers, give me your advice. She who now begs little thought, when she first set foot here, that she would pay so dearly for her honours.

If you will now unite in your complaints / And force them with a constancy, the Cardinal / Cannot stand under them. If you omit / The offer of this time, I cannot promise / But that you shall sustain moe new disgraces, / With these you bear already.

If you will now join together in your complaints and press them steadily, the Cardinal can't withstand them. If you miss the chance this moment offers, I can't promise that you won't suffer more new humiliations on top of the ones you already bear.
I am joyful / To meet the least occasion that may give me / Remembrance of my father-in-law, the Duke, / To be reveng'd on him.
I'm glad of the smallest chance that reminds me of my father-in-law, the Duke, so I can take revenge on him.
Which of the peers / Have uncontemn'd gone by him, or at least / Strangely neglected? When did he regard / The stamp of nobleness in any person / Out of himself?
Which of the peers has he not treated with contempt, or at least strangely ignored? When did he ever respect the mark of nobility in anyone but himself?

My lords, you speak your pleasures. / What he deserves of you and me I know; / What we can do to him, though now the time / Gives way to us, I much fear. If you cannot / Bar his access to the King, never attempt / Anything on him; for he hath a witchcraft / Over the King in 's tongue.

My lords, you say what you like. I know what he deserves from you and me; what we can actually do to him, though the time now favours us, I very much doubt. If you can't stop him getting to the King, never try anything against him, for his tongue has a kind of witchcraft over the King.
O, fear him not; / His spell in that is out. The King hath found / Matter against him that for ever mars / The honey of his language. No, he's settled, / Not to come off, in his displeasure.
Oh, don't fear him; his spell is broken. The King has found something against him that spoils the honey of his words for ever. No, he's fixed in the King's displeasure, never to get out of it.
Sir, / I should be glad to hear such news as this / Once every hour.
Sir, I'd be glad to hear news like this every hour.
Believe it, this is true. / In the divorce his contrary proceedings / Are all unfolded; wherein he appears / As I would wish mine enemy.
Believe me, it's true. His double-dealing over the divorce has all come out, and in it he looks just as I'd wish my enemy to look.
How came / His practices to light?
How did his schemes come to light?

The Cardinal's letters to the Pope miscarried, / And came to the eye o' the King; wherein was read, / How that the Cardinal did entreat his Holiness / To stay the judgement o' the divorce; for if / It did take place, "I do" quoth he "perceive / My king is tangled in affection to / A creature of the Queen's, Lady Anne Bullen."

The Cardinal's letters to the Pope went astray and came before the King's eyes. In them he read that the Cardinal begged his Holiness to hold back the judgement on the divorce, "for if it goes ahead," he said, "I see my King is entangled in love with one of the Queen's women, Lady Anne Bullen."

The King in this perceives him, how he coasts / And hedges his own way. But in this point / All his tricks founder, and he brings his physic / After his patient's death. The King already / Hath married the fair lady.

In this the King sees how he steers round and hedges his own way. But here all his tricks run aground, and he brings his medicine after the patient has died. The King has already married the fair lady.
May you be happy in your wish, my lord! / For, I profess, you have it.
May you be happy in your wish, my lord! For I declare you have it.
Now, all my joy / Trace the conjunction!
Now may all my joy follow this union!

There's order given for her coronation. / Marry, this is yet but young, and may be left / To some ears unrecounted. But, my lords, / She is a gallant creature, and complete / In mind and feature. I persuade me, from her / Will fall some blessing to this land, which shall / In it be memoriz'd.

Orders have been given for her coronation. Indeed, this is still new and may be kept from some ears. But, my lords, she is a splendid creature, perfect in mind and looks. I am convinced some blessing will come from her to this land, which will be remembered for it.
But, will the King / Digest this letter of the Cardinal's? / The Lord forbid!
But will the King swallow this letter of the Cardinal's? God forbid!

No, no; / There be moe wasps that buzz about his nose / Will make this sting the sooner. Cardinal Campeius / Is stolen away to Rome; hath ta'en no leave; / He's left the cause o' the King unhandled, and / Is posted, as the agent of our Cardinal, / To second all his plot. I do assure you / The King cried "Ha!" at this.

No, no; there are more wasps buzzing round his nose that will make this sting sooner. Cardinal Campeius has slipped away to Rome without taking his leave; he has left the King's case undealt with and has rushed off as our Cardinal's agent to back up his whole plot. I assure you the King cried "Ha!" at this.
Now, God incense him, / And let him cry "Ha!" louder!
Now God enrage him, and let him cry "Ha!" louder!
But, my lord, / When returns Cranmer?
But, my lord, when will Cranmer return?

He is return'd in his opinions; which / Have satisfied the King for his divorce, / Together with all famous colleges / Almost in Christendom. Shortly, I believe, / His second marriage shall be publish'd, and / Her coronation. Katherine no more / Shall be call'd Queen, but Princess Dowager / And widow to Prince Arthur.

He has returned in his opinions, which have satisfied the King on his divorce, together with nearly all the famous universities in Christendom. Soon, I believe, his second marriage will be announced, and her coronation. Katherine will no longer be called Queen, but Princess Dowager, widow of Prince Arthur.
This same Cranmer's / A worthy fellow, and hath ta'en much pain / In the King's business.
This Cranmer is a worthy fellow, and has taken great pains over the King's business.
He has; and we shall see him / For it an archbishop.
He has, and we'll see him made an archbishop for it.
Watch, watch; he's in a gloomy mood.
The packet, Cromwell, / Gave't you the King?
The packet, Cromwell: did you give it to the King?
To his own hand, in 's bedchamber.
Into his own hand, in his bedroom.
Look'd he o' the inside of the paper?
Did he look inside the papers?
Presently / He did unseal them; and the first he view'd, / He did it with a serious mind; a heed / Was in his countenance. You he bade / Attend him here this morning.
He unsealed them at once, and he read the first one with a serious mind; there was close attention in his face. He told you to wait on him here this morning.
Is he ready / To come abroad?
Is he ready to come out?
I think, by this he is.
I think he is by now.

[Aside] It shall be to the Duchess of Alencon, / The French king's sister; he shall marry her. / Anne Bullen! No; I'll no Anne Bullens for him; / There's more in't than fair visage. Bullen! / No, we'll no Bullens. Speedily I wish / To hear from Rome. The Marchioness of Pembroke!

(Aside) It shall be the Duchess of Alencon, the French king's sister; he shall marry her. Anne Bullen! No, I'll have no Anne Bullens for him; there's more to it than a pretty face. Bullen! No, we'll have no Bullens. I wish I could hear from Rome quickly. The Marchioness of Pembroke!
May be, he hears the King / Does whet his anger to him.
Maybe he hears the King is sharpening his anger against him.
Sharp enough, / Lord, for thy justice!
Sharp enough, Lord, for your justice!

[Aside] The late queen's gentlewoman, a knight's daughter, / To be her mistress' mistress! the Queen's queen! / This candle burns not clear: 'tis I must snuff it; / Then out it goes. What though I know her virtuous / And well deserving? yet I know her for / A spleeny Lutheran; and not wholesome to / Our cause, that she should lie i' the bosom of / Our hard-rul'd King. Again, there is sprung up / An heretic, an arch one, Cranmer; one / Hath crawl'd into the favour of the King, / And is his oracle.

(Aside) The late queen's lady-in-waiting, a knight's daughter, to become her mistress's mistress, the Queen's queen! This candle doesn't burn clearly; I must snuff it, and then out it goes. What if I know she is virtuous and deserving? I also know she is a hot-headed Lutheran, and it isn't good for our cause that she should lie in the arms of our hard-to-manage King. And again, a heretic has sprung up, an arch-heretic, Cranmer, who has crawled into the King's favour and is his oracle.
I would 'twere something that would fret the string, / The master-cord on 's heart!
I wish it were something that would snap the string, the master-cord of his heart!

What piles of wealth hath he accumulated / To his own portion! and what expense by the hour / Seems to flow from him! How, i' the name of thrift, / Does he rake this together! Now, my lords, / Saw you the Cardinal?

What heaps of wealth he has piled up for himself! And what spending seems to pour from him every hour! How, in the name of thrift, does he rake all this together? Now, my lords, have you seen the Cardinal?

My lord, we have / Stood here observing him. Some strange commotion / Is in his brain; he bites his lip, and starts; / Stops on a sudden, looks upon the ground, / Then lays his finger on his temple; straight / Springs out into fast gait; then stops again, / Strikes his breast hard; and anon he casts / His eye against the moon. In most strange postures / We have seen him set himself.

My lord, we've stood here watching him. Some strange disturbance is in his brain. He bites his lip and starts; stops suddenly, looks at the ground, then puts his finger to his temple; then sets off walking fast; stops again, strikes his chest hard; and then gazes up at the moon. We've seen him put himself into very strange postures.

It may well be; / There is a mutiny in 's mind. This morning / Papers of state he sent me to peruse, / As I requir'd; and wot you what I found / There,—on my conscience, put unwittingly? / Forsooth, an inventory, thus importing / The several parcels of his plate, his treasure, / Rich stuffs, and ornaments of household; which / I find at such proud rate, that it out-speaks / Possession of a subject.

That may well be; there's a mutiny in his mind. This morning he sent me state papers to read, as I had asked; and do you know what I found there, put in, on my conscience, by mistake? An inventory, listing the various pieces of his silver plate, his treasure, rich fabrics and household ornaments, which I find valued so high that it goes far beyond what a subject should own.
It's Heaven's will! / Some spirit put this paper in the packet, / To bless your eye withal.
It's Heaven's will! Some spirit put this paper in the packet to bless your eye with it.

If we did think / His contemplation were above the earth, / And fix'd on spiritual object, he should still / Dwell in his musings; but I am afraid / His thinkings are below the moon, not worth / His serious considering.

If we thought his mind was above the earth and fixed on spiritual things, he could go on with his musing; but I'm afraid his thoughts are below the moon, on worldly things, not worth his serious attention.
Heaven forgive me! / Ever God bless your Highness!
Heaven forgive me! God bless your Highness always!

Good my lord, / You are full of heavenly stuff, and bear the inventory / Of your best graces in your mind; the which / You were now running o'er. You have scarce time / To steal from spiritual leisure a brief span / To keep your earthly audit. Sure, in that / I deem you an ill husband, and am glad / To have you therein my companion.

My good lord, you are full of heavenly matters and carry the inventory of your best graces in your mind, which you were just now going over. You hardly have time to steal a moment from spiritual leisure to keep your earthly accounts. I certainly think you a poor manager there, and I'm glad to have you as my fellow in that.

Sir, / For holy offices I have a time; a time / To think upon the part of business which / I bear i' the state; and Nature does require / Her times of preservation, which perforce / I, her frail son, amongst my brethren mortal, / Must give my tendance to.

Sir, I have a time for holy duties, a time to think about my share of state business; and Nature needs her times of rest and food, which I, her frail son, like my fellow mortals, must necessarily attend to.
And ever may your Highness yoke together, / As I will lend you cause, my doing well / With my well saying!
And may your Highness always link my doing well with my speaking well, as I will give you cause to!

'Tis well said again; / And 'tis a kind of good deed to say well; / And yet words are no deeds. My father lov'd you; / He said he did; and with his deed did crown / His word upon you. Since I had my office, / I have kept you next my heart; have not alone / Employ'd you where high profits might come home, / But par'd my present havings, to bestow / My bounties upon you.

That's well said again, and speaking well is a kind of good deed; and yet words are not deeds. My father loved you; he said he did, and crowned his words with deeds for you. Since I have been king I have kept you closest to my heart; I have not only employed you where great profits could come your way, but cut back my own wealth to give my bounty to you.

Have I not made you / The prime man of the state? I pray you, tell me, / If what I now pronounce you have found true / And, if you may confess it, say withal, / If you are bound to us or no. What say you?
Haven't I made you the first man of the state? Please tell me whether you have found what I say to be true, and if you will admit it, say also whether you are bound to us or not. What do you say?

My sovereign, I confess your royal graces, / Shower'd on me daily, have been more than could / My studied purposes requite, which went / Beyond all man's endeavours. My endeavours / Have ever come too short of my desires, / Yet fil'd with my abilities. Mine own ends / Have been mine so that evermore they pointed / To the good of your most sacred person and / The profit of the state. For your great graces / Heap'd upon me, poor undeserver, I / Can nothing render but allegiant thanks, / My prayers to heaven for you, my loyalty, / Which ever has and ever shall be growing, / Till death, that winter, kill it.

My sovereign, I admit your royal favours, showered on me daily, have been more than my most careful efforts could repay, and they were beyond any man's efforts. My efforts have always fallen short of my wishes, yet matched my abilities. My own aims have been mine only in that they always pointed to the good of your most sacred person and the profit of the state. For your great favours heaped on me, a poor undeserving man, I can give nothing back but loyal thanks, my prayers to heaven for you, and my loyalty, which has always grown and always will, until death, that winter, kills it.

Fairly answer'd. / A loyal and obedient subject is / Therein illustrated. The honour of it / Does pay the act of it, as i' the contrary, / The foulness is the punishment. I presume / That, as my hand has open'd bounty to you, / My heart dropp'd love, my pow'r rain'd honour, more / On you than any, so your hand and heart, / Your brain, and every function of your power, / Should, notwithstanding that your bond of duty, / As 'twere in love's particular, be more / To me, your friend, than any.

A fair answer. It shows a loyal and obedient subject. The honour of loyalty is its own reward, just as the shame of disloyalty is its punishment. I take it that, since my hand has opened bounty to you, my heart dropped love and my power rained honour on you more than on anyone, so your hand and heart, your brain and every power you have should, besides your general bond of duty, be more devoted to me, as your friend in a particular love, than to anyone.

I do profess / That for your Highness' good I ever labour'd / More than mine own, that am, have, and will be— / Though all the world should crack their duty to you, / And throw it from their soul; though perils did / Abound, as thick as thought could make 'em, and / Appear in forms more horrid,—yet my duty, / As doth a rock against the chiding flood, / Should the approach of this wild river break, / And stand unshaken yours.

I declare that I have always worked for your Highness's good more than my own; and that I am, and have been, and will be, though all the world should break its duty to you and throw it out of their souls, though dangers were as thick as thought could make them and appeared in more horrible forms, yet my duty, like a rock against the raging flood, will break the onrush of this wild river and stand unshaken, yours.
'Tis nobly spoken. / Take notice, lords, he has a loyal breast, / For you have seen him open't. Read o'er this;
That's nobly spoken. Take note, lords, he has a loyal heart, for you've seen him open it. Read this through;
And, after, this; and then to breakfast with / What appetite you have.
and afterwards this; and then go to breakfast with whatever appetite you have.

What should this mean? / What sudden anger's this? How have I reap'd it? / He parted frowning from me, as if ruin / Leap'd from his eyes. So looks the chafed lion / Upon the daring huntsman that has gall'd him; / Then makes him nothing. I must read this paper; / I fear, the story of his anger. 'Tis so; / This paper has undone me. 'Tis the account / Of all that world of wealth I have drawn together / For mine own ends; indeed, to gain the popedom / And fee my friends in Rome. O negligence, / Fit for a fool to fall by! What cross devil / Made me put this main secret in the packet / I sent the King? Is there no way to cure this? / No new device to beat this from his brains? / I know 'twill stir him strongly; yet I know / A way, if it take right, in spite of fortune, / Will bring me off again. What's this? "To the Pope!" / The letter, as I live, with all the business / I writ to 's Holiness. Nay then, farewell! / I have touch'd the highest point of all my greatness; / And from that full meridian of my glory, / I haste now to my setting. I shall fall / Like a bright exhalation in the evening, / And no man see me more.

What can this mean? What sudden anger is this? How have I earned it? He left me frowning, as if ruin leapt from his eyes. That's how the enraged lion looks at the bold hunter who has wounded him, before he destroys him. I must read this paper; the story of his anger, I fear. That's it: this paper has ruined me. It's the account of all that world of wealth I have gathered for my own ends, in fact to win the papacy and pay my friends in Rome. Oh, carelessness fit for a fool to fall by! What spiteful devil made me put this vital secret in the packet I sent the King? Is there no way to cure this? No new trick to knock it out of his head? I know it will anger him greatly; yet I know a way that, if it works, will get me off again in spite of fortune. What's this? "To the Pope!" The letter, as I live, with all the business I wrote to his Holiness. Well then, farewell! I have reached the highest point of all my greatness, and from that full noon of my glory I now hurry to my setting. I shall fall like a shooting star in the evening, and no one will see me again.

Hear the King's pleasure, Cardinal! who commands you / To render up the great seal presently / Into our hands; and to confine yourself / To Asher House, my Lord of Winchester's, / Till you hear further from his Highness.
Hear the King's wishes, Cardinal! He commands you to hand over the great seal to us at once, and to confine yourself to Asher House, my Lord of Winchester's, until you hear more from his Highness.
Stay! / Where's your commission, lords? Words cannot carry / Authority so weighty.
Wait! Where is your written commission, lords? Words alone can't carry such weighty authority.
Who dares cross 'em, / Bearing the King's will from his mouth expressly?
Who dares go against them when they bring the King's will straight from his mouth?

Till I find more than will or words to do it, / I mean your malice, know, officious lords, / I dare and must deny it. Now I feel / Of what coarse metal ye are moulded, envy. / How eagerly ye follow my disgraces, / As if it fed ye! and how sleek and wanton / Ye appear in every thing may bring my ruin! / Follow your envious courses, men of malice! / You have Christian warrant for 'em, and, no doubt, / In time will find their fit rewards. That seal / You ask with such a violence, the King, / Mine and your master, with his own hand gave me, / Bade me enjoy it, with the place and honours, / During my life; and, to confirm his goodness, / Tied it by letters-patents. Now, who'll take it?

Until I find more than will and words to do it, I mean your malice, know, you meddling lords, I dare and must refuse. Now I feel what coarse metal you are made of: envy. How eagerly you follow my disgrace, as if it fed you! And how smooth and gleeful you look at anything that may bring my ruin! Follow your envious ways, men of malice! You have Christian authority for them, and no doubt in time they will find their proper rewards. That seal you demand so violently, the King, my master and yours, gave me with his own hand and told me to enjoy it, with the office and honours, for life; and to confirm his goodness, he bound it by letters patent. Now who'll take it?
Thou art a proud traitor, priest.
You are a proud traitor, priest.
Proud lord, thou liest! / Within these forty hours Surrey durst better / Have burnt that tongue than said so.
Proud lord, you lie! Forty hours ago Surrey would rather have burnt that tongue than said so.

Thy ambition, / Thou scarlet sin, robb'd this bewailing land / Of noble Buckingham, my father-in-law. / The heads of all thy brother cardinals, / With thee and all thy best parts bound together, / Weigh'd not a hair of his. Plague of your policy! / You sent me deputy for Ireland, / Far from his succour, from the King, from all / That might have mercy on the fault thou gav'st him; / Whilst your great goodness, out of holy pity, / Absolv'd him with an axe.

Your ambition, you scarlet sin, robbed this mourning land of noble Buckingham, my father-in-law. The heads of all your fellow cardinals, together with you and all your best qualities, weren't worth one of his hairs. A plague on your scheming! You sent me as deputy to Ireland, far from helping him, far from the King, far from everyone who might have shown mercy for the crime you charged him with, while your great goodness, out of holy pity, absolved him with an axe.

This, and all else / This talking lord can lay upon my credit, / I answer is most false. The Duke by law / Found his deserts. How innocent I was / From any private malice in his end, / His noble jury and foul cause can witness. / If I lov'd many words, lord, I should tell you / You have as little honesty as honour, / That in the way of loyalty and truth / Toward the King, my ever royal master, / Dare mate a sounder man than Surrey can be / And all that love his follies.

This, and everything else this talkative lord can blame me for, I answer is completely false. The Duke got what he deserved by law. His noble jury and his foul case can witness how free I was of any private malice in his death. If I liked long speeches, lord, I would tell you that you have as little honesty as honour, and that in loyalty and truth toward the King, my always royal master, I dare match a sounder man than Surrey can be, and all who love his follies.

By my soul, / Your long coat, priest, protects you; thou shouldst feel / My sword i' the life-blood of thee else. My lords, / Can ye endure to hear this arrogance? / And from this fellow? If we live thus tamely, / To be thus jaded by a piece of scarlet, / Farewell nobility! Let his Grace go forward / And dare us with his cap like larks.

By my soul, priest, your long robe protects you; otherwise you'd feel my sword in your life-blood. My lords, can you bear to hear this arrogance, and from this fellow? If we live this tamely, to be treated like old horses by a bit of scarlet cloth, farewell nobility! Let his Grace go on and dazzle us with his red hat like larks caught with a mirror.
All goodness / Is poison to thy stomach.
All goodness is poison to your stomach.

Yes, that goodness / Of gleaning all the land's wealth into one, / Into your own hands, Cardinal, by extortion; / The goodness of your intercepted packets / You writ to the Pope against the King. Your goodness, / Since you provoke me, shall be most notorious. / My Lord of Norfolk, as you are truly noble, / As you respect the common good, the state / Of our despis'd nobility, our issues, / Who, if he live, will scarce be gentlemen, / Produce the grand sum of his sins, the articles / Collected from his life. I'll startle you / Worse than the sacring bell, when the brown wench / Lay kissing in your arms, Lord Cardinal.

Yes, that goodness of gathering all the land's wealth into one place, your own hands, Cardinal, by extortion; the goodness of your intercepted letters that you wrote to the Pope against the King. Since you provoke me, your goodness shall be made well known. My Lord of Norfolk, as you are truly noble, as you care for the common good, the state of our despised nobility and our children, who will hardly be gentlemen if he lives, bring out the grand total of his sins, the charges gathered from his life. I'll startle you worse than the sacring bell at Mass did when the brown-skinned girl lay kissing in your arms, Lord Cardinal.
How much, methinks, I could despise this man, / But that I am bound in charity against it!
How much, I think, I could despise this man, if charity didn't forbid it!
Those articles, my lord, are in the King's hand: / But, thus much, they are foul ones.
Those charges, my lord, are in the King's hands; but this much I can say: they are foul ones.
So much fairer / And spotless shall mine innocence arise, / When the King knows my truth.
All the fairer and more spotless my innocence will rise when the King knows my truth.
This cannot save you. / I thank my memory, I yet remember / Some of these articles; and out they shall. / Now, if you can blush and cry "guilty," Cardinal, / You'll show a little honesty.
That can't save you. Thanks to my memory, I still remember some of these charges, and out they'll come. Now, if you can blush and cry "guilty," Cardinal, you'll show a little honesty.
Speak on, sir; / I dare your worst objections. If I blush, / It is to see a nobleman want manners.
Go on, sir; I defy your worst accusations. If I blush, it's to see a nobleman without manners.
I had rather want those than my head. Have at you! / First, that, without the King's assent or knowledge, / You wrought to be a legate; by which power / You maim'd the jurisdiction of all bishops.
I'd rather lack those than my head. Here goes! First, that without the King's agreement or knowledge you worked to be made papal legate, by which power you crippled the authority of all the bishops.
Then, that in all you writ to Rome, or else / To foreign princes, "Ego et Rex meus" / Was still inscrib'd; in which you brought the King / To be your servant.
Then, that in everything you wrote to Rome or to foreign princes, "Ego et Rex meus," "I and my King," was always written, by which you made the King your servant.
