Then, that, without the knowledge / Either of king or council, when you went / Ambassador to the Emperor, you made bold / To carry into Flanders the great seal.
Then, that without the knowledge of either king or council, when you went as ambassador to the Emperor, you dared to carry the great seal into Flanders.
Item, you sent a large commission / To Gregory de Cassado, to conclude, / Without the King's will or the state's allowance, / A league between his Highness and Ferrara.
Item: you sent a full commission to Gregory de Cassado to conclude, without the King's will or the state's approval, an alliance between his Highness and Ferrara.
That, out of mere ambition, you have caus'd / Your holy hat to be stamp'd on the King's coin.
That, out of sheer ambition, you had your holy hat stamped on the King's coins.

Then, that you have sent innumerable substance— / By what means got, I leave to your own conscience— / To furnish Rome, and to prepare the ways / You have for dignities; to the mere undoing / Of all the kingdom. Many more there are; / Which, since they are of you, and odious, / I will not taint my mouth with.

Then, that you have sent countless riches, how gained I leave to your own conscience, to supply Rome and smooth your way to higher honours, to the utter ruin of the whole kingdom. There are many more, which, since they are yours and hateful, I won't stain my mouth with.
O my lord, / Press not a falling man too far! 'tis virtue. / His faults lie open to the laws; let them, / Not you, correct him. My heart weeps to see him / So little of his great self.
Oh, my lord, don't press a falling man too hard! It's a virtue to spare him. His faults are open to the law; let the law correct him, not you. My heart weeps to see him so shrunk from his great self.

Lord Cardinal, the King's further pleasure is, / Because all those things you have done of late / By your power legatine within this kingdom, / Fall into the compass of a praemunire, / That therefore such a writ be sued against you; / To forfeit all your goods, lands, tenements, / Chattels, and whatsoever, and to be / Out of the King's protection. This is my charge.

Lord Cardinal, the King's further wish is this: because everything you have recently done in this kingdom by your power as legate falls within the scope of a praemunire, a writ of that kind shall be issued against you, so that you forfeit all your goods, lands, houses, possessions and everything else, and are put outside the King's protection. That is my charge.

And so we'll leave you to your meditations / How to live better. For your stubborn answer / About the giving back the great seal to us, / The King shall know it, and, no doubt, shall thank you. / So fare you well, my little good Lord Cardinal.

And so we'll leave you to think about how to live better. As for your stubborn answer about giving back the great seal to us, the King shall hear of it and no doubt will thank you. So farewell, my little good Lord Cardinal.

So farewell to the little good you bear me. / Farewell! a long farewell, to all my greatness! / This is the state of man: to-day he puts forth / The tender leaves of hopes; to-morrow blossoms, / And bears his blushing honours thick upon him; / The third day comes a frost, a killing frost, / And, when he thinks, good easy man, full surely / His greatness is a-ripening, nips his root, / And then he falls, as I do. I have ventur'd, / Like little wanton boys that swim on bladders, / This many summers in a sea of glory, / But far beyond my depth. My high-blown pride / At length broke under me, and now has left me, / Weary and old with service, to the mercy / Of a rude stream, that must for ever hide me. / Vain pomp and glory of this world, I hate ye! / I feel my heart new open'd. O, how wretched / Is that poor man that hangs on princes' favours! / There is, betwixt that smile we would aspire to, / That sweet aspect of princes, and their ruin, / More pangs and fears than wars or women have; / And when he falls, he falls like Lucifer, / Never to hope again.

So farewell to the little good you wish me. Farewell, a long farewell, to all my greatness! This is the state of man: today he puts out the tender leaves of hope; tomorrow he blossoms and wears his blushing honours thick on him; the third day comes a frost, a killing frost, and just when he thinks, the good trusting man, that his greatness is surely ripening, it nips his root, and then he falls, as I do. Like little reckless boys who swim on inflated bladders, I have ventured many summers in a sea of glory, but far out of my depth. My swollen pride finally burst under me, and now has left me, weary and old with service, to the mercy of a rough current that must hide me for ever. Empty pomp and glory of this world, I hate you! I feel my heart opened anew. Oh, how wretched is the poor man who depends on princes' favours! Between the smile we long for, the sweet look of princes, and the ruin they can bring, there are more pangs and fears than wars or women cause; and when he falls, he falls like Lucifer, never to hope again.
I have no power to speak, sir.
What, amaz'd / At my misfortunes? Can thy spirit wonder / A great man should decline? Nay, an you weep, / I am fallen indeed.
What, stunned by my misfortunes? Can your spirit wonder that a great man should fall? No, if you weep, I am fallen indeed.

Why, well, / Never so truly happy, my good Cromwell. / I know myself now; and I feel within me / A peace above all earthly dignities, / A still and quiet conscience. The King has cur'd me, / I humbly thank his Grace; and from these shoulders, / These ruin'd pillars, out of pity, taken / A load would sink a navy, too much honour. / O, 'tis a burden, Cromwell, 'tis a burden / Too heavy for a man that hopes for heaven!

Why, well; never so truly happy, my good Cromwell. I know myself now, and I feel within me a peace above all earthly honours, a calm and quiet conscience. The King has cured me, I humbly thank his Grace, and out of pity has taken from these shoulders, these ruined pillars, a load that would sink a navy: too much honour. Oh, it's a burden, Cromwell, a burden too heavy for a man who hopes for heaven!
I am glad your Grace has made that right use of it.
I'm glad your Grace has used it so rightly.
I hope I have. I am able now, methinks, / Out of a fortitude of soul I feel, / To endure more miseries and greater far / Than my weak-hearted enemies dare offer. / What news abroad?
I hope I have. I think I am now able, through a strength of soul I feel, to endure more and far greater miseries than my faint-hearted enemies dare inflict. What news is there?
The heaviest and the worst / Is your displeasure with the King.
The heaviest and the worst is that you are out of favour with the King.
The next is, that Sir Thomas More is chosen / Lord Chancellor in your place.
The next is that Sir Thomas More has been chosen Lord Chancellor in your place.

That's somewhat sudden; / But he's a learned man. May he continue / Long in his Highness' favour, and do justice / For truth's sake and his conscience; that his bones, / When he has run his course and sleeps in blessings, / May have a tomb of orphans' tears wept on 'em! / What more?

That's rather sudden; but he's a learned man. May he stay long in his Highness's favour and do justice for truth's and conscience's sake, so that when he has run his course and sleeps in blessings, his bones may have a tomb of orphans' tears wept on them! What else?
That Cranmer is return'd with welcome, / Install'd Lord Archbishop of Canterbury.
That Cranmer has returned and been welcomed, and installed as Lord Archbishop of Canterbury.
Last, that the Lady Anne, / Whom the King hath in secrecy long married, / This day was view'd in open as his queen, / Going to chapel; and the voice is now / Only about her coronation.
Lastly, that Lady Anne, whom the King married in secret long ago, was seen in public today as his queen, going to chapel; and now all the talk is of her coronation.

There was the weight that pull'd me down. / O Cromwell, / The King has gone beyond me! All my glories / In that one woman I have lost for ever. / No sun shall ever usher forth mine honours, / Or gild again the noble troops that waited / Upon my smiles. Go, get thee from me, Cromwell! / I am a poor fallen man, unworthy now / To be thy lord and master. Seek the King! / That sun, I pray, may never set! I have told him / What and how true thou art. He will advance thee; / Some little memory of me will stir him— / I know his noble nature—not to let / Thy hopeful service perish too. Good Cromwell, / Neglect him not; make use now, and provide / For thine own future safety.

That was the weight that pulled me down. Oh, Cromwell, the King has outstripped me! In that one woman I have lost all my glories for ever. No sun will ever usher in my honours again, or gild the noble crowds that waited on my smiles. Go, leave me, Cromwell! I am a poor fallen man, unworthy now to be your lord and master. Go to the King, that sun, which I pray may never set! I have told him what you are and how loyal. He will promote you; some small memory of me will move him, I know his noble nature, not to let your promising service die too. Good Cromwell, don't neglect him; take your chance now and provide for your own future safety.

O my lord, / Must I, then, leave you? Must I needs forgo / So good, so noble, and so true a master? / Bear witness, all that have not hearts of iron, / With what a sorrow Cromwell leaves his lord. / The King shall have my service; but my prayers / For ever and for ever shall be yours.

Oh, my lord, must I leave you, then? Must I give up so good, so noble and so true a master? Bear witness, all who don't have hearts of iron, how sorrowfully Cromwell leaves his lord. The King shall have my service, but my prayers shall be yours for ever and ever.

Cromwell, I did not think to shed a tear / In all my miseries; but thou hast forc'd me, / Out of thy honest truth, to play the woman. / Let's dry our eyes; and thus far hear me, Cromwell; / And when I am forgotten, as I shall be, / And sleep in dull cold marble, where no mention / Of me more must be heard of, say, I taught thee; / Say, Wolsey, that once trod the ways of glory, / And sounded all the depths and shoals of honour, / Found thee a way, out of his wreck, to rise in; / A sure and safe one, though thy master miss'd it. / Mark but my fall, and that that ruin'd me. / Cromwell, I charge thee, fling away ambition! / By that sin fell the angels; how can man, then, / The image of his Maker, hope to win by it? / Love thyself last. Cherish those hearts that hate thee; / Corruption wins not more than honesty. / Still in thy right hand carry gentle peace, / To silence envious tongues. Be just, and fear not; / Let all the ends thou aim'st at be thy country's, / Thy God's, and truth's; then if thou fall'st, O Cromwell, / Thou fall'st a blessed martyr! Serve the King! / And, prithee, lead me in. / There take an inventory of all I have, / To the last penny; 'tis the King's. My robe, / And my integrity to Heaven, is all / I dare now call mine own. O Cromwell, Cromwell! / Had I but serv'd my God with half the zeal / I serv'd my king, He would not in mine age / Have left me naked to mine enemies.

Cromwell, I didn't think I would shed a tear in all my miseries; but your honest loyalty has forced me to weep like a woman. Let's dry our eyes, and hear me this far, Cromwell: when I am forgotten, as I shall be, and sleep in dull cold marble where I must never be mentioned again, say I taught you. Say that Wolsey, who once walked the paths of glory and sounded all the depths and shallows of honour, found you a way to rise out of his wreck, a sure and safe one, though your master missed it. Just note my fall and what ruined me. Cromwell, I charge you, throw away ambition! By that sin the angels fell; how then can man, made in his Maker's image, hope to gain by it? Love yourself last. Cherish the hearts that hate you; corruption gains no more than honesty. Always carry gentle peace in your right hand to silence envious tongues. Be just and fear nothing. Let everything you aim at be for your country, your God and truth; then if you fall, Cromwell, you fall a blessed martyr! Serve the King! And please, lead me in. Take an inventory there of everything I own, to the last penny; it's the King's. My robe and my honesty before Heaven are all I now dare call my own. Oh Cromwell, Cromwell! If I had only served my God with half the zeal I served my king, He would not have left me naked to my enemies in my old age.
So I have. Farewell / The hopes of court! My hopes in heaven do dwell.
So I am. Farewell, hopes of court! My hopes now live in heaven.
You come to take your stand here, and behold / The Lady Anne pass from her coronation?
You've come to take your place here and watch Lady Anne pass on her way back from her coronation?
'Tis all my business. At our last encounter, / The Duke of Buckingham came from his trial.
That's all my business. When we last met, the Duke of Buckingham was coming from his trial.
'Tis very true; but that time offer'd sorrow; / This, general joy.
Very true; but that time brought sorrow, this one general joy.

'Tis well. The citizens, / I am sure, have shown at full their royal minds— / As, let 'em have their rights, they are ever forward— / In celebration of this day with shows, / Pageants, and sights of honour.
Good. The citizens, I'm sure, have shown their loyal spirit to the full, for, to give them their due, they are always eager, celebrating this day with shows, pageants and honourable displays.
Never greater, / Nor, I'll assure you, better taken, sir.
Never greater, nor, I assure you, better received, sir.
May I be bold to ask what that contains, / That paper in your hand?
May I be so bold as to ask what that paper in your hand contains?

Yes; 'tis the list / Of those that claim their offices this day / By custom of the coronation. / The Duke of Suffolk is the first, and claims / To be High Steward; next, the Duke of Norfolk, / He to be Earl Marshal. You may read the rest.

Yes; it's the list of those who claim their offices today by custom of the coronation. The Duke of Suffolk is first, and claims to be High Steward; next the Duke of Norfolk, to be Earl Marshal. You can read the rest.
I thank you, sir; had I not known those customs, / I should have been beholding to your paper. / But, I beseech you, what's become of Katherine, / The Princess Dowager? How goes her business?
Thank you, sir; if I didn't know those customs I'd be grateful for your paper. But please, what has become of Katherine, the Princess Dowager? How is her business going?

That I can tell you too. The Archbishop / Of Canterbury, accompanied with other / Learned and reverend fathers of his order, / Held a late court at Dunstable, six miles off / From Ampthill where the Princess lay; to which / She was often cited by them, but appear'd not; / And, to be short, for not appearance and / The King's late scruple, by the main assent / Of all these learned men she was divorc'd, / And the late marriage made of none effect; / Since which she was remov'd to Kimbolton, / Where she remains now sick.

I can tell you that too. The Archbishop of Canterbury, with other learned and reverend fathers of his order, recently held a court at Dunstable, six miles from Ampthill where the Princess was staying. She was summoned to it many times but did not appear. To be brief, because she did not appear and because of the King's recent doubt of conscience, by the general agreement of all these learned men she was divorced and her marriage declared void. Since then she has been moved to Kimbolton, where she now lies ill.
The trumpets sound; stand close, the Queen is coming.
The trumpets are sounding; stand back, the Queen is coming.
A royal train, believe me. These I know. / Who's that that bears the sceptre?
A royal procession, believe me. I know these. Who's that carrying the sceptre?
Marquess Dorset; / And that the Earl of Surrey, with the rod.
Marquess Dorset; and that's the Earl of Surrey, with the rod.
A bold brave gentleman. That should be / The Duke of Suffolk?
A bold, brave gentleman. That must be the Duke of Suffolk?
And that my Lord of Norfolk?
And that's my Lord of Norfolk?

Heaven bless thee! [Looking on the Queen] / Thou hast the sweetest face I ever look'd on. / Sir, as I have a soul, she is an angel; / Our king has all the Indies in his arms, / And more and richer, when he strains that lady. / I cannot blame his conscience.

(Looking at the Queen) Heaven bless you! You have the sweetest face I ever saw. Sir, as I have a soul, she is an angel. Our king holds all the Indies in his arms, and more and richer, when he hugs that lady. I can't blame his conscience.
They that bear / The cloth of honour over her, are four barons / Of the Cinque-ports.
The men carrying the canopy of honour over her are four barons of the Cinque Ports.
Those men are happy; and so are all are near her. / I take it, she that carries up the train / Is that old noble lady, Duchess of Norfolk.
Those men are lucky, and so is everyone near her. I take it the one carrying her train is that old noble lady, the Duchess of Norfolk.
It is; and all the rest are countesses.
It is; and all the rest are countesses.
Their coronets say so. These are stars indeed; / And sometimes falling ones.
Their coronets say so. These are stars indeed, and sometimes falling ones.
God save you, sir! Where have you been broiling?
God save you, sir! Where have you been roasting?
Among the crowds i' the Abbey, where a finger / Could not be wedg'd in more. I am stifled / With the mere rankness of their joy.
In the crowds in the Abbey, where you couldn't have wedged in another finger. I'm stifled by the sheer stink of their joy.
Good sir, speak it to us.
Good sir, tell us about it.

As well as I am able. The rich stream / Of lords and ladies, having brought the Queen / To a prepar'd place in the choir, fell of / A distance from her; while her Grace sat down / To rest a while, some half an hour or so, / In a rich chair of state, opposing freely / The beauty of her person to the people,— / Believe me, sir, she is the goodliest woman / That ever lay by man;—which when the people / Had the full view of, such a noise arose / As the shrouds make at sea in a stiff tempest, / As loud, and to as many tunes. Hats, cloaks,— / Doublets, I think,—flew up; and had their faces / Been loose, this day they had been lost. Such joy / I never saw before. Great-belli'd women, / That had not half a week to go, like rams / In the old time of war, would shake the press / And make 'em reel before 'em. No man living / Could say "This is my wife" there; all were woven / So strangely in one piece.

As well as I can. The rich stream of lords and ladies, having brought the Queen to a place prepared in the choir, drew back a little from her, while her Grace sat down to rest for half an hour or so in a rich chair of state, freely showing the beauty of her person to the people. Believe me, sir, she is the finest woman who ever lay beside a man. When the people got a full view of her, such a noise went up as the rigging makes at sea in a hard storm, as loud and in as many tunes. Hats, cloaks, even doublets I think, flew into the air; and if their faces had been loose, they'd have lost them today. I never saw such joy. Heavily pregnant women with less than half a week to go would shake the crowd like battering rams in old wars and make people reel in front of them. No man alive could say "This is my wife" there; they were all so strangely woven into one piece.

At length her Grace rose, and with modest paces / Came to the altar; where she kneel'd, and saintlike / Cast her fair eyes to heaven and pray'd devoutly; / Then rose again and bow'd her to the people, / When by the Archbishop of Canterbury / She had all the royal makings of a queen, / As holy oil, Edward Confessor's crown, / The rod, and bird of peace, and all such emblems / Laid nobly on her; which perform'd, the choir, / With all the choicest music of the kingdom, / Together sung "Te Deum." So she parted, / And with the same full state pac'd back again / To York Place, where the feast is held.

At last her Grace rose and with modest steps came to the altar, where she knelt and, like a saint, raised her lovely eyes to heaven and prayed devoutly. Then she rose again and bowed to the people, and the Archbishop of Canterbury nobly gave her all the royal marks of a queen: the holy oil, Edward the Confessor's crown, the rod, the dove of peace and all such emblems. When that was done, the choir, with all the finest musicians in the kingdom, sang the "Te Deum" together. Then she left, and with the same full ceremony walked back to York Place, where the feast is being held.
Sir, / You must no more call it York Place, that's past; / For, since the Cardinal fell, that title's lost. / 'Tis now the King's, and call'd Whitehall.
Sir, you mustn't call it York Place any more; that's over. Since the Cardinal fell that name is lost. It's the King's now, and called Whitehall.
I know it; / But 'tis so lately alter'd, that the old name / Is fresh about me.
I know; but it was changed so recently that the old name is still fresh with me.
What two reverend bishops / Were those that went on each side of the Queen?
Who were the two reverend bishops walking on either side of the Queen?
Stokesly and Gardiner; the one of Winchester, / Newly preferr'd from the King's secretary; / The other, London.
Stokesley and Gardiner; the one is Bishop of Winchester, newly promoted from the King's secretary; the other, of London.
He of Winchester / Is held no great good lover of the Archbishop's, / The virtuous Cranmer.
The Bishop of Winchester is said to be no great friend of the Archbishop, the virtuous Cranmer.
All the land knows that. / However, yet there is no great breach; when it comes, / Cranmer will find a friend will not shrink from him.
The whole country knows that. Still, there's no great split yet; when it comes, Cranmer will find a friend who won't shrink from him.
Who may that be, I pray you?
Thomas Cromwell; / A man in much esteem with the King, and truly / A worthy friend. The King has made him master / O' the jewel house, / And one, already, of the privy council.
Thomas Cromwell, a man highly regarded by the King, and truly a worthy friend. The King has made him Master of the Jewel House, and already a member of the Privy Council.
Yes, without all doubt. / Come, gentlemen, ye shall go my way, which / Is to the court, and there ye shall be my guests; / Something I can command. As I walk thither, / I'll tell ye more.
Yes, without any doubt. Come, gentlemen, you shall come my way, which is to court, and there you'll be my guests; I have some influence there. As we walk, I'll tell you more.
We are at your service, sir.

O Griffith, sick to death! / My legs, like loaden branches, bow to the earth, / Willing to leave their burden. Reach a chair. / So; now, methinks, I feel a little ease. / Didst thou not tell me, Griffith, as thou led'st me, / That the great child of honour, Cardinal Wolsey, / Was dead?

Oh, Griffith, sick to death! My legs bend to the earth like loaded branches, wanting to drop their burden. Bring a chair. There; now I think I feel a little easier. Didn't you tell me, Griffith, as you led me, that the great child of honour, Cardinal Wolsey, was dead?
Yes, madam; but I think your Grace, / Out of the pain you suffer'd, gave no ear to't.
Yes, madam; but I think your Grace, because of the pain you were in, didn't listen.
Prithee, good Griffith, tell me how he died. / If well, he stepp'd before me, happily / For my example.
Please, good Griffith, tell me how he died. If he died well, he went before me happily, as an example to me.

Well, the voice goes, madam: / For after the stout Earl Northumberland / Arrested him at York, and brought him forward, / As a man sorely tainted, to his answer, / He fell sick suddenly, and grew so ill / He could not sit his mule.

Well, so people say, madam. After the bold Earl of Northumberland arrested him at York and brought him south, as a man badly disgraced, to answer the charges, he fell suddenly ill and grew so sick he couldn't sit on his mule.

At last, with easy roads, he came to Leicester, / Lodg'd in the abbey; where the reverend abbot, / With all his covent, honourably receiv'd him; / To whom he gave these words: "O, father abbot, / An old man, broken with the storms of state, / Is come to lay his weary bones among ye; / Give him a little earth for charity!" / So went to bed, where eagerly his sickness / Pursu'd him still; and, three nights after this, / About the hour of eight, which he himself / Foretold should be his last, full of repentance, / Continual meditations, tears, and sorrows, / He gave his honours to the world again, / His blessed part to heaven, and slept in peace.

At last, travelling in easy stages, he came to Leicester and lodged in the abbey, where the reverend abbot and all his monks received him with honour. He said to the abbot: "Oh, father abbot, an old man broken by the storms of state has come to lay his weary bones among you; give him a little earth, for charity!" So he went to bed, where his sickness kept pursuing him fiercely; and three nights later, about eight o'clock, the hour he himself had predicted would be his last, full of repentance, constant prayer, tears and sorrow, he gave his honours back to the world and his blessed soul to heaven, and slept in peace.

So may he rest; his faults lie gently on him! / Yet thus far, Griffith, give me leave to speak him, / And yet with charity. He was a man / Of an unbounded stomach, ever ranking / Himself with princes; one that, by suggestion, / Tied all the kingdom. Simony was fair-play; / His own opinion was his law; i' the presence / He would say untruths; and be ever double / Both in his words and meaning. He was never, / But where he meant to ruin, pitiful. / His promises were, as he then was, mighty; / But his performance, as he is now, nothing. / Of his own body he was ill, and gave / The clergy ill example.

So may he rest; may his faults lie lightly on him! Yet let me say this much of him, Griffith, and still with charity. He was a man of boundless pride, always ranking himself with princes; one who by his scheming bound the whole kingdom. He thought selling church offices fair play; his own opinion was his law; in the King's presence he would tell lies, and he was always two-faced in his words and meaning. He never showed pity except where he meant to destroy. His promises were mighty, as he was then; but his performance was nothing, as he is now. He was immoral in his body, and set the clergy a bad example.
Noble madam, / Men's evil manners live in brass; their virtues / We write in water. May it please your Highness / To hear me speak his good now?
Noble madam, men's bad deeds live on in brass; their virtues we write in water. Would it please your Highness to hear me speak of his good qualities now?
Yes, good Griffith; / I were malicious else.
Yes, good Griffith; otherwise I would be malicious.

This Cardinal, / Though from an humble stock, undoubtedly / Was fashion'd to much honour from his cradle. / He was a scholar, and a ripe and good one; / Exceeding wise, fair-spoken, and persuading; / Lofty and sour to them that lov'd him not, / But to those men that sought him, sweet as summer. / And though he were unsatisfied in getting, / Which was a sin, yet in bestowing, madam, / He was most princely: ever witness for him / Those twins of learning that he rais'd in you, / Ipswich and Oxford! one of which fell with him, / Unwilling to outlive the good that did it; / The other, though unfinish'd, yet so famous, / So excellent in art, and still so rising, / That Christendom shall ever speak his virtue. / His overthrow heap'd happiness upon him; / For then, and not till then, he felt himself, / And found the blessedness of being little; / And, to add greater honours to his age / Than man could give him, he died fearing God.

This Cardinal, though from humble stock, was undoubtedly made for great honour from his cradle. He was a scholar, a mature and good one; extremely wise, well-spoken and persuasive; haughty and sour to those who didn't love him, but sweet as summer to those who sought him out. And though he was never satisfied in getting wealth, which was a sin, yet in giving, madam, he was most princely. Let those twin colleges of learning he founded always bear witness for him, Ipswich and Oxford! One of them fell with him, unwilling to outlive the good man who made it; the other, though unfinished, is already so famous, so excellent in learning and still so growing, that Christendom will always speak of his virtue. His fall heaped happiness on him, for then, and not before, he knew himself and found the blessing of being small; and, to add greater honour to his old age than any man could give him, he died fearing God.

After my death I wish no other herald, / No other speaker of my living actions, / To keep mine honour from corruption, / But such an honest chronicler as Griffith. / Whom I most hated living, thou hast made me, / With thy religious truth and modesty, / Now in his ashes honour. Peace be with him! / Patience, be near me still, and set me lower: / I have not long to trouble thee. Good Griffith, / Cause the musicians play me that sad note / I nam'd my knell, whilst I sit meditating / On that celestial harmony I go to.

After my death I want no other herald, no other reporter of my life's actions to keep my honour from decay, than an honest chronicler like Griffith. With your devout truthfulness and fairness, you have made me now honour in his ashes the man I most hated while he lived. Peace be with him! Patience, stay close to me, and lay me lower; I won't trouble you much longer. Good Griffith, have the musicians play me that sad tune I named my funeral bell, while I sit thinking about the heavenly harmony I am going to.
She is asleep. Good wench, let's sit down quiet, / For fear we wake her; softly, gentle Patience.
She's asleep. Good girl, let's sit quietly so we don't wake her; softly, gentle Patience.
Spirits of peace, where are ye? Are ye all gone, / And leave me here in wretchedness behind ye?
Spirits of peace, where are you? Have you all gone and left me behind here in misery?
It is not you I call for. / Saw ye none enter since I slept?
It's not you I'm calling for. Did you see no one come in while I slept?

No? Saw you not, even now, a blessed troop / Invite me to a banquet; whose bright faces / Cast thousand beams upon me, like the sun? / They promis'd me eternal happiness, / And brought me garlands, Griffith, which I feel / I am not worthy yet to wear. I shall, assuredly.

No? Didn't you see just now a blessed company inviting me to a banquet, whose bright faces shone a thousand beams on me like the sun? They promised me eternal happiness and brought me garlands, Griffith, which I feel I am not yet worthy to wear. I surely shall be.
I am most joyful, madam, such good dreams / Possess your fancy.
I am very glad, madam, that such good dreams fill your mind.
Bid the music leave, / They are harsh and heavy to me.
Tell the music to stop; it is harsh and heavy to me.
Do you note / How much her Grace is alter'd on the sudden? / How long her face is drawn! How pale she looks, / And of an earthly cold! Mark her eyes!
Do you see how suddenly her Grace has changed? How drawn her face is! How pale she looks, and cold as earth! Look at her eyes!
She is going, wench. Pray, pray.
She is dying, girl. Pray, pray.
You are a saucy fellow. / Deserve we no more reverence?
You are an insolent fellow. Do we deserve no more respect?
You are to blame, / Knowing she will not lose her wonted greatness, / To use so rude behaviour. Go to, kneel.
You're at fault to behave so rudely, knowing she won't give up her customary rank. Come on, kneel.
I humbly do entreat your Highness' pardon; / My haste made me unmannerly. There is staying / A gentleman, sent from the King, to see you.
I humbly beg your Highness's pardon; my hurry made me rude. A gentleman sent by the King is waiting to see you.
Admit him entrance, Griffith; but this fellow / Let me ne'er see again.
Let him in, Griffith; but let me never see this fellow again.
If my sight fail not, / You should be lord ambassador from the Emperor, / My royal nephew, and your name Capucius.
If my eyesight doesn't fail me, you must be the ambassador from the Emperor, my royal nephew, and your name is Capucius.
O, my lord, / The times and titles now are alter'd strangely / With me since first you knew me. But, I pray you, / What is your pleasure with me?
Oh, my lord, times and titles have changed strangely for me since you first knew me. But please, what do you want with me?

Noble lady, / First, mine own service to your Grace; the next, / The King's request that I would visit you, / Who grieves much for your weakness, and by me / Sends you his princely commendations, / And heartily entreats you take good comfort.

Noble lady, first, to offer my own service to your Grace; next, the King asked me to visit you. He is much grieved by your weakness, sends you his royal greetings through me, and earnestly begs you to take comfort.

O my good lord, that comfort comes too late; / 'Tis like a pardon after execution. / That gentle physic, given in time, had cur'd me; / But now I am past all comforts here, but prayers. / How does his Highness?

Oh, my good lord, that comfort comes too late; it's like a pardon after the execution. That gentle medicine, given in time, would have cured me; but now I am beyond all comforts here except prayers. How is his Highness?
So may he ever do! and ever flourish, / When I shall dwell with worms, and my poor name / Banish'd the kingdom! Patience, is that letter, / I caused you write, yet sent away?
May he always be so, and always flourish, when I live with worms and my poor name is banished from the kingdom! Patience, has that letter I had you write been sent yet?
Sir, I most humbly pray you to deliver / This to my lord the King.
Sir, I most humbly ask you to deliver this to my lord the King.

In which I have commended to his goodness / The model of our chaste loves, his young daughter; / The dews of heaven fall thick in blessings on her! / Beseeching him to give her virtuous breeding,— / She is young, and of a noble modest nature, / I hope she will deserve well,—and a little / To love her for her mother's sake, that lov'd him, / Heaven knows how dearly. My next poor petition / Is, that his noble Grace would have some pity / Upon my wretched women, that so long / Have follow'd both my fortunes faithfully; / Of which there is not one, I dare avow, / And now I should not lie, but will deserve, / For virtue and true beauty of the soul, / For honesty and decent carriage, / A right good husband; let him be a noble; / And, sure, those men are happy that shall have 'em. / The last is, for my men,—they are the poorest, / But poverty could never draw 'em from me— / That they may have their wages duly paid 'em, / And something over to remember me by. / If Heaven had pleas'd to have given me longer life / And able means, we had not parted thus. / These are the whole contents; and, good my lord, / By that you love the dearest in this world, / As you wish Christian peace to souls departed, / Stand these poor people's friend, and urge the King / To do me this last right.

In it I have commended to his goodness the image of our chaste love, his young daughter, may the dews of heaven fall thick with blessings on her, begging him to give her a virtuous upbringing. She is young, and of a noble, modest nature; I hope she will turn out well. And I ask him to love her a little for her mother's sake, who loved him, heaven knows how dearly. My next poor request is that his noble Grace take pity on my wretched women, who have followed me faithfully for so long through good fortune and bad. There is not one of them, I dare swear, and I should not lie now, who will not deserve a really good husband, for virtue and true beauty of soul, for chastity and good behaviour; let him be a nobleman; and surely the men who get them will be happy. The last is for my menservants, who are very poor, though poverty could never draw them away from me: that they may have their wages properly paid, and something extra to remember me by. If Heaven had been pleased to give me longer life and the means, we would not have parted like this. That is all it contains. And, my good lord, by whatever you love most in this world, as you wish Christian peace to departed souls, be a friend to these poor people and urge the King to do me this last justice.
By heaven, I will, / Or let me lose the fashion of a man!
By heaven, I will, or let me lose the shape of a man!

I thank you, honest lord. Remember me / In all humility unto his Highness. / Say his long trouble now is passing / Out of this world; tell him, in death I bless'd him, / For so I will. Mine eyes grow dim. Farewell, / My lord. Griffith, farewell. Nay, Patience, / You must not leave me yet. I must to bed; / Call in more women. When I am dead, good wench, / Let me be us'd with honour. Strew me over / With maiden flowers, that all the world may know / I was a chaste wife to my grave. Embalm me, / Then lay me forth. Although unqueen'd, yet like / A queen, and daughter to a king, inter me. / I can no more.

Thank you, honest lord. Remember me in all humility to his Highness. Tell him the one who troubled him so long is now passing out of this world; tell him I blessed him in death, for so I will. My eyes are growing dim. Farewell, my lord. Griffith, farewell. No, Patience, you mustn't leave me yet. I must go to bed; call in more women. When I am dead, good girl, let me be treated with honour. Scatter maiden flowers over me, so the whole world may know I was a chaste wife to my grave. Embalm me, then lay me out. Though I am no longer queen, bury me like a queen and a king's daughter. I can say no more.
It's one o'clock, boy, is't not?
It's one o'clock, boy, isn't it?

These should be hours for necessities, / Not for delights; times to repair our nature / With comforting repose, and not for us / To waste these times. Good hour of night, Sir Thomas! / Whither so late?
These should be hours for needs, not pleasures; times to restore our bodies with comforting rest, not for us to waste. Good night, Sir Thomas! Where are you going so late?
Came you from the King, my lord?
Have you come from the King, my lord?
I did, Sir Thomas; and left him at primero / With the Duke of Suffolk.
I have, Sir Thomas, and left him playing primero with the Duke of Suffolk.
I must to him too, / Before he go to bed. I'll take my leave.
I must go to him too, before he goes to bed. I'll say goodbye.

Not yet, Sir Thomas Lovell. What's the matter? / It seems you are in haste. An if there be / No great offence belongs to't, give your friend / Some touch of your late business. Affairs, that walk, / As they say spirits do, at midnight, have / In them a wilder nature than the business / That seeks despatch by day.

Not yet, Sir Thomas Lovell. What's the matter? You seem in a hurry. If there's no great harm in it, give your friend some hint of your business tonight. Affairs that walk at midnight, as they say ghosts do, have a wilder nature than business that is done by day.
My lord, I love you; / And durst commend a secret to your ear / Much weightier than this work. The Queen's in labour, / They say in great extremity; and fear'd / She'll with the labour end.
My lord, I love you, and I'd dare trust a secret to your ear much weightier than this errand. The Queen is in labour, they say in great danger, and they fear she will die in childbirth.
The fruit she goes with / I pray for heartily, that it may find / Good time, and live; but for the stock, Sir Thomas, / I wish it grubb'd up now.
I pray with all my heart that the fruit she carries may be born safely and live; but as for the tree, Sir Thomas, I wish it were dug up now.
Methinks I could / Cry thee amen; and yet my conscience says / She's a good creature, and, sweet lady, does / Deserve our better wishes.
I think I could say amen to that; and yet my conscience tells me she's a good creature, and, sweet lady, deserves better wishes from us.

But, sir, sir, / Hear me, Sir Thomas. You're a gentleman / Of mine own way; I know you wise, religious; / And, let me tell you, it will ne'er be well, / 'Twill not, Sir Thomas Lovell, take't of me, / Till Cranmer, Cromwell, her two hands, and she, / Sleep in their graves.

But sir, sir, listen to me, Sir Thomas. You are a gentleman of my own persuasion; I know you are wise and religious. Let me tell you, it will never be well, it won't, Sir Thomas Lovell, take it from me, until Cranmer, Cromwell, her two hands, and she herself sleep in their graves.

Now, sir, you speak of two / The most remark'd i' the kingdom. As for Cromwell, / Beside that of the jewel house, is made master / O' the rolls, and the King's secretary; further, sir, / Stands in the gap and trade of moe preferments, / With which the time will load him. The Archbishop / Is the King's hand and tongue; and who dare speak / One syllable against him?

Now, sir, you're speaking of the two most prominent men in the kingdom. As for Cromwell, besides the Jewel House, he's been made Master of the Rolls and the King's secretary; and further, sir, he stands in the path of more promotions, which time will load on him. The Archbishop is the King's hand and tongue; who dares say one word against him?

Yes, yes, Sir Thomas, / There are that dare; and I myself have ventur'd / To speak my mind of him: and indeed this day, / Sir, I may tell it you, I think I have / Incens'd the lords o' the council, that he is, / For so I know he is, they know he is, / A most arch heretic, a pestilence / That does infect the land; with which they moved / Have broken with the King, who hath so far / Given ear to our complaint, of his great grace / And princely care foreseeing those fell mischiefs / Our reasons laid before him, hath commanded / To-morrow morning to the council-board / He be convented. He's a rank weed, Sir Thomas, / And we must root him out. From your affairs / I hinder you too long. Good-night, Sir Thomas.

Yes, yes, Sir Thomas, there are those who dare, and I myself have risked speaking my mind about him. Indeed, sir, I can tell you, today I think I have convinced the lords of the council that he is, for I know he is, and they know he is, a most arch-heretic, a plague infecting the land. Moved by this, they have raised it with the King, who has listened so far to our complaint that, out of his great grace and royal care, foreseeing the deadly harm our arguments set before him, he has ordered him to be summoned before the council tomorrow morning. He's a rank weed, Sir Thomas, and we must root him out. I'm keeping you too long from your business. Good night, Sir Thomas.
Many good-nights, my lord! I rest your servant.
Many good nights, my lord! I remain your servant.
Charles, I will play no more to-night. / My mind's not on't; you are too hard for me.
Charles, I won't play any more tonight. My mind isn't on it; you're too good for me.
Sir, I did never win of you before.
Sir, I never beat you before.
But little, Charles; / Nor shall not, when my fancy's on my play. / Now, Lovell, from the Queen what is the news?
Only a little, Charles; and you won't when my mind is on my game. Now, Lovell, what news from the Queen?

I could not personally deliver to her / What you commanded me, but by her woman / I sent your message; who return'd her thanks / In the great'st humbleness, and desir'd your Highness / Most heartily to pray for her.
I couldn't deliver your message to her in person, but I sent it by her woman, who brought back her thanks in the greatest humility and asked your Highness most earnestly to pray for her.
What say'st thou, ha? / To pray for her? What, is she crying out?
What are you saying, ha? To pray for her? What, is she crying out in labour?
So said her woman; and that her suff'rance made / Almost each pang a death.
So her woman said, and that her suffering made almost every pang a death.
God safely quit her of her burden, and / With gentle travail, to the gladding of / Your Highness with an heir!
May God deliver her safely of her burden, with an easy labour, and gladden your Highness with an heir!
'Tis midnight, Charles; / Prithee, to bed; and in thy prayers remember / The estate of my poor queen. Leave me alone; / For I must think of that which company / Will not be friendly to.
It's midnight, Charles; please go to bed, and remember my poor queen's condition in your prayers. Leave me alone, for I must think of something company will not help.
I wish your Highness / A quiet night; and my good mistress will / Remember in my prayers.
I wish your Highness a peaceful night, and I will remember my good mistress in my prayers.
Sir, I have brought my lord the Archbishop, / As you commanded me.
Sir, I have brought my lord the Archbishop, as you ordered.
That's right; where is he, Denny?
[Aside] This is about that which the bishop spake. / I am happily come hither.
(Aside) This is about what the bishop was talking about. I've come here at a lucky moment.
Avoid the gallery. [Lovell seems to stay] / Ha! I have said. Be gone. / What!
Clear the gallery. (Lovell seems to stay) Ha! I've said so. Go. What!
[Aside] I am fearful; wherefore frowns he thus? / 'Tis his aspect of terror. All's not well.
(Aside) I'm afraid; why is he frowning like this? It's his look of terror. All is not well.
How now, my lord! you do desire to know / Wherefore I sent for you.
Well, my lord! You want to know why I sent for you.
[Kneeling] It is my duty / To attend your Highness' pleasure.
(Kneeling) It is my duty to wait on your Highness's wishes.

Pray you, arise, / My good and gracious Lord of Canterbury. / Come, you and I must walk a turn together; / I have news to tell you. Come, come, me your hand. / Ah, my good lord, I grieve at what I speak, / And am right sorry to repeat what follows. / I have, and most unwillingly, of late / Heard many grievous, I do say, my lord, / Grievous complaints of you; which, being consider'd, / Have mov'd us and our council, that you shall / This morning come before us; where, I know, / You cannot with such freedom purge yourself / But that, till further trial in those charges / Which will require your answer, you must take / Your patience to you, and be well contented / To make your house our Tower. You a brother of us, / It fits we thus proceed, or else no witness / Would come against you.

Please rise, my good and gracious Lord of Canterbury. Come, you and I must take a walk together; I have news to tell you. Come, come, give me your hand. Ah, my good lord, I grieve at what I'm saying, and am truly sorry to repeat what follows. Recently, and very unwillingly, I have heard many serious, I say, my lord, serious complaints about you. Having considered them, we and our council have decided that you shall come before us this morning; where, I know, you cannot clear yourself so freely but that, until there is a further trial of the charges you must answer, you must be patient and be content to make your home in our Tower. Since you are one of our council, it is right we proceed this way, or else no witness would dare come forward against you.

[Kneeling] I humbly thank your Highness; / And am right glad to catch this good occasion / Most throughly to be winnowed, where my chaff / And corn shall fly asunder; for, I know, / There's none stands under more calumnious tongues / Than I myself, poor man.

(Kneeling) I humbly thank your Highness, and am very glad of this good chance to be thoroughly winnowed, so that my chaff and grain will fly apart; for I know no one suffers under more slanderous tongues than I do, poor man.

Stand up, good Canterbury! / Thy truth and thy integrity is rooted / In us, thy friend. Give me thy hand, stand up; / Prithee, let's walk. Now, by my holidame, / What manner of man are you? My lord, I look'd / You would have given me your petition, that / I should have ta'en some pains to bring together / Yourself and your accusers; and to have heard you, / Without indurance, further.

Stand up, good Canterbury! Your truth and integrity are rooted in us, your friend. Give me your hand; stand up. Please, let's walk. Now, by Our Lady, what kind of man are you? My lord, I expected you to petition me to take some trouble to bring you and your accusers face to face, and to hear you further without imprisonment.

Most dread liege, / The good I stand on is my truth and honesty. / If they shall fail, I, with mine enemies, / Will triumph o'er my person; which I weigh not, / Being of those virtues vacant. I fear nothing / What can be said against me.

Most feared sovereign, the good I stand on is my truth and honesty. If they fail, I will join my enemies in triumphing over my person, which I don't value if it lacks those virtues. I fear nothing that can be said against me.

Know you not / How your state stands i' th' world, with the whole world? / Your enemies are many, and not small; their practices / Must bear the same proportion; and not ever / The justice and the truth o' the question carries / The due o' the verdict with it. At what ease / Might corrupt minds procure knaves as corrupt / To swear against you? Such things have been done. / You are potently oppos'd, and with a malice / Of as great size. Ween you of better luck, / I mean, in perjur'd witness, than your Master, / Whose minister you are, whiles here He liv'd / Upon this naughty earth? Go to, go to! / You take a precipice for no leap of danger, / And woo your own destruction.

Don't you know how you stand in the world, with the whole world? Your enemies are many, and not small; their plots must be just as great. And the justice and truth of a case do not always bring the verdict it deserves. How easily corrupt minds could find rogues just as corrupt to swear against you! Such things have been done. You are powerfully opposed, and with malice just as great. Do you expect better luck with perjured witnesses than your Master, whose minister you are, had while He lived on this wicked earth? Come on, come on! You take a cliff edge for no dangerous leap, and court your own destruction.
God and your Majesty / Protect mine innocence, or I fall into / The trap is laid for me!
God and your Majesty protect my innocence, or I fall into the trap that has been set for me!

Be of good cheer; / They shall no more prevail than we give way to. / Keep comfort to you; and this morning see / You do appear before them. If they shall chance, / In charging you with matters, to commit you, / The best persuasions to the contrary / Fail not to use, and with what vehemency / The occasion shall instruct you. If entreaties / Will render you no remedy, this ring / Deliver them, and your appeal to us / There make before them. Look, the good man weeps! / He's honest, on mine honour. God's blest mother! / I swear he is true-hearted; and a soul / None better in my kingdom. Get you gone, / And do as I have bid you.

Cheer up; they shall get no further than we allow. Keep your courage, and see that you appear before them this morning. If, in charging you, they happen to commit you to prison, don't fail to use the best arguments against it, as forcefully as the moment teaches you. If pleading gets you no remedy, give them this ring and make your appeal to us there in front of them. Look, the good man is weeping! He's honest, on my honour. By God's blessed mother, I swear he is true-hearted, and there's no better soul in my kingdom. Go now, and do as I've told you.
He has strangled his language in his tears.
His tears have choked his words.
(Within) Come back! What do you mean by it?
I'll not come back; the tidings that I bring / Will make my boldness manners. Now, good angels / Fly o'er thy royal head, and shade thy person / Under their blessed wings!
I won't come back; the news I bring will turn my boldness into good manners. Now may good angels fly over your royal head and shade you under their blessed wings!
Now, by thy looks / I guess thy message. Is the Queen deliver'd? / Say ay; and of a boy.
Now, from your looks I guess your message. Has the Queen given birth? Say yes, and to a boy.

Ay, ay, my liege; / And of a lovely boy. The God of Heaven / Both now and ever bless her! 'tis a girl, / Promises boys hereafter. Sir, your queen / Desires your visitation, and to be / Acquainted with this stranger. 'Tis as like you / As cherry is to cherry.

Yes, yes, my lord, and to a lovely boy. May the God of Heaven bless her now and always! It's a girl, which promises boys later. Sir, your queen wants you to visit her and meet this newcomer. It's as like you as one cherry is to another.
Give her an hundred marks. I'll to the Queen.
Give her a hundred marks. I'm going to the Queen.

An hundred marks! By this light, I'll ha' more. / An ordinary groom is for such payment. / I will have more, or scold it out of him. / Said I for this, the girl was like to him? / I will have more, or else unsay't; and now, / While it is hot, I'll put it to the issue.

A hundred marks! By this daylight, I'll have more. That's payment for an ordinary servant. I'll have more, or scold it out of him. Did I say the girl looked like him for this? I'll have more, or else take it back; and now, while it's hot, I'll settle it.
I hope I am not too late; and yet the gentleman, / That was sent to me from the council, pray'd me / To make great haste. All fast? what means this? Ho! / Who waits there? Sure, you know me?
I hope I'm not too late; and yet the gentleman the council sent me begged me to hurry. All locked? What does this mean? Hello! Who's on duty there? Surely you know me?
Yes, my lord; / But yet I cannot help you.
Yes, my lord; but still I can't help you.
Your Grace must wait till you be call'd for.
Your Grace must wait until you are called.
[Aside] This is a piece of malice. I am glad / I came this way so happily; the King / Shall understand it presently.
(Aside) This is a piece of malice. I'm glad I happened to come this way; the King shall know of it at once.

[Aside] 'Tis Butts, / The King's physician. As he pass'd along, / How earnestly he cast his eyes upon me! / Pray Heaven, he sound not my disgrace! For certain, / This is of purpose laid by some that hate me— / God turn their hearts! I never sought their malice— / To quench mine honour; they would shame to make me / Wait else at door, a fellow-counsellor, / 'Mong boys, grooms, and lackeys. But their pleasures / Must be fulfill'd, and I attend with patience.

(Aside) That's Butts, the King's physician. How intently he looked at me as he passed! Heaven grant he isn't sounding out my disgrace! Surely this has been arranged on purpose by some who hate me, God change their hearts, I never sought their malice, to snuff out my honour; otherwise they'd be ashamed to make me, a fellow councillor, wait at the door among boys, grooms and footmen. But their wishes must be carried out, and I'll wait patiently.
I'll show your Grace the strangest sight—
I'll show your Grace the strangest sight —
I think your Highness saw this many a day.
I think your Highness hasn't seen this for many a day.
Body o' me, where is it?
There, my lord, / The high promotion of his Grace of Canterbury; / Who holds his state at door, 'mongst pursuivants, / Pages, and footboys.
There, my lord: the high promotion of his Grace of Canterbury, who holds court at the door among messengers, pages and footboys.

Ha! 'tis he, indeed. / Is this the honour they do one another? / 'Tis well there's one above 'em yet. I had thought / They had parted so much honesty among 'em, / At least, good manners, as not thus to suffer / A man of his place, and so near our favour, / To dance attendance on their lordships' pleasures, / And at the door too, like a post with packets. / By holy Mary, Butts, there's knavery. / Let 'em alone, and draw the curtain close; / We shall hear more anon.

Ha! It's him indeed. Is this the honour they pay one another? It's a good thing there's still one above them. I'd have thought they had enough honesty among them, or at least good manners, not to let a man of his rank, so close to our favour, dance attendance on their lordships' pleasure, and at the door too, like a messenger with letters. By holy Mary, Butts, there's villainy here. Leave them alone, and draw the curtain shut; we'll hear more soon.
Speak to the business, master secretary. / Why are we met in council?
Come to the business, master secretary. Why are we meeting in council?
Please your honours, / The chief cause concerns his Grace of Canterbury.
If it please your honours, the main matter concerns his Grace of Canterbury.
Has he had knowledge of it?
Has he been told of it?
My Lord Archbishop; / And has done half an hour, to know your pleasures.
My Lord Archbishop, and he has been for half an hour, waiting to know your wishes.
Your Grace may come in now.

My good Lord Archbishop, I'm very sorry / To sit here at this present, and behold / That chair stand empty; but we all are men, / In our own natures frail, and capable / Of our flesh; few are angels: out of which frailty / And want of wisdom, you, that best should teach us, / Have misdemean'd yourself, and not a little, / Toward the King first, then his laws, in filling / The whole realm, by your teaching and your chaplains, / For so we are inform'd, with new opinions / Divers and dangerous, which are heresies / And, not reform'd, may prove pernicious.

My good Lord Archbishop, I'm very sorry to sit here now and see that chair stand empty. But we are all men, frail by nature and subject to the weakness of the flesh; few are angels. Out of that frailty and lack of wisdom, you, who ought most to teach us, have behaved wrongly, and not a little, toward the King first and then his laws, by filling the whole kingdom, through your teaching and your chaplains, as we are informed, with new opinions, varied and dangerous, which are heresies and, if not reformed, may prove deadly.

Which reformation must be sudden too, / My noble lords; for those that tame wild horses / Pace 'em not in their hands to make 'em gentle, / But stop their mouth with stubborn bits and spur 'em / Till they obey the manage. If we suffer, / Out of our easiness and childish pity / To one man's honour, this contagious sickness, / Farewell all physic! And what follows then? / Commotions, uproars, with a general taint / Of the whole state; as, of late days, our neighbours, / The upper Germany, can dearly witness, / Yet freshly pitied in our memories.

And that reform must be quick too, my noble lords. People who tame wild horses don't walk them about in their hands to make them gentle; they stop their mouths with hard bits and spur them until they obey their training. If, out of our softness and childish pity for one man's honour, we allow this infectious sickness, farewell to all medicine! And what follows then? Riots and uproars, with the whole state infected, as our neighbours in upper Germany can bitterly witness, still freshly pitied in our memories.

My good lords, hitherto in all the progress / Both of my life and office, I have labour'd, / And with no little study, that my teaching / And the strong course of my authority / Might go one way, and safely; and the end / Was ever, to do well; nor is there living, / I speak it with a single heart, my lords, / A man that more detests, more stirs against, / Both in his private conscience and his place, / Defacers of a public peace, than I do. / Pray Heaven, the King may never find a heart / With less allegiance in it! Men that make / Envy and crooked malice nourishment / Dare bite the best. I do beseech your lordships, / That, in this case of justice, my accusers, / Be what they will, may stand forth face to face / And freely urge against me.

My good lords, until now, in the whole course of my life and office, I have worked, with no small study, to make my teaching and the firm exercise of my authority go one way, and safely; and my aim was always to do good. There is no man alive, I say it with an honest heart, my lords, who hates more, or works harder against, those who disturb the public peace, both in his private conscience and his office, than I do. I pray Heaven the King may never find a heart with less loyalty in it! Men who feed on envy and crooked malice dare bite the best. I beg your lordships that, in this matter of justice, my accusers, whoever they are, may stand face to face with me and freely make their charges.
Nay, my lord, / That cannot be. You are a counsellor, / And, by that virtue, no man dare accuse you.
No, my lord, that can't be. You are a member of the council, and because of that no man dares accuse you.

My lord, because we have business of more moment, / We will be short with you. 'Tis his Highness' pleasure / And our consent, for better trial of you, / From hence you be committed to the Tower; / Where, being but a private man again, / You shall know many dare accuse you boldly, / More than, I fear, you are provided for.

My lord, because we have more important business, we'll be brief with you. It is his Highness's wish, and our decision, for a fuller trial of you, that you be taken from here to the Tower; where, being only a private man again, you'll find many who dare accuse you boldly, more than you are prepared for, I fear.

Ah, my good Lord of Winchester, I thank you. / You are always my good friend; if your will pass, / I shall both find your lordship judge and juror, / You are so merciful. I see your end; / 'Tis my undoing. Love and meekness, lord, / Become a churchman better than ambition. / Win straying souls with modesty again, / Cast none away. That I shall clear myself, / Lay all the weight ye can upon my patience, / I make as little doubt as you do conscience / In doing daily wrongs. I could say more, / But reverence to your calling makes me modest.

Ah, my good Lord of Winchester, I thank you. You are always my good friend; if you get your way, I'll find your lordship both judge and jury, you're so merciful. I see your aim; it's my ruin. Love and meekness, my lord, suit a churchman better than ambition. Win back straying souls with gentleness; cast none away. Lay all the weight you can on my patience; I have as little doubt that I will clear myself as you have conscience in doing daily wrongs. I could say more, but respect for your office keeps me modest.
My lord, my lord, you are a sectary, / That's the plain truth. Your painted gloss discovers, / To men that understand you, words and weakness.
My lord, my lord, you are a sectarian; that's the plain truth. To men who understand you, your painted gloss reveals mere words and weakness.
My Lord of Winchester, you are a little, / By your good favour, too sharp; men so noble, / However faulty, yet should find respect / For what they have been. 'Tis a cruelty / To load a falling man.
My Lord of Winchester, with respect, you are a little too sharp. Men so noble, however much at fault, should still be respected for what they have been. It is cruel to pile weight on a falling man.
Good master secretary, / I cry your honour mercy. You may, worst / Of all this table, say so.
Good master secretary, I beg your honour's pardon. You, least of anyone at this table, have the right to say so.
Do not I know you for a favourer / Of this new sect? Ye are not sound.
Don't I know you are a supporter of this new sect? You're not sound.
Would you were half so honest! / Men's prayers then would seek you, not their fears.
I wish you were half as honest! Then men would pray for you instead of fearing you.
I shall remember this bold language.
I shall remember this bold talk.
Do. / Remember your bold life too.
Do. Remember your bold life too.
This is too much. / Forbear, for shame, my lords.
This is too much. Stop, for shame, my lords.

Then thus for you, my lord: it stands agreed, / I take it, by all voices, that forthwith / You be convey'd to the Tower a prisoner; / There to remain till the King's further pleasure / Be known unto us. Are you all agreed, lords?

Then this is for you, my lord: it is agreed, I take it, by everyone, that you be taken to the Tower as a prisoner at once, to stay there until the King's further wishes are made known to us. Are you all agreed, lords?
Is there no other way of mercy, / But I must needs to the Tower, my lords?
Is there no other merciful way? Must I go to the Tower, my lords?
What other / Would you expect? You are strangely troublesome. / Let some o' the guard be ready there.
What other way would you expect? You are strangely troublesome. Have some of the guard ready there.
For me? / Must I go like a traitor thither?
For me? Must I go there like a traitor?
Receive him, / And see him safe i' the Tower.
Take him, and see him safely in the Tower.

Stay, good my lords, / I have a little yet to say. Look there, my lords; / By virtue of that ring, I take my cause / Out of the gripes of cruel men, and give it / To a most noble judge, the King my master.
Wait, my good lords, I have a little more to say. Look there, my lords. By the power of that ring, I take my case out of the grip of cruel men and give it to a most noble judge, the King my master.
'Tis the right ring, by heaven! I told ye all, / When we first put this dangerous stone a-rolling, / 'Twould fall upon ourselves.
It's the real ring, by heaven! I told you all, when we first set this dangerous stone rolling, it would fall back on us.
Do you think, my lords, / The King will suffer but the little finger / Of this man to be vex'd?
Do you think, my lords, the King will allow even this man's little finger to be harmed?
'Tis now too certain. / How much more is his life in value with him? / Would I were fairly out on't!
That's now only too certain. How much more must his life be worth to him? I wish I were well out of this!
My mind gave me, / In seeking tales and informations / Against this man, whose honesty the devil / And his disciples only envy at, / Ye blew the fire that burns ye. Now have at ye!
I had a feeling that, in hunting for tales and reports against this man, whose honesty only the devil and his followers envy, you were blowing on the fire that burns you. Now look out!

Dread sovereign, how much are we bound to Heaven / In daily thanks, that gave us such a prince; / Not only good and wise, but most religious; / One that, in all obedience, makes the Church / The chief aim of his honour; and, to strengthen / That holy duty, out of dear respect, / His royal self in judgement comes to hear / The cause betwixt her and this great offender.

Dread sovereign, how much we owe Heaven daily thanks for giving us such a prince, not only good and wise but most devout, one who in all obedience makes the Church the chief aim of his honour; and who, to strengthen that holy duty, out of loving respect, comes in his royal person to hear the case between her and this great offender.

You were ever good at sudden commendations, / Bishop of Winchester. But know, I come not / To hear such flattery now, and in my presence; / They are too thin and bare to hide offences. / To me you cannot reach you play the spaniel, / And think with wagging of your tongue to win me; / But, whatsoe'er thou tak'st me for, I'm sure / Thou hast a cruel nature and a bloody. / [To Cranmer] Good man, sit down. Now let me see the proudest / He, that dares most, but wag his finger at thee: / By all that's holy, he had better starve / Than but once think this place becomes thee not.

You were always good at sudden compliments, Bishop of Winchester. But know that I have not come to hear such flattery now, and in my presence; it is too thin and bare to hide offences. You can't reach me; you play the fawning spaniel and think you can win me with a wagging tongue; but whatever you take me for, I'm sure you have a cruel and bloody nature. (To Cranmer) Good man, sit down. Now let me see the proudest of them, the boldest, so much as wag his finger at you. By all that's holy, he would do better to starve than even think once that this place doesn't suit you.

No, sir, it does not please me. / I had thought I had had men of some understanding / And wisdom of my council; but I find none. / Was it discretion, lords, to let this man, / This good man,—few of you deserve that title,— / This honest man, wait like a lousy footboy / At chamber-door? and one as great as you are? / Why, what a shame was this! Did my commission / Bid ye so far forget yourselves? I gave ye / Power as he was a councillor to try him,— / Not as a groom. There's some of ye, I see, / More out of malice than integrity, / Would try him to the utmost, had ye mean; / Which ye shall never have while I live.

No, sir, it does not please me. I thought I had men of some understanding and wisdom on my council, but I find none. Was it sensible, lords, to let this man, this good man, few of you deserve that title, this honest man, wait like a lice-ridden footboy at the chamber door, and a man as great as you? Why, what a disgrace this was! Did my commission tell you to forget yourselves so far? I gave you power to try him as a councillor, not as a servant. I see some of you, more from malice than honesty, would try him to the utmost if you had the means; which you shall never have while I live.

Thus far, / My most dread sovereign, may it like your Grace / To let my tongue excuse all. What was purpos'd / Concerning his imprisonment was rather, / If there be faith in men, meant for his trial / And fair purgation to the world, than malice, / I'm sure, in me.

My most dread sovereign, may it please your Grace to let my tongue excuse us all this far. What was planned concerning his imprisonment was meant, if men can be trusted, rather for his trial and fair clearing before the world than out of malice, certainly in my case.

Well, well, my lords, respect him; / Take him, and use him well, he's worthy of it. / I will say thus much for him, if a prince / May be beholding to a subject, I / Am, for his love and service, so to him. / Make me no more ado, but all embrace him. / Be friends, for shame, my lords! My Lord of Canterbury, / I have a suit which you must not deny me; / That is, a fair young maid that yet wants baptism, / You must be godfather, and answer for her.

Well, well, my lords, respect him. Accept him and treat him well; he deserves it. I'll say this much for him: if a prince can be indebted to a subject, I am to him, for his love and service. Make no more fuss, but all embrace him. Be friends, for shame, my lords! My Lord of Canterbury, I have a request you mustn't refuse me: there is a fair young girl who still needs baptising; you must be her godfather and answer for her.
The greatest monarch now alive may glory / In such an honour; how may I deserve it, / That am a poor and humble subject to you?
The greatest king alive could be proud of such an honour; how can I deserve it, being a poor and humble subject of yours?

Come, come, my lord, you'd spare your spoons. / You shall have two noble partners with you, the old Duchess / of Norfolk and Lady Marquess Dorset. Will these please you? / Once more, my Lord of Winchester, I charge you, embrace and / love this man.

Come, come, my lord, you'd like to save the cost of the christening spoons. You shall have two noble partners with you, the old Duchess of Norfolk and Lady Marquess Dorset. Will these please you? Once more, my Lord of Winchester, I order you: embrace and love this man.
With a true heart / And brother-love I do it.
I do it with a true heart and brotherly love.
And let Heaven / Witness how dear I hold this confirmation.
And let Heaven witness how dearly I value this pledge.

Good man, those joyful tears show thy true heart. / The common voice, I see, is verified / Of thee, which says thus, "Do my Lord of Canterbury / A shrewd turn, and he is your friend for ever." / Come, lords, we trifle time away; I long / To have this young one made a Christian. / As I have made ye one, lords, one remain; / So I grow stronger, you more honour gain.

Good man, those tears of joy show your true heart. I see the common saying about you is proved true: "Do my Lord of Canterbury a bad turn, and he is your friend for ever." Come, lords, we're wasting time; I long to have this little one made a Christian. As I have made you one, lords, stay one; so I grow stronger, and you gain more honour.
You'll leave your noise anon, ye rascals; do you take / the court for Paris-garden? Ye rude slaves, leave your gaping.
You'll stop your noise soon, you rascals. Do you take the court for the Paris Garden bear-pit? You rude slaves, stop your bawling.
[Within] Good master porter, I belong to the larder.
(Within) Good master porter, I belong to the larder.

Belong to the gallows, and be hang'd, ye rogue! Is this / a place to roar in? Fetch me a dozen crab-tree staves, and strong / ones; these are but switches to 'em. I'll scratch your heads. You / must be seeing christenings? Do you look for ale and cakes here, / you rude rascals?

Belong to the gallows and be hanged, you rogue! Is this a place to roar in? Fetch me a dozen crab-apple clubs, and strong ones; these are only switches compared to them. I'll scratch your heads. You must see christenings, must you? Do you expect ale and cakes here, you rude rascals?

Pray, sir, be patient. 'Tis as much impossible— / Unless we sweep 'em from the door with cannons— / To scatter 'em, as 'tis to make 'em sleep / On May-day morning; which will never be. / We may as well push against Paul's, as stir 'em.

Please, sir, be patient. Unless we sweep them from the door with cannons, it's as impossible to scatter them as it is to make them sleep on May Day morning, which will never happen. We might as well push against Saint Paul's as try to move them.
How got they in, and be hang'd?
How did they get in, damn them?
Alas, I know not: how gets the tide in? / As much as one sound cudgel of four foot— / You see the poor remainder—could distribute, / I made no spare, sir.
Alas, I don't know. How does the tide get in? As much as one good four-foot cudgel could hand out, and you see the poor stump left of it, I didn't hold back, sir.

I am not Samson, nor Sir Guy, nor Colbrand, / To mow 'em down before me; but if I spar'd any / That had a head to hit, either young or old, / He or she, cuckold or cuckold-maker, / Let me ne'er hope to see a chine again; / And that I would not for a cow, God save her!

I'm not Samson, nor Sir Guy, nor Colbrand the giant, to mow them down before me; but if I spared anyone who had a head to hit, young or old, he or she, cuckold or cuckold-maker, may I never hope to see a joint of meat again; and I wouldn't want that for a cow, God save her!
I shall be with you presently, good master puppy.— / Keep the door close, sirrah.
I'll be with you in a minute, good master puppy. Keep the door shut, fellow.
What would you have me do?
What do you want me to do?

What should you do, but knock 'em down by the dozens? Is this / Moorfields to muster in? Or have we some strange Indian with the / great tool come to court, the women so besiege us? Bless me, what / a fry of fornication is at door! On my Christian conscience, this / one christening will beget a thousand; here will be father, / godfather, and all together.

What should you do but knock them down by the dozen? Is this Moorfields, to drill soldiers in? Or has some strange Indian with a great tool come to court, that the women besiege us like this? Bless me, what a swarm of fornication is at the door! On my Christian conscience, this one christening will breed a thousand; here will be father, godfather and all together.

The spoons will be the bigger, sir. There is a fellow somewhat / near the door, he should be a brazier by his face, for, o' my / conscience, twenty of the dog-days now reign in's nose; all that / stand about him are under the line, they need no other penance: / that fire-drake did I hit three times on the head, and three / times was his nose discharged against me; he stands there, like a / mortar-piece, to blow us. There was a haberdasher's wife of / small wit near him, that rail'd upon me till her pink'd porringer / fell off her head, for kindling such a combustion in the state. I / miss'd the meteor once, and hit that woman; who cried out / "Clubs!" when I might see from far some forty truncheoners draw / to her succour, which were the hope o' the Strand, where she was / quartered. They fell on; I made good my place; at length they / came to the broomstaff to me; I defied 'em still; when suddenly a / file of boys behind 'em, loose shot, deliver'd such a shower of / pebbles, that I was fain to draw mine honour in, and let 'em win / the work. The devil was amongst 'em, I think, surely.

The christening spoons will be bigger, sir. There's a fellow near the door who must be a brass-worker by his face, for on my conscience twenty dog-days of heat rule in his nose; everyone standing round him is at the equator and needs no other penance. I hit that fiery dragon on the head three times, and three times his nose fired at me; he stands there like a mortar ready to blow us up. There was a haberdasher's wife of little sense near him who abused me till her decorated hat fell off her head, for starting such a fire in the state. I missed the shooting star once and hit that woman, who shouted "Clubs!", and I saw from far off about forty club-carrying apprentices, the flower of the Strand where she lodged, come to her rescue. They charged; I held my ground; at last they came at me with broomsticks; I still defied them; when suddenly a line of boys behind them, skirmishers, let fly such a shower of pebbles that I was glad to withdraw my honour and let them win the fort. The devil was among them, I'm sure.

These are the youths that thunder at a playhouse, and fight for / bitten apples; that no audience but the tribulation of Tower-hill / or the limbs of Limehouse, their dear brothers, are able to / endure. I have some of 'em in Limbo Patrum, and there they are / like to dance these three days; besides the running banquet of / two beadles that is to come.

These are the young men who thunder at a playhouse and fight over bitten apples, whom no audience can stand except the rabble of Tower Hill or the gangs of Limehouse, their dear brothers. I have some of them locked up in the lockup, and there they're likely to dance for three days, besides the whipping by two beadles still to come.

Mercy o' me, what a multitude are here! / They grow still too; from all parts they are coming / As if we kept a fair here! Where are these porters, / These lazy knaves? Ye have made a fine hand, fellows. / There's a trim rabble let in. Are all these / Your faithful friends o' the suburbs? We shall have / Great store of room, no doubt, left for the ladies, / When they pass back from the christening.

Mercy on me, what a crowd there is here! And they're still growing; they're coming from everywhere as if we were holding a fair! Where are these porters, these lazy rogues? You've made a fine job of it, fellows. That's a pretty rabble you've let in. Are all these your faithful friends from the suburbs? No doubt we'll have plenty of room left for the ladies when they come back from the christening.
An't please your honour, / We are but men; and what so many may do, / Not being torn a-pieces, we have done. / An army cannot rule 'em.
