If it please your honour, we're only men; and we've done what so few could do without being torn to pieces. An army couldn't control them.

As I live, / If the King blame me for't, I'll lay ye all / By the heels, and suddenly; and on your heads / Clap round fines for neglect. Ye're lazy knaves; / And here ye lie baiting of bombards, when / Ye should do service. Hark! the trumpets sound; / They're come already from the christening. / Go, break among the press, and find a way out / To let the troops pass fairly; or I'll find / A Marshalsea shall hold ye play these two months.

As I live, if the King blames me for this, I'll put you all in the stocks, and quickly, and slap heavy fines on your heads for neglect. You're lazy rogues, and here you lie drinking from leather jugs when you should be doing your job. Listen! The trumpets are sounding; they've already come from the christening. Go, push into the crowd and clear a way for the procession to pass properly, or I'll find a Marshalsea prison to keep you amused for the next two months.
Make way there for the princess.
Make way there for the princess.
You great fellow, / Stand close up, or I'll make your head ache.
You big fellow, stand back, or I'll make your head ache.
You i' the camlet, get up o' the rail; / I'll peck you o'er the pales else.
You in the camlet cloth, get off the rail, or I'll pitch you over the fence.
Heaven, from thy endless goodness, send prosperous / life, long and ever happy, to the high and mighty Princess of / England, Elizabeth!
Heaven, from your endless goodness, send a prosperous life, long and always happy, to the high and mighty Princess of England, Elizabeth!

[Kneeling] And to your royal Grace, and the good queen, / My noble partners, and myself, thus pray: / All comfort, joy, in this most gracious lady, / Heaven ever laid up to make parents happy, / May hourly fall upon ye!

(Kneeling) And for your royal Grace and the good queen, my noble partners and I pray this: may all the comfort and joy Heaven ever stored up to make parents happy fall on you hourly through this most gracious lady!
Thank you, good Lord Archbishop. / What is her name?
Thank you, good Lord Archbishop. What is her name?
With this kiss take my blessing: God protect thee! / Into whose hand I give thy life.
With this kiss take my blessing: God protect you! Into His hand I give your life.
My noble gossips, ye have been too prodigal. / I thank ye heartily; so shall this lady, / When she has so much English.
My noble godparents, you have been too generous. I thank you heartily, and so will this lady when she has enough English.

Let me speak, sir, / For Heaven now bids me; and the words I utter / Let none think flattery, for they'll find 'em truth. / This royal infant—Heaven still move about her!— / Though in her cradle, yet now promises / Upon this land a thousand thousand blessings, / Which time shall bring to ripeness. She shall be— / But few now living can behold that goodness— / A pattern to all princes living with her, / And all that shall succeed. Saba was never / More covetous of wisdom and fair virtue / Than this pure soul shall be. All princely graces, / That mould up such a mighty piece as this is, / With all the virtues that attend the good, / Shall still be doubled on her. Truth shall nurse her, / Holy and heavenly thoughts still counsel her. / She shall be lov'd and fear'd: her own shall bless her; / Her foes shake like a field of beaten corn, / And hang their heads with sorrow. Good grows with her. / In her days every man shall eat in safety, / Under his own vine, what he plants, and sing / The merry songs of peace to all his neighbours. / God shall be truly known; and those about her / From her shall read the perfect ways of honour, / And by those claim their greatness, not by blood. / Nor shall this peace sleep with her; but as when / The bird of wonder dies, the maiden phoenix, / Her ashes new create another heir / As great in admiration as herself; / So shall she leave her blessedness to one, / When heaven shall call her from this cloud of darkness, / Who from the sacred ashes of her honour / Shall star-like rise as great in fame as she was, / And so stand fix'd. Peace, plenty, love, truth, terror, / That were the servants to this chosen infant, / Shall then be his, and like a vine grow to him. / Wherever the bright sun of heaven shall shine, / His honour and the greatness of his name / Shall be, and make new nations. He shall flourish, / And, like a mountain cedar, reach his branches / To all the plains about him. Our children's children / Shall see this, and bless Heaven.

Let me speak, sir, for Heaven now commands me; and let no one think my words flattery, for they will find them true. This royal infant, may Heaven always watch over her, though still in her cradle, already promises this land a thousand thousand blessings, which time will bring to ripeness. She shall be, though few now living will see that goodness, a model to all princes of her time and all who come after. The Queen of Sheba was never more eager for wisdom and virtue than this pure soul will be. All the royal graces that shape such a mighty person as this, with all the virtues that go with goodness, shall be doubled in her. Truth shall nurse her; holy and heavenly thoughts shall always guide her. She shall be loved and feared; her own people shall bless her; her enemies shall shake like a field of flattened corn and hang their heads in sorrow. Good grows with her. In her days every man shall eat in safety what he plants under his own vine, and sing merry songs of peace to all his neighbours. God shall be truly known; and those around her shall learn from her the perfect ways of honour, and claim their greatness by those, not by birth. Nor shall this peace die with her; but as when the miraculous bird, the virgin phoenix, dies, her ashes create a new heir as wonderful as herself, so she shall leave her blessedness to one who, when heaven calls her from this cloud of darkness, shall rise like a star from the sacred ashes of her honour, as great in fame as she was, and stay fixed there. Peace, plenty, love, truth and awe, which served this chosen infant, shall then be his and grow round him like a vine. Wherever the bright sun of heaven shines, his honour and the greatness of his name shall be there and found new nations. He shall flourish and, like a mountain cedar, spread his branches over all the plains around him. Our children's children shall see this and bless Heaven.

She shall be, to the happiness of England, / An aged princess; many days shall see her, / And yet no day without a deed to crown it. / Would I had known no more! but she must die, / She must, the saints must have her; yet a virgin, / A most unspotted lily shall she pass / To the ground, and all the world shall mourn her.

She shall be, to England's happiness, an aged princess; many days shall see her, and yet no day without a deed to crown it. I wish I knew no more! But she must die; she must, the saints must have her. Yet she shall go to the grave a virgin, a perfectly spotless lily, and the whole world shall mourn her.

O Lord Archbishop, / Thou hast made me now a man! Never, before / This happy child, did I get anything. / This oracle of comfort has so pleas'd me, / That when I am in heaven I shall desire / To see what this child does, and praise my Maker. / I thank ye all. To you, my good Lord Mayor, / And you, good brethren, I am much beholding; / I have receiv'd much honour by your presence, / And ye shall find me thankful. Lead the way, lords. / Ye must all see the Queen, and she must thank ye, / She will be sick else. This day, no man think / Has business at his house; for all shall stay. / This little one shall make it holiday.

Oh, Lord Archbishop, you have made me a man now! Before this happy child I never fathered anything. This comforting prophecy has pleased me so much that when I am in heaven I shall want to see what this child does, and praise my Maker. I thank you all. To you, my good Lord Mayor, and you, good aldermen, I am much obliged; I have received great honour by your presence, and you shall find me grateful. Lead the way, lords. You must all see the Queen, and she must thank you, or she'll be ill. Let no man think he has business at home today, for everyone shall stay. This little one shall make it a holiday.

'Tis ten to one this play can never please / All that are here. Some come to take their ease, / And sleep an act or two; but those, we fear, / We have frighted with our trumpets; so, 'tis clear, / They'll say 'tis nought: others, to hear the city / Abus'd extremely, and to cry "That's witty!" / Which we have not done neither: that, I fear, / All the expected good we're like to hear / For this play at this time, is only in / The merciful construction of good women; / For such a one we show'd 'em. If they smile / And say 'twill do, I know, within a while / All the best men are ours; for 'tis ill hap / If they hold when their ladies bid 'em clap.

It's ten to one this play can never please everyone here. Some come to relax and sleep through an act or two, but we fear we have woken those with our trumpets, so clearly they'll say it's worthless; others come to hear the city mocked mercilessly and cry "That's witty!", which we haven't done either. So I fear all the praise we are likely to hear for this play at present lies only in the kind judgement of good women, for we showed them such a woman. If they smile and say it will do, I know that before long all the best men will be ours; for it's bad luck if the men hold back when their ladies tell them to clap.
